title: CS229 2018 Lecture Notes
text:
Lectures
The course runs to twenty lectures and one discussion section, and every one has a chapter; the roadmap groups them by theme.


Lecture 1
Introduction
What machine learning is, the five areas the course covers, and the board pictures every later lecture is drawn on.
Complete


Lecture 2
Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
Fitting a hypothesis by least squares: batch and stochastic gradient descent, and the normal equations that skip iteration altogether.
Complete


Lecture 3
Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression
Least squares as maximum likelihood, a regression that refits around every query, and the logistic model for classification with Newton’s method.
Complete


Lecture 4
Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models
The perceptron, the exponential family, and the recipe that turns a choice of distribution into a learning algorithm, softmax regression included.
Complete


Lecture 5
GDA and Naive Bayes
Modelling how each class generates its inputs instead of the boundary between them: Gaussian discriminant analysis and naive Bayes.
Complete


Lecture 6
Support Vector Machines
Laplace smoothing and the event models for text, then the geometric margin and the optimisation problem that maximises it.
Complete


Lecture 7
Kernels
The dual of the margin problem, inner products in feature spaces you never compute, and the soft margin for data that will not separate.
Complete


Lecture 8
Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation
Bias and variance, regularisation, and how to choose a model with data you did not train on.
Complete


Discussion section
Learning Theory
Why training error says anything about test error: the union bound, Hoeffding’s inequality, uniform convergence and the VC dimension.
Complete


Lecture 9
Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
Greedy recursive splits, the losses that choose them, and the bagging, random forests and boosting that make trees competitive.
Complete


Lecture 10
Introduction to Neural Networks
Logistic regression as a single neuron, and what stacking them into layers buys.
Complete


Lecture 11
Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
Backpropagation worked out by hand, then initialisation, normalisation and the optimisers that make training work in practice.
Complete


Lecture 12
Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis
Diagnosing a learning algorithm that does not work: bias versus variance, optimisation versus objective, and error and ablative analysis.
Complete


Lecture 13
Expectation-Maximization Algorithms
Clustering with k-means, mixtures of Gaussians, and the EM algorithm that fits a model with latent variables.
Complete


Lecture 14
EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis
EM’s concrete updates and its view as coordinate ascent, and factor analysis for few examples in many dimensions.
Complete


Lecture 15
PCA and ICA
Projecting data onto the directions of greatest variance, when that helps and when it does not, and the cocktail-party problem ICA solves.
Complete


Lecture 16
Independent Component Analysis and RL
Finishing ICA by maximum likelihood, then Markov decision processes and the Bellman equations.
Complete


Lecture 17
MDPs and Value/Policy Iteration
Solving an MDP by value iteration and policy iteration, and learning its model from experience.
Complete


Lecture 18
Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation
Discretization and its limits, learning a simulator from flight logs, and fitted value iteration for continuous states.
Complete


Lecture 19
Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator
State-action rewards, finite horizons and non-stationary policies, linearization, and the linear quadratic regulator.
Complete


Lecture 20
RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
The helicopter diagnostics in RL notation, stochastic policies, REINFORCE and its variance, partial observability.
Complete

title: CS229 2018 Lecture Notes
text:
What these notes are
The official CS229 notes are the formal account of the course, and a good one. What they cannot carry is the lecture itself: the order in which Andrew Ng motivates an idea before he formalises it, the picture he draws to make an update rule obvious, the question from the room that exposes the step everyone was about to skip.
These notes are written from the Autumn 2018 recordings rather than from the official notes, and they are meant to sit beside both. Each page aims to be:

Faithful to the lecture — it follows what was taught and why, and links each section to the moment in the video where it happens.
Complete in its mathematics — the derivations done at the board are written out in full, with every symbol defined.
A bridge, not a copy — where the official notes go further, the chapter says which section to read next rather than reproducing it.

The whole book is also a single PDF. For an AI assistant, llms.txt maps every chapter to a Markdown copy with the maths in TeX, and llms-full.txt holds the book in one file. The same treatment of Stanford’s deep learning for computer vision course is in the companion CS231n 2025 Lecture Notes.

title: CS229 2018 Lecture Notes
text:
Roadmap


Supervised learning — linear and logistic regression, generalized linear models, generative learning, support vector machines and kernels
Generalization — bias and variance, model selection, learning theory
Trees and neural networks — decision trees and ensembles, neural networks and backpropagation
Applying machine learning — debugging learning algorithms and error analysis
Unsupervised learning — k-means, EM, factor analysis, PCA and ICA
Reinforcement learning — MDPs, value and policy iteration, continuous states, LQR

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 What the course assumes
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
The first lecture of CS229 does two things. It places the course among Stanford’s other machine-learning courses, and it draws, in about forty minutes at the board, the map the remaining nineteen lectures fill in: learning from labelled examples, learning to apply learning algorithms well, deep learning, learning from data with no labels, and learning from reward. No algorithm is derived. What the lecture supplies instead is the set of pictures — a scatter of house prices, a row of noughts and crosses, two clouds of unlabelled points — that every later derivation is drawn on top of, and it is worth having them clearly in mind before the mathematics arrives.
10:22 The stated prerequisites are modest on paper: familiarity with basic probability and statistics, basic linear algebra, and enough programming to write non-trivial code. In 2018 the assignments moved from MATLAB and Octave to Python and NumPy, which Ng presented as following the field rather than leading it.
The more useful guidance came from a question at 28:37 about how CS229 differs from CS229A and CS230. Ng’s answer was not a list of topics but a statement about depth. CS229A, taught as a flipped classroom built on his online course, covers a similarly broad set of algorithms with much less mathematics; CS230 is narrower, deep learning only, and also more applied. CS229 is the one that derives things, and he was candid that the derivations make it a heavy course. His advice to anyone unsure whether they were ready was to take CS229A first. He also pointed out that the three overlap less than their titles suggest — students who took two at once saw the same algorithms from different angles rather than the same lectures twice — and closed with the remark that frames the rest of the course: AI is larger than machine learning, and machine learning is larger than deep learning.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Two definitions
36:17 Ng offers two definitions of machine learning, an informal one and an operational one.
The informal one is usually credited to Arthur Samuel: machine learning is the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. That exact sentence does not appear in Samuel’s paper, Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers (1959), and is better read as a later paraphrase of it. Samuel’s own wording describes programming a computer “to behave in a way which, if done by human beings or animals, would be described as involving the process of learning”. The result the lecture attaches to it is in the paper, and it is what made the work famous. Samuel’s program, given the rules of checkers and a list of board features with unknown weights, learned to play a better game than Samuel himself, partly by playing against a copy of itself and keeping whichever set of weights won. The abstract puts the training time at eight to ten hours of machine-playing time.
Ng’s point about this is historical. At the time the open question was whether a computer could do anything it had not been explicitly told to do, and a program that beat its own author was a direct answer. Today it is routine for a learning algorithm to outperform people on a narrow task — a particular kind of speech recognition, or Go given enormous amounts of computation and self-play — and he stresses the word narrow. Samuel’s checkers player was among the first cases of that pattern.
The operational definition is Tom Mitchell’s, from his 1997 textbook Machine Learning, which calls something a well-posed learning problem when three things are named. A program learns from experience E with respect to a task T and a performance measure P if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with E. 38:43 Applied to checkers, T is playing the game, E is the large number of games the program plays against itself, and P is the probability of winning its next game against a new opponent. The value of the definition is that it forces all three to be stated. A good deal of what goes wrong in applied machine learning, which the course returns to in its lectures on strategy, is a project where one of them was never pinned down: the team is measuring a P that does not track the T they care about, or gathering an E that does not resemble the situations the system will face.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Supervised learning: regression
40:12 The most widely used kind of machine learning, and the subject of the first third of the course, is supervised learning. Ng introduces it with the example the next lecture formalises. Plot the size of each house in a dataset on the horizontal axis and its sale price on the vertical, call the first x and the second y, and ask for the relationship between them. If you own a house of 1,250 square feet and want to know what to ask for it, one answer is to fit a straight line to the data and read the price off the line above 1,250.






Figure 1.1: House size against price, with a straight line and a quadratic each fitted to the same points by least squares, and the price each predicts for a 1,250 ft² house. The data are synthetic, drawn to resemble the board sketch. Computed by figures/01-introduction/make_diagrams.py.



That is the whole shape of supervised learning. You are given a training set of inputs x paired with the correct outputs y, and the job is to learn a mapping from x to y good enough to apply to an x you have not seen. The problem is called regression when y is continuous. Prices are rounded to the cent and so are not literally real numbers, Ng notes, but nobody prices a house at \pi million dollars and for every practical purpose they are continuous.
A straight line is close to the simplest learning algorithm there is, and Figure 1.1 shows why it is not the only candidate. A quadratic follows the flattening of prices at the top end and has lower error on the training points (an RMSE of 25.4 against 29.6 on this data). That comparison cannot settle the question, though. A quadratic can never fit its training data worse than a line, because every line is a quadratic whose x^2 coefficient is zero, and this particular quadratic peaks at about 2,400 square feet and predicts that every house larger than that is worth less. How to choose between models — the line, the quadratic, or something richer, whether by hand or automatically — is one of the questions Ng flags as recurring all quarter. It becomes the bias–variance discussion of lecture 8.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Supervised learning: classification
43:04 The second example comes from a medical problem some of Ng’s collaborators worked on: deciding from a breast tumour’s size whether it is malignant or benign. Plot size on the horizontal axis and, on the vertical, y = 1 for malignant and y = 0 for benign. When a new patient arrives with a tumour of a given size, the learning algorithm should say how likely it is to be malignant. Because y now takes one of a small number of discrete values, this is classification. With two values it is binary classification, and with, say, five types of cancer it is still classification, just with five classes.
45:37 Ng then redraws the same data in a form the course uses from then on. Every example is pushed up onto a single horizontal line, and the label is carried by the symbol rather than by the height: a nought for a negative example (y = 0), a cross for a positive one (y = 1). Nothing is lost — Figure 1.2 shows both views of identical data — but the second frees the vertical axis to hold a second input.






Figure 1.2: The tumour problem twice. Above, size against the label plotted as a height; below, the same examples on one axis with the label carried by the symbol. Synthetic data. Computed by figures/01-introduction/make_diagrams.py.



47:07 That is the step he takes next. Real problems rarely give you one number to predict another; with the patient’s age as a second feature, x becomes a two-dimensional vector of tumour size and age, and each example becomes a nought or a cross in the plane. The task is now to separate the two kinds of mark, and the algorithm the course reaches for first draws a straight line between them. That algorithm is logistic regression, taken up in lecture 3, and it is what fitted the boundary in Figure 1.3.






Figure 1.3: Two features, tumour size and patient age. The line is the decision boundary logistic regression fits to these points by Newton’s method; one malignant example falls on the benign side of it. Synthetic data. Computed by figures/01-introduction/make_diagrams.py.

title: 1  Introduction
section: 1.5 More features than you can draw
text:
1.5 More features than you can draw
48:41 The two-feature picture is a teaching device. The group Ng describes used many more measurements of each tumour: clump thickness, uniformity of cell size, uniformity of cell shape, marginal adhesion. Those are attributes of the Wisconsin breast cancer data (Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Original)), which scores each of nine cytological features on a scale of one to ten. Nine dimensions cannot be plotted. The algorithms of the coming weeks are therefore written for an input vector x \in \mathbb{R}^n of any length, and the board pictures are the n = 2 case drawn to build intuition.
50:11 Ng then makes the remark of the lecture that most deserves a second look. The support vector machine, he says, can represent each patient not by two numbers or a million, but by an infinite list of features. His question is the one a reader should ask: a computer cannot store infinitely many numbers, so how can that work?
The answer, which lecture 7 develops, is that the algorithm never needs the features themselves. It only ever needs inner products between pairs of feature vectors, and for well-chosen feature maps that inner product has a closed form. A one-dimensional example shows it. Map a scalar x to the infinite vector

\phi(x) = e^{-x^2/2}\left(1,\; x,\; \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{2!}},\; \frac{x^3}{\sqrt{3!}},\; \dots\right).
\tag{1.1}
The inner product of two such vectors is a power series that sums exactly:

\phi(x)^\top \phi(z) = e^{-x^2/2}\, e^{-z^2/2} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(xz)^k}{k!}
= e^{-x^2/2 - z^2/2 + xz} = e^{-(x-z)^2/2}.
\tag{1.2}
The left-hand side is an inner product in infinitely many dimensions; the right-hand side is one subtraction and one exponential. The generator for this chapter checks the identity numerically. For x = 0.7 and z = -0.4, the first five coordinates of \phi already match the exact value e^{-(1.1)^2/2} \approx 0.5461 to within 10^{-5}, and ten match it to about 10^{-12}. A function like the right-hand side of Equation 1.2 is called a kernel, and this one is the Gaussian kernel. The SVM is written so that features appear only inside such inner products, and that is the whole of the trick Ng is foreshadowing.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.6 Learning to steer: ALVINN
52:05 The idea underneath all of this, Ng says, is that during training the algorithm sees inputs x together with their labels y, and its job is to find a mapping that produces the right y for a new x. To show how far that idea goes, he plays an old video of Dean Pomerleau’s ALVINN at Carnegie Mellon, a neural network that learned to steer a vehicle.
The set-up is supervised learning with a human as the labeller. While a person drives, the vehicle repeatedly digitises the camera image of the road ahead, downsampled to a small greyscale picture, and records the steering direction the driver chose at that moment. The image is x and the driver’s steering is y. On screen the label is a bright blob on a bar, a little left of centre when the driver is turning slightly left, and the network’s output is drawn on a second bar beneath it. At the start of training the network’s output is a grey smear across the whole bar, its way of saying it has no idea which way to steer. As training proceeds the smear contracts to a sharp blob that tracks the driver’s. Then the driver takes their hands off the wheel and the network steers. A later version in the video trains separate networks for one-lane and two-lane roads, with an arbitrator choosing between them, and switches from one to the other as the road changes.
Ng is clear that this is not how self-driving cars are built now. The example is in the lecture because it is a supervised learning problem whose labels cost nothing except someone driving, and because the techniques that make it work — gradient descent and backpropagation — are the ones the course teaches in its first weeks and in lectures 10 and 11.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.7 Machine learning strategy
58:01 The second area of the course, which the class notes file under learning theory, is what Ng calls machine learning strategy, and his motivation for it is drawn from practice rather than from theory. Visiting machine-learning teams at large technology companies, he finds an enormous difference in how effectively two teams apply the same algorithm. The failure he describes is a team that has spent six months on an approach, where a look at the data shows that it was never going to work, and that could have been seen at the start.
The decisions behind that are the everyday ones: whether to collect more data and which data, whether to try a different algorithm, whether to rent faster GPUs and train for longer, which architecture to use. 1:01:08 A learning algorithm, he says, almost never works the first time, so what separates teams is how they debug. His two analogies are both about debugging by principle rather than by reflex. One is a friend who dealt with compiler errors by deleting every line that had one. The other is the difference between an inexperienced engineer who starts optimising code at once and an experienced one who runs a profiler first and changes only the bottleneck. The aim is to turn what has been “black magic”, tribal knowledge held by people with decades of experience, into an engineering discipline that can be taught. That material comes in lecture 8, the learning-theory discussion section, and lecture 12 on debugging and error analysis.
Deep learning is the third area. Ng describes it as the part of the field moving fastest and treats it as one tool among many. CS229 covers enough to train a neural network from scratch in lectures 10 and 11, and leaves the depth to CS230.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.8 Unsupervised learning
1:04:57 Ng introduces unsupervised learning by redrawing the classification picture and deleting the labels. You are given only the inputs x, no y, and asked to find interesting structure in them. In the data on the board the structure is visible at a glance — two clusters — and an algorithm the course covers, k-means clustering, finds it. Figure 1.4 runs that algorithm on synthetic points like the board’s. Starting from two arbitrary points as centres, it reaches a stable split in three rounds of reassignment.






Figure 1.4: Unsupervised learning on the same kind of picture as Figure 1.3, but without labels. Left, all the algorithm receives; right, the two groups k-means assigns, with each group’s centre marked. Synthetic data. Computed by figures/01-introduction/make_diagrams.py.



The applications Ng lists show how much of clustering is grouping things that nobody has named. Google News gathers thousands of articles a day by different reporters into a single story, such as the BP oil-well spill. Genetic microarray data group individuals by shared characteristics. Clustering groups machines in a data centre by related workloads, finds the cohesive communities in a social network, and splits a customer database into market segments that can be addressed separately. A colleague of his has used it to group galaxies in astronomical data.
1:08:12 A student asked the natural question: is unsupervised learning just clustering? It is not. Unsupervised learning means any use of unlabelled data to find something interesting, and clustering is one instance. Ng’s second example is the cocktail party problem. Put several microphones in a room where several people are talking at once. Each microphone records an overlapping mixture of every voice, and the task is to recover each speaker’s voice cleanly. Nothing labels which sound came from whom, which is what makes the problem unsupervised. The algorithm that solves it, independent component analysis, is in lectures 15 and 16 and is a programming exercise later in the course. His third example is text. From unlabelled text alone, word representations can be learned that capture analogies such as man is to woman as king is to queen and Tokyo is to Japan as Washington, D.C. is to the United States, the result popularised by Mikolov et al. (2013).
He also offered a judgement on the economics. Most of the value machine learning was creating in 2018 came from supervised learning, while unsupervised learning had important uses and was where much of the research frontier lay.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.9 Reinforcement learning
1:11:19 The fifth area starts from a problem that defeats supervised learning: if you were handed the keys to Stanford’s autonomous helicopter, how would you write a program to fly it? The difficulty is that nobody knows the optimal way to move a helicopter’s two control sticks, so there is no y to label each state with, and no expert whose every action is worth imitating as ALVINN imitated its driver.
1:12:18 Ng’s analogy is training a dog. You cannot show a dog the optimal way to behave either. You let it do what it wants and say “good dog” when it does something you like and “bad dog” when it does not, and over time it does more of the first and less of the second. Reinforcement learning replaces the label with that signal, called the reward. The helicopter flies however it likes, gets “good helicopter” for an accurate manoeuvre and “bad helicopter” when it crashes, and the algorithm’s job is to find a way of acting that collects more reward over time. The helicopter in the video is the Stanford autonomous helicopter, whose aerobatic flight is described in Abbeel et al., 2006, and a second clip applies the same reward-driven learning to a legged robot dog learning to climb over obstacles.
The best-known successes of reinforcement learning were in games, Atari and AlphaGo. Ng said he was as excited, or more, by its growing traction in robotics and in optimising logistics systems. The course’s last five lectures build it up from Markov decision processes.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.10 The map of the course
1:11:11 Ng closes the overview with the list of the five areas. They map onto this book as follows.



Table 1.1: The five areas of CS229 and the lectures that cover them.










Area
What it is about
Lectures




Supervised learning
learning a mapping from labelled pairs (x, y)
2–7, 9


Learning theory and strategy
why learning works, and how to make it work in practice
8, learning theory, 12


Deep learning
training neural networks
10–11


Unsupervised learning
finding structure in x alone
13–16


Reinforcement learning
learning to act from a reward signal
16–20






The order is deliberate. Supervised learning comes first because it is where both the mathematics and the economic value are most developed, and every later area borrows its notation. The next chapter starts there, with the house-price scatter of Figure 1.1 and the first algorithm for fitting it.

title: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
2.1 The housing problem and the hypothesis
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
The second lecture builds the first complete learning algorithm of the course and then solves the same problem a second way. Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of features; the weights are chosen to make the squared error on the training set as small as possible; and that minimum can be found either by walking downhill on the error surface, one gradient step at a time, or by solving a linear system for it directly. Gradient descent is the half that matters later: the normal equations work for linear regression and its weighted variant and nothing else in the course, while the walk downhill reappears in logistic regression, generalised linear models and neural networks. Ng uses this lecture to set up the vocabulary all of them share — hypothesis, parameters, cost function, learning rate — and it is worth getting that vocabulary straight here, where the mathematics is still simple enough to check by hand.
1:55 The running example is the one that closed lecture 1: predict the asking price of a house from its size. Ng’s data are real, a few dozen listings from Portland, Oregon collected off Craigslist — a 2,104 ft² house listed at $400,000, a 1,416 ft² one at $232,000, and so on — and the task is to fit a straight line through them.
Before writing any formula he describes the shape every supervised algorithm in the course will have. A training set goes into a learning algorithm, and what comes out is a function, by convention called the hypothesis h, which takes the size of a house it has never seen and returns an estimated price. The learning algorithm’s job is to produce h; h’s job is to make predictions. 4:43 The first design decision is therefore not how to fit, but how to represent h, and for linear regression the answer is
h_\theta(x) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \theta_2 x_2,
\tag{2.1}
with x_1 the size and x_2 the number of bedrooms. Ng concedes the point a mathematician in the room would raise: with the \theta_0 term this is an affine function, not a linear one, and machine learning calls it linear anyway.
The intercept is awkward to carry around, so it is absorbed into the sum by inventing a feature that is always one, x_0 = 1. Then x and \theta are both vectors in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}, and
h_\theta(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \theta_j x_j = \theta^\top x .
\tag{2.2}
The rest of the notation is fixed here for the whole quarter. The \theta_j are the parameters, and choosing them is all that learning means for this model. m is the number of training examples (rows of the table), n the number of features (two here, so x and \theta are three-dimensional), x the input features and y the output or target. The i-th training example is written (x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}), and the superscript in parentheses is an index into the table, not a power: x^{(1)}_1 =
2104 is the size of the first house. Ng is open that some of this terminology is an accident of history — he does not think “hypothesis” is a good name, but someone used it in a paper decades ago and the field is stuck with it.
crumbs: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent

title: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
2.2 The least-squares cost
14:41 “Choose \theta so that h(x) is close to y on the training examples” needs a number that measures closeness, and Ng builds it one piece at a time on the board: the squared difference between prediction and truth for one house, summed over all m houses, with a factor of one half in front:

J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( h_\theta(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right)^2 .
\tag{2.3}
J is the cost function, and linear regression — ordinary least squares — is the choice of \theta that minimises it. The one half changes nothing about where the minimum is; it is there so that the 2 brought down by differentiating a square cancels it, as it will in Section 2.4.
16:39 The question Ng says he is asked most often is why the error is squared rather than taken in absolute value or raised to the fourth power. His answer here is a deferral with a hint: squared error corresponds to assuming the noise in y is Gaussian, and linear regression turns out to be one member of a family, the generalised linear models, in which that choice is derived rather than assumed. The next lecture makes the Gaussian argument precise.
crumbs: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent

title: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
2.3 Gradient descent
18:27 The algorithm for minimising J starts from some initial \theta — the zero vector is a reasonable default, a random start is also fine — and keeps changing \theta in a way that lowers J.
19:40 Ng’s picture for it is a landscape. Put \theta_0 and \theta_1 on the two horizontal axes and J as the height (with three parameters the surface lives in four dimensions, which is why the picture uses two). Stand at the starting point, turn through 360 degrees, and ask: if I took one tiny step, which direction would take me downhill fastest? Take that step, look around again from the new spot, and repeat.
22:03 The picture also exposes the method’s weakness. On a landscape with more than one valley, where you end up depends on where you start: begin a few steps to one side and the same procedure walks you into a different local minimum (Figure 2.1). For linear regression this turns out not to matter, for a reason Section 2.5 gives, but it matters a great deal for most of what comes later in the course.






Figure 2.1: Gradient descent on a one-parameter cost with two valleys. Started just left of the hump, it runs into the deeper valley; started just right, it stops in the shallower one and has no way of knowing a better minimum exists. Computed by figures/02-linear-regression/make_diagrams.py.



23:54 Formally, one step of gradient descent updates every parameter at once:

\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_j} J(\theta), \qquad j = 0, 1, \dots, n .
\tag{2.4}
The partial derivative gives the direction of steepest ascent, so subtracting a multiple of it goes downhill. The multiple \alpha is the learning rate, which sets the size of the step. The := is assignment, and Ng is deliberate about it: a := a
+ 1 increments a, whereas a = b asserts a fact, and he promises never to write a
= a + 1. Throughout the update, the training set is fixed and J is a fixed function of \theta; only \theta moves.
26:04 A student asked at once how to choose \alpha. “There’s a theory and there’s a practice,” and the practice, to laughter, is 0.01. The serious version followed: if the features are scaled to roughly [-1, 1], start at 0.01 and try larger and smaller values to see which drives J down fastest. Section 2.5 says why the scaling clause is not optional.
crumbs: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent

title: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
2.4 The LMS update
27:27 To run Equation 2.4 the partial derivative has to be computed, and Ng does it for a training set of a single example (x, y) first, so that the sum does not get in the way. The chain rule brings the 2 down from the square, where it cancels the half, and leaves the derivative of what was inside:

\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_j} \frac{1}{2}\left(h_\theta(x) - y\right)^2
= \left(h_\theta(x) - y\right) \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_j}
\left( \theta_0 x_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \dots + \theta_n x_n - y \right)
= \left(h_\theta(x) - y\right) x_j .
\tag{2.5}
Of all the terms in the expanded sum only \theta_j x_j depends on \theta_j, so every other term differentiates to zero and this one to x_j.
31:43 With m examples, the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and the full algorithm is

\text{repeat until convergence:} \quad
\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( h_\theta(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right) x_j^{(i)}
\quad \text{for every } j .
\tag{2.6}
This is the least-mean-squares or Widrow–Hoff rule, and it reads well once written out. Each example pushes \theta_j in proportion to its own error: a house whose price is already predicted almost exactly barely moves the parameters, one that is badly mispredicted moves them a lot, and the push on \theta_j is weighted by how large the feature x_j was for that house. The generator behind this chapter checks Equation 2.6’s sum against finite differences of J on the housing data, and it agrees.






NoteIn the official notes



The same derivation, and the remark that the update is proportional to the error, are in cs229-notes1, section 1.
crumbs: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent

title: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
section: 2.5 A bowl, and the learning rate
text:
2.5 A bowl, and the learning rate
33:52 The local-minimum worry of Figure 2.1 disappears for this cost. J is a sum of squares of functions linear in \theta, so it is a quadratic in \theta, and a quadratic of this kind is a single bowl: its only local minimum is the global one. Looked at from above, its contours are nested ellipses, and Ng adds a fact he half-remembers from school — “I think it’s true” — that each step of steepest descent crosses the contour it starts on at right angles. It is true: the gradient is normal to the level set through any point, and the generator confirms it on the housing cost to within a cosine of 0.003.
What the board picture does not show is how thin the bowl can be. Figure 2.2 runs gradient descent on synthetic housing data shaped like Ng’s, with size in thousands of square feet, starting from \theta = 0. The first step drops almost straight across the contours into the floor of a long valley; every step after that inches along the floor towards the minimum, and it takes more than four hundred of them to bring the intercept within $500 of its final value. The ratio of the bowl’s steepest to its shallowest curvature — the eigenvalues of X^\top X, in the notation of Section 2.8 — is about a hundred here, and gradient descent’s pace is set by the shallow direction while its step size is capped by the steep one.






Figure 2.2: Batch and stochastic gradient descent on the contours of the least-squares cost, both from \theta = 0, on 47 synthetic houses shaped after the Portland data. Batch descent (left) reaches the valley floor in one step and then crawls along it; the stochastic version (right) takes the same route noisily and keeps moving near the minimum, marked by the dot. Computed by figures/02-linear-regression/make_diagrams.py.



That cap is the precise version of Ng’s 36:08 advice on the learning rate. Too small and the algorithm needs very many iterations; too large and each step overshoots the minimum, lands higher on the far side, and diverges (Figure 2.3). For a quadratic the boundary is exact: with \lambda_{\max} the largest eigenvalue of X^\top X, gradient descent converges for \alpha <
2/\lambda_{\max} and diverges above it, which the generator checks on both sides of the line. His practical rules follow from watching J rather than computing eigenvalues. If J goes up over iterations, the learning rate is almost certainly too large. And rather than search finely, try values on a roughly doubling scale — 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.08 — and keep whichever drives J down fastest.






Figure 2.3: Gradient descent on J(\theta) = \theta^2, where the update multiplies \theta by 1 - 2\alpha. A small learning rate creeps down one side; a moderate one reaches the bottom in a few steps; above \alpha = 1 every step overshoots to the other side, higher than before. Computed by figures/02-linear-regression/make_diagrams.py.



The same bound explains the feature-scaling clause in “set it to 0.01”. On the synthetic data with size measured in raw square feet, \lambda_{\max} is so large that the stable range ends at \alpha \approx 4 \times 10^{-9}, and 0.01 diverges immediately; with size rescaled to about [-1, 1] the limit is about 0.04, and 0.01 is comfortably safe. One further caveat follows from writing J as a sum. \lambda_{\max} grows with m, so the safe learning rate shrinks as the training set grows, and 0.01 that works on 47 houses will not on 47,000. Many implementations average the squared error instead of summing it, which removes that dependence; the minimum is unchanged either way.
37:14 Ng’s second view of the same run is in the data rather than in parameter space. With \theta = 0 the hypothesis is the horizontal line h(x) = 0, predicting every house free; each step of gradient descent replaces it with a line that fits a little better, until it settles on the least-squares fit (Figure 2.4).






Figure 2.4: The hypothesis after successive steps of batch gradient descent from \theta = 0, drawn over the synthetic housing data; the solid line is the least-squares fit the steps converge to. Computed by figures/02-linear-regression/make_diagrams.py.



39:30 A student asked why the update subtracts \alpha times the gradient rather than adding it. Ng’s suggestion was to work one case by hand, and it settles the matter: take J(\theta) = \theta^2 at \theta = 1. The derivative there is 2 (Ng said 1 at the board; the sign is what matters), positive, and to reach the minimum at zero \theta has to decrease — so the step must go against the gradient. Adding it would climb.
crumbs: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent

title: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
2.6 Stochastic gradient descent
41:05 Equation 2.6 is called batch gradient descent because every single update looks at the whole training set as one batch. That is its weakness. If m is the size of the US census rather than of a Craigslist scrape — Ng mentions training on hundreds of millions of examples — then one step requires a full pass over the data, possibly terabytes read from disk, before \theta moves at all, and convergence can take hundreds or thousands of such steps.
44:13 Stochastic gradient descent updates after every example instead:

\text{loop: for } i = 1, \dots, m: \quad
\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \left( h_\theta(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right) x_j^{(i)}
\quad \text{for every } j .
\tag{2.7}
46:02 In Ng’s words it looks at one house and adjusts the parameters to predict that house better, then the next house, then the next. No single house’s gradient points straight at the minimum, so the path is noisy, but on average it heads downhill, and it starts making progress after the first example rather than after the millionth. The price is that it never quite converges: because each update chases a different house, \theta keeps wandering around the minimum, as on the right of Figure 2.2. For a large dataset that trade is almost always worth making.
The questions from the room fill in how it is used in practice. Asked 47:58 whether one could start stochastic and switch to batch near the end, Ng said yes, and that it does no harm — but that people rarely bother, because batch steps on a large dataset are too slow to be worth it, and because the parameters stochastic gradient descent ends near are usually perfectly good even if they are not exactly the global minimum. The middle ground, which he names and leaves to CS230, is mini-batch gradient descent, which updates on a hundred or so examples at a time. What is common instead is 50:03 to decrease the learning rate slowly over time: the oscillations shrink with the step size, so \theta ends up bouncing around a smaller region closer to the minimum. Asked when to stop, his answer was to plot J over time and stop when it stops going down — easy here, where there are no local optima to confuse the picture, and much harder for the neural networks later in the course.
51:35 The last question was whether stochastic gradient descent’s learning rate should be 1/m times batch’s. No, Ng said, it is usually much bigger, since otherwise it would be as slow as batch. The arithmetic behind that answer is worth having. Because J is a sum, a full pass of Equation 2.7 at rate \alpha adds up, to first order in \alpha, to one batch step at the same \alpha; the generator confirms the gap between them shrinking as \alpha does. Dividing by m would therefore make a whole pass of stochastic updates worth only 1/m of a batch step. And a single-example update tolerates a far larger rate in the first place: its stability limit is 2 /
\lVert x^{(i)} \rVert^2 rather than 2 / \lambda_{\max} of the whole of X^\top X, which on the synthetic housing data is a factor of about 25 more room.
51:51 Ng’s own rule of thumb closes the topic. With a dataset of hundreds or thousands of examples, where a pass is cheap, he would almost always use batch gradient descent, because it is one less thing to fiddle with — no oscillating parameters to worry about. When the data are too large for that, almost everyone uses stochastic gradient descent or something like it.
crumbs: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent

title: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
2.7 Matrix derivatives and the trace
53:25 For linear regression, and for exactly linear regression — none of the models of the following lectures beyond its weighted variant in lecture 3 — there is a way to skip the iterations altogether and jump to the minimum in one step. Deriving it means setting the gradient of J to zero and solving, and Ng’s aim is to do that “in roughly four lines of linear algebra rather than pages and pages”, which takes a little notation first. In his experience, he says, the right notation is what makes such problems tractable.
56:02 For a function J : \mathbb{R}^{n+1} \to \mathbb{R}, the derivative with respect to the vector \theta is the vector of partial derivatives,

\nabla_\theta J = \begin{bmatrix} \partial J / \partial \theta_0 \\ \vdots \\ \partial J / \partial \theta_n \end{bmatrix} ,
\tag{2.8}
and more generally, for a function f that maps an m \times n matrix A to a real number, \nabla_A f(A) is the m \times n matrix whose (i, j) entry is \partial f /
\partial A_{ij}. Ng’s example 58:32 is a made-up function of a 2 \times 2 matrix, f(A) = A_{11} + A_{12}^2, so that f applied to the matrix with rows (5, 6) and (7, 8) is 5 + 36 = 41, and

\nabla_A f(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2A_{12} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .
\tag{2.9}
A student asked whether the vector definition was a special case of the matrix one; it is — a vector is an (n+1) \times 1 matrix, and the two agree.
1:03:35 The second tool is the trace of a square matrix, the sum of its diagonal entries, \operatorname{tr} A = \sum_i A_{ii}. Transposing a matrix leaves its diagonal where it was, so \operatorname{tr} A = \operatorname{tr} A^\top. The trace of a product is unchanged by moving the last factor to the front, \operatorname{tr} AB = \operatorname{tr} BA and \operatorname{tr} ABC =
\operatorname{tr} CAB, and its derivative has a clean form:

\nabla_A \operatorname{tr} AB = B^\top .
\tag{2.10}
1:06:23 Ng then gives one identity as the matrix analogue of \frac{d}{da}
a^2 c = 2ac, a rule to be used without re-deriving it every time, the way one uses the derivative of x^2. The analogy is a good way to remember the shape of the result, but the generator caught that the shorthand needs a condition the board left out:

\nabla_A \operatorname{tr}\!\left(A A^\top C\right) = \left(C + C^\top\right) A ,
\tag{2.11}
which equals 2CA only when C is symmetric. For a random non-symmetric C, the numerical gradient matches Equation 2.11 and misses 2CA by a visible margin; for the symmetric part of the same C the two coincide. In the derivation that follows A is \theta and the matrix playing the role of C is X^\top X, which is symmetric, so nothing goes wrong, but the general rule is the one with C + C^\top. The official notes state the fully general version, \nabla_A \operatorname{tr} ABA^\top C = CAB + C^\top A
B^\top, which reduces to Equation 2.11 when B is the identity.
crumbs: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent

title: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
2.8 The normal equations
1:08:39 To write J with matrices, stack the training inputs as the rows of the design matrix X, an m \times (n+1) matrix whose i-th row is (x^{(i)})^\top, and stack the targets into a vector \vec{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m. Then X\theta is the vector of every prediction at once, since its i-th entry is (x^{(i)})^\top \theta = h_\theta(x^{(i)}), and X\theta - \vec{y} is the vector of every error. A vector dotted with itself is the sum of its squared entries, z^\top z =
\sum_i z_i^2, so

J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \left( X\theta - \vec{y} \right)^\top \left( X\theta - \vec{y} \right) .
\tag{2.12}
1:13:08 Now take the gradient and set it to zero. Expanding the product the way one expands (ax - b)^2 gives four terms, \theta^\top X^\top X \theta - \theta^\top
X^\top \vec{y} - \vec{y}^\top X \theta + \vec{y}^\top \vec{y}. The last does not depend on \theta; the middle two are the same scalar, each the transpose of the other; and the trace rules of Section 2.7 differentiate the first to 2X^\top X\theta and the middle pair to 2X^\top\vec{y}. Halving,

\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = X^\top X \theta - X^\top \vec{y} .
\tag{2.13}
This is Equation 2.6’s sum written in matrix form, which is a useful check on both. 1:16:19 Setting it to zero gives the normal equations,

X^\top X \theta = X^\top \vec{y} ,
\qquad
\theta = \left( X^\top X \right)^{-1} X^\top \vec{y} .
\tag{2.14}
A few matrix products land on the global minimum of the bowl in one step, the same point that gradient descent spends hundreds of steps approaching in Figure 2.2; the generator runs both and confirms they agree to six decimal places. On the real Portland data the official notes report the fit \theta_0 = 71.27, \theta_1 =
0.1345: about $71,000 plus $134.50 per square foot.
1:17:01 The common question is what to do if X^\top X is not invertible. That usually means the features are linearly dependent — redundant — and the matrix pseudo-inverse will still return a sensible answer. But Ng’s preferred fix is diagnostic: a singular X^\top X most often means the same feature is in the data twice (size in square feet and size in square metres, say), and the right move is to find the duplicate and drop it. With a feature duplicated, every way of splitting its weight between the two copies gives exactly the same predictions and the same J, which is why no single \theta can be picked out by the equations; the generator checks this on a copy of the housing data with the size column repeated.
His last answer, to a final question on how to choose the learning rate, came back to where Section 2.3 left it: it is empirical, and most people try several values and keep the one that works.






NoteIn the official notes



The matrix-derivative identities and the full derivation of the normal equations, including the trace manipulation Ng skips, are in cs229-notes1, sections 2.1 and 2.2. Section 3 justifies the least-squares cost as maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise, which is where the next lecture begins.
crumbs: 2  Linear Regression and Gradient Descent

title: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression
text:
3.1 Features, or a different algorithm
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
This lecture takes the linear regression of lecture 2 in three directions. Locally weighted regression keeps the least-squares machinery but refits it around every query point, which lets a straight-line method trace a curve no single set of features would fit. A probabilistic reading of linear regression then shows that least squares is not an arbitrary choice: it is what maximum likelihood gives when the noise is Gaussian. And the same two-step recipe — assume a distribution for y given x, then maximise the likelihood — produces logistic regression, the first classification algorithm of the course, along with Newton’s method to fit it in a handful of iterations. Ng ranks linear and logistic regression as the two learning algorithms he uses most.
2:20 Lecture 2 fitted a straight line to house prices, but the data may bend. One answer is to change the features: fit \theta_0 + \theta_1 x + \theta_2 x^2 by defining x_2 = x^2, and the linear-regression machinery runs unchanged, because “linear” refers to the parameters, not to x. The trouble is choosing. A quadratic eventually curves back down, which for house prices says a bigger house is cheaper; \sqrt{x} or \log x might bend the right way; and for data that rise, dip and rise again, Ng says frankly that finding the right set of features — square root, log, cube, x^{2/3} — is hard. Feature-selection algorithms that automate the choice come later in the course.
5:53 Locally weighted regression sidesteps the question, and it introduces a distinction worth having early. A parametric learning algorithm fits a fixed set of parameters, after which the training set can be erased: linear regression keeps only \theta. A non-parametric algorithm has to keep the data, and the amount it stores grows — linearly here — with the size of the training set. That is the cost of not having to choose features, and it is why Ng warns that such methods may not suit a really massive dataset.
crumbs: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression

title: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression
text:
3.2 Locally weighted regression
8:33 Linear regression makes a prediction at x by fitting \theta once to all the data and returning \theta^\top x. Locally weighted regression postpones the fit until it knows where the prediction is wanted. Given the query point x, it fits a straight line that pays most attention to the training examples with inputs near x, glances at the ones further away, and uses that local line to predict at x; a different query point gets a different line. Formally it chooses \theta to minimise a weighted cost,

\sum_{i=1}^{m} w^{(i)} \left( y^{(i)} - \theta^\top x^{(i)} \right)^2,
\qquad
w^{(i)} = \exp\!\left( -\frac{\left(x^{(i)} - x\right)^2}{2\tau^2} \right),
\tag{3.1}
and returns \theta^\top x. 12:09 When x^{(i)} is close to the query the weight is near e^0 = 1 and that example’s error counts in full; when it is far the weight is near zero and its error term all but disappears from the sum. (Ng first wrote the exponent without the square on \tau; a student caught it, and it is \tau^2.) The left panel of Figure 3.1 shows one such fit.






Figure 3.1: Locally weighted regression on synthetic data. Left: at the query x = 6, points are shaded by their weight, the bump below is the weight function, and the line is the weighted least-squares fit whose value at x = 6 is the prediction. Right: repeating that at every x traces the whole curve, for three bandwidths. Computed by figures/03-locally-weighted-logistic/make_diagrams.py.



15:27 The weight function is shaped like a Gaussian bell, and Ng heads off the obvious confusion: it has nothing to do with a Gaussian density. Its peak is 1, it does not integrate to 1, and it is not a probability of anything — just a convenient bump. The bump’s width is the bandwidth \tau, a hyperparameter, and 16:46 it decides how large a neighbourhood each local fit sees. Ng leaves its effect for the problem set, saying only that it controls overfitting and underfitting; the right panel of Figure 3.1 shows both. With \tau = 0.12 only a couple of points carry weight in each fit, and the curve chases the noise into spikes; with \tau = 4 nearly every point carries weight everywhere, and the curve flattens towards a single straight line. In the limit it is that line: the generator checks that a bandwidth of 10^4 reproduces the ordinary least-squares fit to four decimal places. At \tau
= 0.6 the curve follows the rise, the dip and the plateau without being told what features describe them.
The questions that followed are the practical ones. Asked 18:53 about predicting outside the range of the data, Ng said the formulas still work but the results may be poor — locally weighted regression is not good at extrapolation, but then most learning algorithms are not. Asked about letting \tau vary across the input space, he said yes: there is a large literature on choosing it from the local density of points, and on replacing the bell with other shapes, such as a triangle that reaches zero outside a window. His own rule 19:58 is to reach for locally weighted regression when the number of features is small, two or three, there is a lot of data, and you do not want to think about which features to use.
20:29 On cost, his answer at the board needs one correction. Each prediction solves a weighted version of the normal equations, X^\top W X \theta = X^\top W
\vec{y} with W the diagonal matrix of weights, and that is a system of dimension n + 1 — the number of parameters — not of the number of training examples, as the lecture puts it. What does grow with m is the work of forming the system, since every training example contributes a weighted term, and that work is repeated for every query. So a prediction costs time proportional to m, which is why a few thousand examples are no problem and millions call for data structures such as k-d trees that find the nearby points without visiting all of them.






NoteIn the official notes



Locally weighted linear regression, with the same weight function, is cs229-notes1, section 4; the problem set explores the bandwidth.
crumbs: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression

title: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression
text:
3.3 Least squares as maximum likelihood
22:24 Lecture 2 promised a reason for squaring the error. Ng’s answer starts by assuming how the data were generated: each house’s price is a linear function of its features plus an error,

y^{(i)} = \theta^\top x^{(i)} + \epsilon^{(i)},
\qquad
\epsilon^{(i)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),
\tag{3.2}
where \epsilon^{(i)} gathers everything the model leaves out — the seller’s mood that day, unmodelled features — and random noise. The density of the error is the Gaussian \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp\!\left(-\epsilon^2 / 2\sigma^2\right), which, unlike the bump of Section 3.2, does integrate to one. 25:45 The large assumption is that the errors are IID — independent and identically distributed across houses — and Ng is candid that it is false: if one house on a street is priced unusually high, its neighbours probably are too. It is one of those assumptions that is probably not true and is good enough to give a useful model.
Together the assumptions say that, given x and \theta, the price is Gaussian around the line:

p\left(y^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}; \theta\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
\exp\!\left( -\frac{\left( y^{(i)} - \theta^\top x^{(i)} \right)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right).
\tag{3.3}
28:16 The semicolon is read “parameterised by”. Writing a comma would mean conditioning on \theta, which is not a random variable in this frequentist view; Ng keeps the distinction, he says, mostly to avoid upsetting statistician friends, and admits it changes nothing about the code one writes.
30:57 Because the errors are independent, the probability of all the observed prices is the product of the individual densities, and viewed as a function of \theta with the data fixed that product is the likelihood,

L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} p\left(y^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}; \theta\right).
\tag{3.4}
32:44 Ng’s vocabulary rule is worth adopting. The likelihood of the parameters and the probability of the data are the same number; which name you use says which argument you are varying. So one speaks of the likelihood of the parameters and the probability of the data, never the reverse.
37:49 Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the \theta that makes the observed data most probable. The logarithm is strictly increasing, so it is easier and equivalent to maximise the log-likelihood \ell(\theta) = \log L(\theta), which turns the product into a sum:

\ell(\theta) = m \log \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
- \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( y^{(i)} - \theta^\top x^{(i)} \right)^2 .
\tag{3.5}
The first term does not involve \theta, and \sigma^2 is a positive constant, so maximising \ell is exactly minimising the least-squares cost J(\theta) of lecture 2 — and the answer does not depend on \sigma at all. Least squares is maximum likelihood under IID Gaussian noise.
Asked 35:31 why the noise should be Gaussian, Ng pointed to the central limit theorem: an error made of many small, not-too-correlated contributions — the seller’s mood, the school district, the weather, transport — sums to something close to Gaussian, which is why it became the default. The same derivation also answers lecture 2’s question about absolute error, which Ng deferred. Assume instead that the errors follow a Laplace distribution, with density proportional to \exp(-|\epsilon|/b), and the log-likelihood becomes a constant minus a multiple of \sum_i |y^{(i)} - \theta^\top x^{(i)}|: maximum likelihood is then least absolute deviations. The difference is not cosmetic. With an intercept alone the Gaussian answer is the mean and the Laplace answer is the median, and the generator checks both against a grid search on a sample of twenty values around 3 plus one at 25: the Gaussian estimate is pulled to 4.09 by the single outlier, the Laplace one stays at 2.93. The choice of noise model is a choice of how much to trust the extreme points.
Asked 41:07 whether some other cost would ever be better, Ng said that under these assumptions none is — the derivation makes least squares the answer. If you know the errors are badly non-IID, more sophisticated models exist, but in practice he rarely bothers: assumptions known to be not quite true are often kept because they make the algorithm efficient.






NoteIn the official notes



The same derivation is cs229-notes1, section 3, which also notes that the conclusion does not depend on \sigma.
crumbs: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression

title: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression
section: 3.4 Why not linear regression for classification
text:
3.4 Why not linear regression for classification
43:42 The recipe — assume p(y \mid x; \theta), then maximise the likelihood — now goes to a problem where y is 0 or 1: binary classification, with lecture 1’s tumours as the example. The tempting shortcut is to fit a straight line to the 0/1 labels and call anything above 0.5 a 1. Ng’s objection 44:43 is a single extra example. Add one malignant tumour far to the right, a point whose label nobody would dispute, and the least-squares line tilts to reach it; the place it crosses 0.5 slides right, and malignant tumours that were correctly classified are now called benign. In Figure 3.2 the threshold moves from 3.17 to 4.11, and the number of misclassified tumours goes from one to three, because of a point that contained no new information about where the boundary is. There is also the unnatural fact that a line outputs values below 0 and above 1 for something that can only be 0 or 1. Ng says some people use linear regression for classification and sometimes get lucky; he never does.






Figure 3.2: One malignant tumour at size 20 drags the least-squares line (dashed without it, solid with it), moving the size at which it crosses 0.5 past three malignant tumours. The logistic regression curve, fitted with the extra example, keeps its boundary at the same place. Synthetic data. Computed by figures/03-locally-weighted-logistic/make_diagrams.py.
crumbs: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression

title: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression
text:
3.5 The logistic model
46:46 A classifier’s hypothesis should output a number between 0 and 1, so logistic regression passes the linear function through the sigmoid or logistic function — the two names mean the same thing:

h_\theta(x) = g\!\left(\theta^\top x\right) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^\top x}},
\qquad
g(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} .
\tag{3.6}
g starts near 0 for very negative z, passes through \tfrac12 at z = 0 and approaches 1. Ng is open that he is pulling it “out of a hat” for now: many functions have that shape, and lecture 4 derives this one from the generalised linear model framework. Section 3.6 adds a reason of its own.
50:23 The probabilistic assumption is that the hypothesis is the probability of the positive class — the chance that the tumour is malignant:

P(y = 1 \mid x; \theta) = h_\theta(x), \qquad P(y = 0 \mid x; \theta) = 1 - h_\theta(x).
\tag{3.7}
A student asked whether the roles could be swapped; they could, and nothing would change except which class is called positive. 52:46 Since y is 0 or 1, the two lines compress into one,

p(y \mid x; \theta) = h_\theta(x)^{\,y} \left(1 - h_\theta(x)\right)^{1 - y},
\tag{3.8}
because whichever factor carries a zero exponent becomes 1 and drops out, leaving the line that applies. The trick is only notation, but it is what makes the likelihood a single product.
crumbs: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression

title: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression
text:
3.6 Maximum likelihood and gradient ascent
56:03 With Equation 3.8 the likelihood is \prod_i h(x^{(i)})^{y^{(i)}}
(1 - h(x^{(i)}))^{1 - y^{(i)}}, and its log is

\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} y^{(i)} \log h_\theta\!\left(x^{(i)}\right)
+ \left(1 - y^{(i)}\right) \log\!\left(1 - h_\theta\!\left(x^{(i)}\right)\right).
\tag{3.9}
To fit, 58:54 Ng uses batch gradient ascent: the same walk as lecture 2, but uphill, since the goal is now to maximise \ell rather than minimise J, so the minus sign in the update becomes a plus. Working out the derivative, which Ng leaves to the notes, gives

\theta_j := \theta_j + \alpha \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( y^{(i)} - h_\theta\!\left(x^{(i)}\right) \right) x_j^{(i)} .
\tag{3.10}
The generator checks this gradient against finite differences of Equation 3.9.
1:03:06 Ng then put a question to the room. Flip the sign and swap the two terms in the bracket, and Equation 3.10 is character for character the LMS rule of lecture 2 — yet the lecture had just argued that linear regression is wrong for classification. What changed? The hypothesis: h_\theta is now g(\theta^\top x), not \theta^\top x, so the same-looking update does something different. The resemblance is not a coincidence; it holds for the whole family of generalised linear models, and Ng adds that the likeness caused priority disputes in the field’s early history, between people who thought the algorithms were one and people who saw they were not.
1:02:15 Asked whether \ell has local maxima, Ng said no: for logistic regression the log-likelihood is concave, so the only maximum is the global one. The Hessian makes that checkable, \nabla^2 \ell = -\sum_i h(1-h)\, x^{(i)} x^{(i)\top}, a negative sum of outer products, and the generator confirms it is negative semidefinite at two hundred random parameter values. He then gave this as another reason to choose the logistic function over other S-shaped functions — that it guarantees a single maximum. That is true but not unique to it, and the generator says where the property actually comes from. \ell is concave because \log g(z) and \log(1 - g(z)) are both concave in z, and that is a property of the S-curve, not of logistic regression. The normal CDF, which gives probit regression, has it too. The Cauchy CDF, \tfrac12 + \arctan(z)/\pi, an S-curve with heavy tails, does not: its log bends upward in the left tail (Figure 3.3), and on a three-example dataset the resulting log-likelihood has positive curvature at \theta = -0.9, so the argument that rules out local maxima no longer applies. The logistic function is one of a class of choices with a single maximum, not the only one; its claim to being the choice is the generalised-linear-model derivation of lecture 4.






Figure 3.3: Left: three S-shaped choices of g — logistic, the normal CDF (probit) and the Cauchy CDF. Right: their logarithms. The first two bend downward everywhere, which is what makes the log-likelihood concave; the Cauchy curve bends upward in its left tail. Computed by figures/03-locally-weighted-logistic/make_diagrams.py.



Asked 1:04:53 whether logistic regression has an equivalent of the normal equations, Ng’s short answer was no: there is no known closed form for the maximising \theta, so an iterative method is always needed.






NoteIn the official notes



The derivative of the sigmoid, g'(z) = g(z)(1 - g(z)), and the derivation of Equation 3.10 from it are in cs229-notes1, section 5.
crumbs: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression

title: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression
text:
3.7 Newton’s method
1:05:36 Gradient ascent takes baby steps. Ng’s comparison is a problem that needs a hundred or a thousand gradient iterations and only ten of Newton’s method, each of which costs more. To explain it he solves a different problem first: given a function f of a single real \theta, find where f(\theta) = 0. Maximising \ell is such a problem, since at the maximum \ell'(\theta) = 0, so in the end f will be \ell'.
1:08:33 The picture is a sequence of tangents. From the current guess, draw the line tangent to f and follow it down to where it crosses zero; that crossing is the next guess. Repeat, and within a few iterations the guesses sit on the root (Figure 3.4). If the tangent at \theta_0 meets the axis a horizontal distance \Delta away, its slope is the height over the run, f'(\theta_0) = f(\theta_0) /
\Delta, so \Delta = f(\theta_0)/f'(\theta_0) and

\theta^{(t+1)} := \theta^{(t)} - \frac{f\left(\theta^{(t)}\right)}{f'\left(\theta^{(t)}\right)}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\theta^{(t+1)} := \theta^{(t)} - \frac{\ell'\left(\theta^{(t)}\right)}{\ell''\left(\theta^{(t)}\right)} .
\tag{3.11}






Figure 3.4: Newton’s method on f(\theta) = \ell'(\theta), the derivative of a one-parameter logistic log-likelihood on synthetic data. Each tangent from the current guess meets the axis at the next guess; the gap to the root shrinks faster at every step, and by the fifth the guess has all but reached it, marked by the dot. Computed by figures/03-locally-weighted-logistic/make_diagrams.py.



The update uses only where \ell' vanishes, so it is the same whether the goal is a maximum or a minimum — the official notes leave this as a question, and that is the answer. What makes it the right tool here is that \ell is concave, so its only stationary point is the maximum.
1:14:22 The speed has a name, quadratic convergence, which Ng calls “not a great name”. Informally, once Newton’s method is close, the error is roughly squared at each step: an error of 0.01 becomes about 0.0001 and then about 0.00000001, so the number of correct digits doubles per iteration. On the problem of Figure 3.4 the generator’s errors run 0.053, then 0.0014, then 9 \times 10^{-7}. The doubling only starts near the root; from the start at zero the first few steps shrink the error more slowly.
1:16:03 With \theta a vector, the first derivative becomes the gradient and the second the Hessian H, the (n+1) \times (n+1) matrix of second partial derivatives H_{ij} = \partial^2 \ell / \partial\theta_i \partial\theta_j:

\theta := \theta - H^{-1} \nabla_\theta \ell(\theta) .
\tag{3.12}
1:17:22 That matrix is the catch. Each iteration solves a linear system in it, or inverts it, which is nothing for ten parameters and prohibitive for a hundred thousand. Ng’s rule of thumb follows: with ten or fifty parameters he would very likely use Newton’s method and be done in a few iterations; with ten thousand or more he would use gradient descent. The gap in iteration counts can be far larger than his hundred-to-ten. On the tumour data of Figure 3.2, which are nearly separable and so put the maximum far out at \theta \approx (-14.9, 4.4), Newton’s method reaches it to six decimal places in 9 iterations; gradient ascent with the safe fixed step \alpha = 4/\lambda_{\max}(X^\top X) needs about 117,000.






NoteIn the official notes



Newton’s method and its vector form are cs229-notes1, section 7, which adds that Newton’s method applied to the logistic log-likelihood is also called Fisher scoring.
crumbs: 3  Locally Weighted and Logistic Regression

title: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models
text:
4.1 The perceptron
Based on the lecture by Anand Avati — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Lectures 2 and 3 derived linear regression and logistic regression separately, and both ended with the same update, \theta_j := \theta_j + \alpha\,(y - h_\theta(x))\,x_j. This lecture, given by Anand Avati while Ng was away, explains why. Both models are instances of a generalized linear model: pick a distribution for y from the exponential family, let its natural parameter be a linear function of x, and the hypothesis, the likelihood and the update all follow — the same update every time, with only h_\theta changing. The sigmoid, which lecture 3 introduced without justification, falls out of this recipe once y is assumed Bernoulli. The lecture opens with the perceptron, which has the same update for a different reason, and closes with softmax regression, which extends logistic regression to many classes.
1:35 The perceptron replaces logistic regression’s sigmoid with a hard threshold, g(z) = 1 if z \ge 0 and 0 otherwise, so h_\theta(x) = g(\theta^\top x) outputs a label rather than a probability. The update is the one from lecture 3, written for one example at a time:
\theta := \theta + \alpha \left(y^{(i)} - h_\theta(x^{(i)})\right) x^{(i)} .
\tag{4.1}
Avati reads it from the inside out. Since y and h_\theta(x) are both 0 or 1, the bracket can take only three values: 0 when the prediction is right, so nothing happens; +1 when a positive example was called negative; and -1 in the opposite case. A correctly classified example therefore leaves \theta alone, and a misclassified one adds or subtracts a multiple of itself.
7:27 The geometric picture makes that rule look inevitable rather than arbitrary. The decision boundary \theta^\top x = 0 is the line perpendicular to \theta, and \theta^\top x is positive for inputs on the side \theta points toward. We want \theta to have a positive dot product with the positive examples and a negative one with the negative examples — to be similar to the first and dissimilar to the second. When a positive x lands on the wrong side, the most naive way to make \theta more like x is to add a bit of x to it. That rotates \theta toward x, and the boundary rotates with it (Figure 4.1).
The lecture calls \alpha “some small learning rate”, but for the perceptron as usually run it has no effect at all. Starting from \theta = 0, every update adds \pm\alpha
x^{(i)}, so \theta is always \alpha times a sum of examples, and the sign of \theta^\top x — the only thing the prediction depends on — does not depend on \alpha. The generator checks this: on a separable set of 40 points, \alpha = 1 and \alpha = 0.001 make the same 8 mistakes in the same order and finish with parameter vectors that differ by exactly the factor of 1000. The learning rate starts to matter only if it changes over time, which is where a student question led.
12:39 Asked why the perceptron is not used in practice, Avati gives two reasons. It has no probabilistic interpretation: it draws a boundary but says nothing about how confident it is. And it has a famous limitation. The perceptron was celebrated in the late 1950s as a model of the brain (Rosenblatt, 1958); the 1969 book Perceptrons by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert (the lecture remembers it as a paper by Minsky) set out what a single linear threshold unit cannot compute, and the smallest example is XOR — two positive and two negative points at the corners of a square, diagonally opposite, which no line separates. Interest in the model collapsed afterwards.
13:39 A second question asked when to stop training. If the data are linearly separable, the answer is a theorem the lecture does not state: the perceptron stops making mistakes after finitely many updates. If every \lVert x^{(i)} \rVert \le R and some unit vector u separates the classes with margin \gamma, the number of mistakes is at most (R/\gamma)^2, whatever the order of the examples (Novikoff, 1962). On the generator’s 40 points the bound is 55 and the perceptron makes 8. If the data are not separable, it never settles — on XOR it is still making mistakes on all four points in the thousandth pass — so Avati’s practical advice is to anneal: shrink \alpha with every example until \theta stops moving much. That is exactly the case where \alpha is no longer irrelevant, since later updates then count for less than earlier ones.
13:31 Avati also offers the cleanest way to place the perceptron beside the previous lecture: logistic regression is a soft version of it. The step function is the limit of g(kz) = 1/(1 + e^{-kz}) as the slope k grows (Figure 4.2); at k = 12 the two already differ by less than 0.003 everywhere outside |z| < 0.5. What the sigmoid buys in exchange for that softness is a likelihood, and with it everything that follows.

title: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models
text:
4.2 The exponential family
14:53 The exponential family is a class of distributions with convenient mathematics, and it is the bridge to generalized linear models. A distribution belongs to it if its density (or, for discrete y, its probability mass function) can be written

p(y; \eta) = b(y) \exp\!\left( \eta^\top T(y) - a(\eta) \right) .
\tag{4.2}
Avati names each piece. The variable is called y, not x, on purpose: these distributions will model the output of a supervised problem, and x enters only when the model is built. \eta is the natural parameter. T(y) is the sufficient statistic, in the statistician’s sense, but for every distribution in this course T(y) = y, and the lecture tells the reader to make that substitution and move on. b(y) is the base measure, which may depend only on y; and a(\eta) is the log-partition function, which may depend only on \eta. In most of the course y and \eta are scalars; softmax will need a vector \eta.
18:48 The name of a explains its job. Moving it out of the exponent gives p(y;\eta) = b(y)\, e^{\eta T(y)} / e^{a(\eta)}, so e^{a(\eta)} is the normalising constant — the partition function — that makes the density integrate to one, and a(\eta) is its log. That has a consequence worth making explicit, because the lecture says one can choose a, b and T freely as long as the result integrates to one. The condition is not a side constraint on a; it determines it. Once b and T are fixed,

a(\eta) = \log \int b(y)\, e^{\eta T(y)}\, dy ,

with a sum in place of the integral for discrete y. Choosing b and T chooses the family; a comes with it. The generator confirms, for the three families below, that the a(\eta) read off by pattern matching equals this normaliser computed by brute-force summation.
21:44 To show that a familiar distribution is a member, write its density in the usual form and massage it until it matches Equation 4.2. For the Bernoulli with mean \phi, the density \phi^y (1-\phi)^{1-y} — an “if–else written in maths”, as Avati puts it, since it equals \phi when y = 1 and 1 - \phi when y = 0 — becomes, after wrapping it in \exp\log,

p(y; \phi) = \exp\!\left( y \log\frac{\phi}{1-\phi} + \log(1-\phi) \right) .

Matching term by term gives b(y) = 1, T(y) = y, the natural parameter \eta = \log\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}, and a(\eta) = -\log(1-\phi). 26:14 Inverting the expression for \eta gives

\phi = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}} ,
\tag{4.3}
the sigmoid, which arrives here without being asked for. Substituting it into a gives a(\eta) = \log(1 + e^{\eta}), now a function of \eta alone as the definition requires.
28:41 The Gaussian works the same way once its variance is fixed. With \sigma^2 = 1 — and lecture 3 showed that the variance has no effect on the fitted \theta in least squares, so nothing is lost —

\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left( -\tfrac12 (y - \mu)^2 \right)
= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-y^2/2}}_{b(y)} \,
\exp\!\Big( \mu\, y - \underbrace{\tfrac12 \mu^2}_{a(\eta)} \Big),

so \eta = \mu and a(\eta) = \eta^2 / 2. A student asked what happens if the variance is unknown: the Gaussian is still in the family, but \eta becomes a two-dimensional vector and T(y) = (y, y^2). The Poisson, which the lecture uses later without deriving, fits the same mould: \lambda^y e^{-\lambda} / y! has b(y) = 1/y!, \eta = \log \lambda and a(\eta) = e^{\eta}.






NoteIn the official notes



The Bernoulli and Gaussian derivations are cs229-notes1, section 8, which also lists the multinomial, Poisson, gamma, exponential, beta and Dirichlet as members.
