title: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models
section: 4.3 Why the exponential family is convenient
text:
4.3 Why the exponential family is convenient
33:10 Three properties make the family worth the trouble, and Avati states them without proof — they are an exercise in the first problem set. First, maximum likelihood in the natural parameter is a concave problem, so it has no spurious local maxima; the negative log-likelihood, its cost-function form, is convex. Second and third, the log-partition function produces the moments by differentiation:

\mathbb{E}[y; \eta] = \frac{\partial a}{\partial \eta} ,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[y; \eta] = \frac{\partial^2 a}{\partial \eta^2} .
\tag{4.4}
35:08 The point Avati makes about these is practical: computing a mean or a variance normally means integrating against the density, and here it means differentiating a single function, which is far easier. For the Bernoulli, a'(\eta) = 1/(1+e^{-\eta}) = \phi and a''(\eta) = \phi(1-\phi); for the Gaussian, a' = \eta = \mu and a'' = 1; for the Poisson, both derivatives are e^\eta = \lambda, the textbook fact that a Poisson’s mean equals its variance. The generator checks all three by computing a' and a'' by finite differences and the mean and variance by summing over the support. The first property follows from the third: a variance is never negative, so a is convex, and the log-likelihood \log b(y) + \eta y - a(\eta) is linear minus convex, which is concave. 36:06 When \eta is a vector, as for a Gaussian with unknown variance, a student asked how this generalises; the gradient of a gives the mean of T(y) and its Hessian the covariance.
crumbs: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models

title: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models
text:
4.4 Generalized linear models
36:35 A generalized linear model attaches the inputs to an exponential-family distribution, and the lecture frames it as three design choices.

y \mid x; \theta is distributed according to some member of the exponential family, with natural parameter \eta.
The natural parameter is linear in the input: \eta = \theta^\top x, with \theta, x \in \mathbb{R}^n.
At test time, the prediction for x is the mean of that distribution: h_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid x; \theta].

38:36 The first choice is the modelling decision, and it is dictated by what kind of quantity y is. Real-valued outputs such as house prices call for a Gaussian; binary labels for a Bernoulli; counts — non-negative integers, such as the number of visitors to a website — for a Poisson; positive reals such as a volume or the time until an event for a gamma or an exponential. Avati warns that the exponential distribution and the exponential family are different things, though the first is a member of the second, and the list ends with distributions over probabilities, the beta and the Dirichlet, which mostly appear in Bayesian statistics. Whether a GLM is a classifier or a regressor is therefore not a property of GLMs at all: it is decided by the distribution put in the first slot.
42:55 The picture to keep in mind has two halves. On the left is a linear model: x goes in, a learnable \theta multiplies it, and out comes a number. On the right is a distribution from the exponential family, and that number becomes its natural parameter. 45:40 Only \theta is learned. A student asked whether training adjusts the distribution’s parameters, and the answer separates two uses of the word “parameter”: \eta is not a variable that gradient descent touches, it is the output of the linear model for one particular x. Training is maximum likelihood over \theta,

\max_\theta \; \sum_{i=1}^m \log p\!\left(y^{(i)}; \eta = \theta^\top x^{(i)}\right) ,

which is concave in \theta because it is concave in \eta and \eta is linear in \theta.
48:46 Here the recipe pays off. One would expect each new distribution to need its own algebra: write p as a function of \theta^\top x, differentiate, simplify. It does not, because for every GLM built this way the stochastic gradient-ascent update is

\theta_j := \theta_j + \alpha \left( y^{(i)} - h_\theta(x^{(i)}) \right) x^{(i)}_j ,
\tag{4.5}
with h_\theta(x) = a'(\theta^\top x) the only thing that changes. The derivation is one line: the log-likelihood of one example is \log b(y) + \theta^\top x\, y -
a(\theta^\top x), and its gradient is (y - a'(\theta^\top x))\, x, which by Equation 4.4 is (y - h_\theta(x))\, x. This is why linear regression, logistic regression and Poisson regression share an update: the first is the Gaussian GLM with h = \theta^\top x, the second the Bernoulli with h = 1/(1+e^{-\theta^\top x}), the third the Poisson with h = e^{\theta^\top x}. The generator checks the expression against a numerical gradient of the log-likelihood for all three.
“Every GLM” carries a qualification the lecture leaves implicit: the identity holds because the natural parameter itself is set to \theta^\top x. A model that instead connects \theta^\top x to the mean through some other function does not inherit it. The probit model of lecture 3, P(y = 1 \mid x) = \Phi(\theta^\top x) with \Phi the standard normal CDF, is a Bernoulli model with exactly the same shape, and the update that looks right for it — Equation 4.5 with h = \Phi(\theta^\top x) — is not its gradient: at a test point on synthetic data it has the right direction but a length off by 41 percent. That would be harmless if it only rescaled the step, but it also moves the place where the step vanishes. Iterated to convergence, the look-alike update stops at \theta = (-0.200, 0.697), while the probit maximum-likelihood estimate is (-0.210, 0.707). The two links are close, so the error is small, but the algorithm is now solving a different equation from the one it claims to.
50:43 For batch training, sum the update over the examples. Asked about Newton’s method, Avati calls it probably the most common way to fit a GLM, provided the number of features is below a few thousand, so that the Hessian is affordable — the same rule of thumb Ng gave in lecture 3. Concavity is what makes it safe: on a Poisson regression with 200 synthetic counts, Newton’s method reaches the maximum in 7 iterations, at the same \theta that plain gradient ascent eventually finds.
crumbs: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models

title: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models
text:
4.5 Three parametrisations
52:03 The lecture pauses on terminology, because a GLM has three sets of numbers called parameters and they are easy to confuse (Figure 4.3). The model parameters \theta are what learning adjusts. The natural parameter \eta is the linear model’s output, one per example. The canonical parameters are the ones the distribution is usually written in: \phi for a Bernoulli, \mu (and \sigma^2) for a Gaussian, \lambda for a Poisson. The step from \theta to \eta is linear by design choice 2. The step from \eta to the mean has a name: g(\eta) = \mathbb{E}[y;\eta] =
a'(\eta) is the canonical response function, and its inverse g^{-1} is the canonical link function.






Figure 4.3: The three parametrisations of a GLM. Only \theta is learned; \eta = \theta^\top x is the natural parameter of the distribution for one input; the response function g = a' maps it to the mean, and the canonical link g^{-1} maps back.



56:23 With the vocabulary in place, logistic regression stops being a choice and becomes a consequence. For a binary label the natural distribution is the Bernoulli; design choice 3 says the hypothesis is its mean, h_\theta(x) = \phi; and Equation 4.3 says \phi = 1/(1 + e^{-\eta}) with \eta = \theta^\top x. Lecture 3 pulled the logistic function “out of thin air” because it squashes the real line into (0, 1). Here, as Avati puts it, it simply pops out: the sigmoid is the canonical response function of the Bernoulli. The same steps applied to the Gaussian return h_\theta(x) = \theta^\top x, ordinary least squares.
The idea and the name are due to Nelder and Wedderburn (1972), who showed that one fitting procedure covered regression models that had been treated separately.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes1, section 9, constructs the GLM from the same three assumptions and derives ordinary least squares (9.1) and logistic regression (9.2) from them.
crumbs: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models

title: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models
section: 4.6 What the assumptions say about the data
text:
4.6 What the assumptions say about the data
1:00:03 Avati’s last pass over GLMs draws the assumptions as a story about how the data were generated. For the Gaussian, take a line \theta^\top x; at every x, stand a unit-variance Gaussian on the line; and draw each training y from the Gaussian above its x (Figure 4.4, left). Learning runs the story backwards: each choice of \theta is a different line, and maximum likelihood picks the line from whose Gaussians the observed points were most likely to have come.
1:04:50 For classification the story has one more step. The line now gives \eta, which can be any real number; passing it through the sigmoid gives \phi, the probability that y = 1 at that x; and each label is a coin flip with that bias, so labels are mostly 0 where the curve is low and mostly 1 where it is high (Figure 4.4, right). Logistic regression asks which \theta would have produced a sigmoid from which these labels were most likely drawn.






Figure 4.4: The data-generating process each GLM assumes, sampled from the model. Left: Gaussian y around the line \theta^\top x, with the density drawn sideways at three inputs. Right: Bernoulli labels whose probability of being 1 follows g(\theta^\top x). Computed by figures/04-perceptron-glm/make_diagrams.py.
crumbs: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models

title: 4  Perceptron and Generalized Linear Models
text:
4.7 Softmax regression
1:07:58 Softmax regression extends logistic regression to k classes. The notes present it as one more GLM, built on the multinomial distribution; the lecture deliberately takes another route and presents it as cross-entropy minimisation, an interpretation worth having because it is how classifiers with thousands of classes are usually described.
1:11:04 The labels are one-hot vectors: a vector of k zeros with a single 1 in the position of the correct class. Where logistic regression had one parameter vector, softmax has one per class, \theta_1, \dots, \theta_k, which together form an n \times k matrix. For an input x, each class gets a score \theta_c^\top x, called a logit, which can be any real number. 1:16:24 To turn the scores into a probability distribution over classes, exponentiate them, which makes them all positive, and divide by their sum, which makes them add to one:

\hat p(y = c \mid x) = \frac{\exp(\theta_c^\top x)}{\sum_{j=1}^k \exp(\theta_j^\top x)} .
\tag{4.6}
1:19:09 The label is read as a distribution too, p(y), which puts probability 1 on the correct class. Learning makes \hat p look like p by minimising the cross entropy between them,

\mathrm{CE}(p, \hat p) = -\sum_{c=1}^k p(c) \log \hat p(c) = -\log \hat p(y \mid x) ,
\tag{4.7}
where the sum collapses because p is zero everywhere except at the true class y. (The minus sign is missing from the board the first time; it belongs there, since the loss has to be non-negative.) Figure 4.5 follows one example through the pipeline: an input whose true class is triangle but which scores highest for square receives \hat p(\text{triangle}) = 0.19 and a loss of 1.67. The last expression in Equation 4.7 is the negative log-likelihood of a multinomial model, so the lecture’s route and the notes’ arrive at the same objective. Its gradient for class c is (\hat p(c \mid x) - \mathbb{1}\{y = c\})\, x, the same “prediction minus truth, times input” shape as Equation 4.5; and with k = 2 the softmax probability of class 1 is exactly 1/(1 + e^{-(\theta_1 - \theta_2)^\top x}), logistic regression with \theta = \theta_1 - \theta_2.






Figure 4.5: Softmax regression for one example. The logits are exponentiated, then normalised into a distribution \hat p over the three classes; the label is a one-hot distribution on triangle, and the cross-entropy loss is -\log \hat p(\text{triangle} \mid x). Computed by figures/04-perceptron-glm/make_diagrams.py.



1:12:53 That two-class reduction exposes something the board picture hides. The lecture draws one line per class, \theta_c^\top x = 0, with each class’s own region on the positive side, as though each \theta_c carves out its class independently. But Equation 4.6 is unchanged if the same vector c is added to every \theta_j: the factor e^{c^\top x} cancels between numerator and denominator. Only the differences \theta_i - \theta_j matter, so the decision boundary between two classes is (\theta_i - \theta_j)^\top x = 0, and the individual lines \theta_c^\top x = 0 can be moved anywhere without changing a single prediction (Figure 4.6). On the fitted model in the figure, the board’s picture — exactly one positive score, and it belongs to the predicted class — holds on only 45 percent of the plotted square even before any shift. This redundancy is why the official notes give softmax only k - 1 parameter vectors and fix \theta_k = 0: the k-th vector adds nothing a shift could not remove.






Figure 4.6: The same softmax model with every \theta_c shifted by one common vector. The shaded decision regions are identical; the dashed lines \theta_c^\top x = 0 move to entirely different places, because they carry no meaning on their own. Fitted by gradient descent in figures/04-perceptron-glm/make_diagrams.py.









NoteIn the official notes
