title: 5  GDA and Naive Bayes
text:
5.1 Two ways to build a classifier
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Every algorithm so far has been discriminative: it models p(y \mid x) directly, or maps x to a label, and learns by searching for a boundary between the classes. This lecture introduces the other family. A generative learning algorithm models what each class looks like, p(x \mid y), together with how common each class is, p(y), and classifies a new example by asking which class model it fits better. Gaussian discriminant analysis (GDA) does this with a Gaussian per class and turns out to imply exactly the logistic form of lecture 3 — but with stronger assumptions, which help when data are scarce and hurt when they are wrong. Naive Bayes does it for text, with one binary feature per word and an assumption Ng calls flatly untrue, and still makes a serviceable spam filter.
1:09 Ng starts from the tumour data again, two features and two classes. Logistic regression initialises a line and lets gradient descent move it until it separates the malignant from the benign examples; it is searching for a boundary. A generative algorithm never looks for a boundary. It takes the malignant tumours alone and fits a model of where they live — roughly inside one ellipse — then does the same for the benign tumours. When a new patient arrives, it compares their features against the two models and picks the class whose model the patient resembles more.
3:56 In symbols, a discriminative algorithm learns p(y \mid x), or a function from x to labels. A generative one learns p(x \mid y) — what the features are like given the class — and the class prior p(y), the odds that a tumour is malignant before the patient has even been examined. 5:50 Bayes’ rule converts those two into the quantity a classifier needs:
p(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{p(x \mid y = 1)\, p(y = 1)}{p(x)},
\qquad
p(x) = p(x \mid y = 1)\, p(y = 1) + p(x \mid y = 0)\, p(y = 0) .
\tag{5.1}
35:49 If all that is wanted is the most likely label, the denominator can be skipped. p(x) does not depend on y, so
\arg\max_y\, p(y \mid x) = \arg\max_y\, p(x \mid y)\, p(y) ,
and implementations often never compute p(x) at all. Ng’s aside on notation is worth keeping: \min_z (z - 5)^2 is 0, the smallest value attained, while \arg\min_z (z-5)^2 is 5, the input that attains it.

title: 5  GDA and Naive Bayes
text:
5.2 The multivariate Gaussian
9:46 GDA needs a Gaussian over vectors. A random vector z \in \mathbb{R}^n is distributed \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma), with mean vector \mu \in \mathbb{R}^n and covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, symmetric and positive definite, if its density is

p(z; \mu, \Sigma) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2} \lvert\Sigma\rvert^{1/2}}
\exp\!\left( -\tfrac12 (z - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (z - \mu) \right),
\tag{5.2}
where \Sigma = \mathbb{E}[(z - \mu)(z - \mu)^\top]. Ng’s view is that almost nobody memorises this formula until they have used it enough times, and that pictures teach it better. 12:00 Ng projected a sequence of three-dimensional plots; Figure 5.1 recomputes them as contour maps, every panel at the same four density heights so that panels can be compared.






Figure 5.1: Contours of two-dimensional Gaussians with mean zero, each panel drawn at the same four density heights. Shrinking \Sigma makes the bump taller and narrower — at 0.6I the highest level appears; enlarging it lowers the peak until only the lowest level remains. Positive off-diagonal entries tilt the contours along z_1 = z_2, negative ones the other way; the dashed line is the leading eigenvector of \Sigma. Computed by figures/05-gda-naive-bayes/make_diagrams.py.



With \mu = 0 and \Sigma = I — the standard Gaussian — the contours are circles. Multiplying \Sigma by 0.6 shrinks the spread, and because the density must still integrate to one, it grows taller: in two dimensions the peak 1/(2\pi\lvert\Sigma
\rvert^{1/2}) scales by 1/0.6, from 0.159 to 0.265. Doubling \Sigma halves it. Raising the off-diagonal entries makes z_1 and z_2 positively correlated, and the circles stretch into ellipses along the diagonal, narrower as the entry rises to 0.8; negative entries tilt them the other way. One coincidence in the figure is a useful check on the formula: the off-diagonal-0.8 Gaussian has the same peak as 0.6I, because both have \lvert\Sigma\rvert = 0.36. Changing \mu moves the bump without changing its shape.
16:26 A student asked whether the columns of \Sigma point in meaningful directions. Ng’s answer is that single columns are not worth reading in isolation — the matrix is symmetric — but its eigenvectors are: they are the principal axes of the elliptical contours, the long axis belonging to the largest eigenvalue. For the off-diagonal-0.8 panel the eigenvalues are 1.8 and 0.2, with the long axis along (1, 1)/\sqrt2. This is the idea principal component analysis builds on later in the course.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes2, section 1.1, defines the multivariate normal and shows the same family of surface plots.

title: 5  GDA and Naive Bayes
section: 5.3 The GDA model and its fit
text:
5.3 The GDA model and its fit
19:02 Gaussian discriminant analysis assumes that each class’s features are Gaussian, with a mean of their own and a covariance they share, and that the label is a coin flip:

\begin{aligned}
y &\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\phi), \\
x \mid y = 0 &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \Sigma), \\
x \mid y = 1 &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \Sigma) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.3}
For generative models Ng drops the convention x_0 = 1, so x \in \mathbb{R}^n. The parameters are \phi \in (0, 1), \mu_0, \mu_1 \in \mathbb{R}^n and \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}. 20:24 A shared \Sigma is a choice, not a necessity — separate \Sigma_0 and \Sigma_1 are perfectly reasonable — and the reason for it becomes clear when the decision boundary is drawn.
23:05 The fit is where the two families part. Logistic regression chose \theta to maximise the conditional likelihood \prod_i p(y^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}; \theta). GDA maximises the joint likelihood,

L(\phi, \mu_0, \mu_1, \Sigma) = \prod_{i=1}^m p\!\left(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\right)
= \prod_{i=1}^m p\!\left(x^{(i)} \mid y^{(i)}\right) p\!\left(y^{(i)}\right) .

26:56 Taking logs, differentiating and setting the derivatives to zero gives closed forms — the derivation is a problem-set exercise, and Ng gives the answers along with the intuition for each:

\begin{aligned}
\phi &= \frac1m \sum_{i=1}^m 1\{y^{(i)} = 1\}, &
\mu_k &= \frac{\sum_i 1\{y^{(i)} = k\}\, x^{(i)}}{\sum_i 1\{y^{(i)} = k\}}, \\
\Sigma &= \frac1m \sum_{i=1}^m \left(x^{(i)} - \mu_{y^{(i)}}\right)\left(x^{(i)} - \mu_{y^{(i)}}\right)^\top .
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.4}
The indicator 1\{\cdot\} is 1 when its argument is true and 0 when it is false. The estimate of \phi is the fraction of malignant tumours in the training set, as the maximum-likelihood bias of a coin is the fraction of heads. Each mean is the average of its class’s feature vectors: the indicator in the numerator keeps only that class’s examples, the one in the denominator counts them. And \Sigma is the average outer product of each example’s deviation from its own class mean — one covariance fitted to both clouds at once. Ng is careful to say that this intuition is not the derivation; the derivation is calculus on \log L. The generator takes the shortcut of checking the result instead: on 80 synthetic points, 500 random perturbations of the closed-form estimates all lower the joint log-likelihood.
There is no iteration anywhere in Equation 5.4: fitting GDA is computing two means and a covariance. That will matter when Ng explains why GDA is still worth using.






NoteIn the official notes



The model and its maximum-likelihood estimates are cs229-notes2, section 1.2.

title: 5  GDA and Naive Bayes
text:
5.4 GDA’s boundary is logistic
37:07 On the same two-feature data, Ng shows logistic regression’s line migrating over about twenty iterations of gradient descent, then GDA fitting one Gaussian to each class and classifying by Bayes’ rule. Both produce straight boundaries, and the two lines are close but not the same (Figure 5.2, left).






Figure 5.2: Left: GDA with a shared covariance on synthetic data, with the fitted Gaussians’ contours at one and two standard deviations, the GDA boundary, and logistic regression’s boundary on the same 80 points. Right: classes with very different spreads, each given its own covariance; the boundary becomes a conic, here a hyperbola. Computed by figures/05-gda-naive-bayes/make_diagrams.py.



39:42 A student asked why the model uses two means but one covariance. With a shared \Sigma the boundary is linear, which is what many problems want. With \Sigma_0 and \Sigma_1 the model also works, but the boundary is no longer a line, and Ng says the parameter count roughly doubles. That holds for the covariance part, and for the whole model only when n is large: counting \phi and the means too, a shared covariance needs 1 + 2n + n(n+1)/2 parameters and two covariances 1 + 2n + n(n+1), a ratio of 1.38 at n = 2, 1.72 at n = 10 and 1.96 at n = 100. 58:13 Asked later what the posterior looks like with separate covariances, Ng’s recollection was that it is still a logistic function, but with quadratic terms inside it. That is right: the log-odds becomes a quadratic in x, and its zero set is a conic (Figure 5.2, right).
41:02 The connection to logistic regression is the lecture’s most interesting property of GDA. Fix the parameters and, for a single feature, evaluate p(y = 1 \mid x) by Bayes’ rule at point after point along the axis. 43:31 Far to the left, almost any point must have come from the class-0 Gaussian, so the posterior is near 0; far to the right it is near 1; at the midpoint between the two means, Ng says, you cannot tell, so it is 0.5. Joining the dots gives an S-shaped curve, and 47:13 it is exactly a sigmoid (Figure 5.3). With a shared covariance the quadratic terms of the two Gaussians’ exponents cancel in the log-odds, leaving

p(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\theta^\top x + \theta_0)}},
\qquad
\theta = \Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1 - \mu_0),
\quad
\theta_0 = -\tfrac12\left(\mu_1^\top \Sigma^{-1}\mu_1 - \mu_0^\top \Sigma^{-1}\mu_0\right) + \log\frac{\phi}{1-\phi} .
\tag{5.5}
The generator confirms the identity at 200 random points against Bayes’ rule computed directly.






Figure 5.3: The posterior along one feature. Two unit-variance class densities (thin), five training points from each class, and p(y = 1 \mid x) computed by Bayes’ rule (thick): a sigmoid crossing 0.5 midway between the means when \phi = 0.5, and at x = 1.69 when \phi = 0.2. Computed by figures/05-gda-naive-bayes/make_diagrams.py.



The midpoint claim holds only when the classes are equally likely. The last term of \theta_0 is the prior log-odds, and it shifts the curve. For one feature the crossing point is

x_{1/2} = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\log\frac{1 - \phi}{\phi} ,

so with means 0 and 2, unit variance and a prior of 0.2 on class 1, the boundary moves from x = 1 to x = 1.69: a rarer class needs stronger evidence. On a malignant/benign problem, where \phi is usually far from one half, this term is anything but negligible.
47:53 So both algorithms end up with a sigmoid in x, but they do not end up with the same sigmoid. GDA’s \theta is a byproduct of fitting the joint likelihood; it is not the \theta that maximises the conditional likelihood, which is what logistic regression computes. On the 80 points of Figure 5.2, logistic regression reaches a conditional log-likelihood of -29.73, and the \theta GDA implies scores -29.97 on the same objective. Neither is wrong; they are answering different questions.

title: 5  GDA and Naive Bayes
text:
5.5 Which one to use
48:57 Ng frames the comparison as an implication that runs only one way. If Equation 5.3 holds, then p(y = 1 \mid x) is logistic — that was the previous section. But assuming that p(y = 1 \mid x) is logistic says nothing about x \mid y being Gaussian. 53:08 Ng’s counterexample: if x \mid y = 0 and x \mid y = 1 are Poisson with means \lambda_0 and \lambda_1, the posterior is again logistic, since the log-odds is x \log(\lambda_1/\lambda_0) - (\lambda_1 - \lambda_0) + \log\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}, linear in x. The same holds, Ng adds, whenever the two class-conditionals are the same exponential family differing only in the natural parameter, with T(x) = x. GDA therefore makes the stronger assumptions and logistic regression the weaker.
54:46 The principle that follows is one Ng says will recur throughout the course. Stronger modelling assumptions, when they are roughly right, let an algorithm learn from less data, because the assumptions are information it no longer has to extract from examples. When they are wrong, they cost accuracy that more data cannot recover. Weaker assumptions are more robust: if you do not know whether the data are Gaussian or Poisson or something else from the family, logistic regression is correct in all those cases.
Figure 5.4 puts numbers on this. In a world built to satisfy GDA’s assumptions, GDA’s average test error is lower than logistic regression’s from 10 to about 100 training examples, by up to half a percentage point, and both converge to the Bayes error of 0.201 — though at 6 examples logistic regression, with a slight ridge penalty to keep it finite on separable samples, is ahead. With two features the advantage is real but small; Ng and Jordan (2002) analysed the same trade-off for naive Bayes against logistic regression and found it grows with the number of features: the generative model can approach its (higher) asymptotic error with a number of examples logarithmic in n, the discriminative one with roughly linear. In the Poisson world GDA is misspecified, and still it is slightly ahead at 6 and 10 examples — the assumptions are wrong but informative. The curves cross near 25 examples, and from there logistic regression pulls ahead, reaching 0.160 at 400 examples against GDA’s 0.168. With 20,000 examples logistic regression sits at the Bayes error of 0.158 while GDA stalls at 0.162, an error no amount of data removes.






Figure 5.4: Mean test error over 400 training sets at each size; the vertical axes do not start at zero. Left, data satisfying GDA’s assumptions: GDA is slightly ahead from 10 to about 100 examples. Right, Poisson classes, where logistic regression is correctly specified and GDA is not: GDA’s error levels off above the Bayes error. Computed by figures/05-gda-naive-bayes/make_diagrams.py.



56:13 Ng’s own practice follows from this. With large datasets, which is most problems now, Ng would usually reach for logistic regression, because data can make up for what the algorithm was not told. There are two sources of knowledge, in Ng’s account: the assumptions you build in and what is learned from data. With plenty of the second you can afford fewer of the first. 56:56 When Ng does use GDA today it is more for computation than accuracy — two means and a covariance, no iterative optimisation.
58:45 Should one test whether the data are Gaussian before using GDA? In practice, Ng says, if you have enough data to run a statistical test and believe it, you probably have enough to use logistic regression. What people actually do is plot the data, rule out GDA if it is obviously non-Gaussian, and otherwise — with, say, fifty healthcare records — use judgment, perhaps by asking doctors whether the distribution is plausibly Gaussian. 59:47 This leads Ng to a broader view: the field has somewhat overhyped big data. More data almost never hurts, but many applications have a hundred examples rather than a million, and there the designer’s skill — including the choice of what to assume — matters far more: on a million-image benchmark many teams do well, while with a hundred examples the skilled teams do much better than the rest. 1:02:42 Asked whether the comparison carries over to more than two classes, Ng says it does, with softmax regression as the discriminative counterpart.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes2, section 1.3, makes the same comparison and states that GDA is asymptotically efficient when its assumptions hold.

title: 5  GDA and Naive Bayes
text:
5.6 Naive Bayes
1:04:08 GDA needs continuous features. Naive Bayes is a generative algorithm for discrete ones, and Ng builds it around spam filtering, though the same method applies to any text classification — the lecture mentions eBay sorting free-text listings into product categories.
1:05:08 The first question is how to turn an e-mail into a feature vector. Take a list of words — conceptually the dictionary, from “a” and “aardvark” to “zymurgy”, in practice the 10,000 most frequent words in your own training set, so that “CS229” makes the list even though no dictionary has it — and set x_j = 1 if word j appears in the e-mail and 0 if not. So x \in \{0, 1\}^n with n = 10{,}000.
1:09:28 Modelling p(x \mid y) directly is hopeless: a distribution over all 2^{10{,}000} binary vectors needs 2^{10{,}000} - 1 parameters for each class, a number with 3,011 digits. 1:10:00 Naive Bayes assumes that the x_j are conditionally independent given y. The chain rule of probability, which is always true, writes the joint as p(x_1 \mid y)\, p(x_2 \mid x_1, y)\, p(x_3 \mid x_1, x_2, y)
\cdots; the assumption drops every conditioning variable except y,

p(x_1, \dots, x_n \mid y) = \prod_{j=1}^n p(x_j \mid y) .
\tag{5.6}
In words: once you know whether an e-mail is spam, learning that it contains “buy” tells you nothing about whether it contains “aardvark”. Figure 5.5 shows this as the graphical model Ng sketches for those who have met them.






Figure 5.5: The naive Bayes assumption as a graphical model: the label points to every word indicator, and no word indicator points to another.



1:11:53 Ng does not defend the assumption as true. It is not, mathematically — words in an e-mail are obviously correlated — but, as with data that are not quite Gaussian, it may be not so wrong that you cannot get away with it. Where it does bite is worth seeing. Suppose a word appears in 60 percent of spam and 10 percent of other mail, and a second feature happens to be an exact copy of it (in real text, a word and its plural, or “click” and “here”). The true posterior from seeing the word, with equal priors, is 0.857; the second feature adds no information, but naive Bayes multiplies its likelihood in again and reports 0.973. Correlated features are counted as independent evidence, which makes naive Bayes overconfident even when its decisions are reasonable.
1:13:46 The parameters are \phi_{j \mid y=1} = p(x_j = 1 \mid y = 1), the chance that word j appears in a spam e-mail, \phi_{j \mid y=0} for non-spam, and the prior \phi_y = p(y = 1) — 2n + 1 numbers, 20,001 for the 10,000-word vocabulary, instead of a number with three thousand digits. 1:15:00 Maximising the joint likelihood, exactly as for GDA, gives counts:

\phi_y = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m 1\{y^{(i)} = 1\},
\qquad
\phi_{j \mid y=1} = \frac{\sum_i 1\{x^{(i)}_j = 1,\; y^{(i)} = 1\}}{\sum_i 1\{y^{(i)} = 1\}} ,
\tag{5.7}
and the same with y = 0. Of all the spam e-mails in the training set, what fraction contain “buy”? That fraction is \phi_{\text{buy} \mid y=1}. Prediction multiplies these numbers by Equation 5.6 and applies Bayes’ rule.
Naive Bayes has the same relationship to logistic regression that GDA has. Its log-odds is a sum over words of terms that depend on x_j only through x_j \in \{0, 1\}, so it is exactly linear: \log \frac{p(y=1 \mid x)}{p(y=0 \mid x)} = b + w^\top x with w_j = \log \frac{\phi_{j \mid 1}(1 - \phi_{j \mid 0})}{\phi_{j \mid 0}(1 - \phi_{j \mid
1})}. The generator checks this on every input of a six-word vocabulary. Naive Bayes is a linear classifier whose weights are set by counting rather than by optimisation.
1:17:32 Ng’s verdict is that naive Bayes is “not too horrible”, that logistic regression does better almost all the time, and that naive Bayes is nonetheless very efficient: fitting is counting, prediction is multiplying, and the counts can be updated as new labelled mail arrives without refitting anything. This is the regime Ng and Jordan studied: naive Bayes reaches its own, higher, asymptotic error with fewer examples. 1:18:14 Ng flags one flaw that makes the version above “nearly work”: zeros. If a word never appears in any training e-mail, its estimate is 0 in both classes, an e-mail containing it gets p(x \mid y) = 0 under both, and the posterior is 0/0. Even a word seen only in non-spam drives the spam probability of any e-mail containing it to exactly zero, however spammy the rest. The fix, Laplace smoothing, opens the next lecture.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes2, section 2, develops naive Bayes for the same spam example; Laplace smoothing (2.1) and the multinomial event model for text (2.2) come with lecture 6.

title: 6  Support Vector Machines
text:
6.1 Laplace smoothing
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Naive Bayes, as lecture 5 left it, breaks the first time a word turns up that the training set never contained: every class gets probability zero and the posterior is 0/0. The fix is to add one to every count, and that rule, Laplace smoothing, is what a Bayesian with a uniform prior would compute anyway. With smoothing in place the lecture builds a second naive Bayes for text, the multinomial event model, which counts how often each word occurs instead of only whether it does, and then steps back to argue that an algorithm this cheap is the right first thing to build. The second half starts the support vector machine. Before kernels, an SVM is a linear classifier chosen for one property: of all the lines that separate the training data, it takes the one that stays furthest from every example. Most of the work is in defining “furthest” so that it cannot be gamed.
4:42 Ng’s example of the zero problem is a word that is new to your inbox but not to the world. Suppose “NIPS”, the machine learning conference, is word 6017 of a 10,000-word vocabulary, and nobody has yet e-mailed you about it. The maximum likelihood estimates from lecture 5 are fractions of e-mails containing the word, so both \phi_{6017 \mid y=1} and \phi_{6017 \mid y=0} come out as 0. 8:03 Months later your project team writes about submitting to NIPS. The product \prod_j p(x_j \mid y) now contains a factor of zero for both classes, and the classifier’s posterior is 0 / (0 + 0). The division by zero is the visible symptom; the underlying error, Ng says, is statistical — estimating the probability of something as zero because you have not seen it yet.
9:58 He sets spam aside to make the point with a smaller example. One season, Stanford’s football team played four out-of-state games — Wake Forest, Oregon State, Arizona and, Ng adds for the room, Caltech — and lost all four. You followed them to every one. What is the chance they win the next? Maximum likelihood counts wins over games played, 0/4 = 0: absolute certainty of a loss, which is unkind and also unreasonable. 11:59 Laplace smoothing pretends you saw one more of each outcome than you did — one extra win and one extra loss — so the estimate becomes (0 + 1)/(4 + 2) = 1/6.
12:58 The rule is not arbitrary. Laplace derived it for the probability that the sun rises tomorrow: having seen it rise every day so far, you should be very confident but not certain. Ng compresses the justification into one sentence, which is worth unpacking. If the unknown win probability p is given a uniform prior on [0, 1] and you observe s wins in n games, the posterior is proportional to p^s (1 - p)^{n - s}, and its mean is
\mathbb{E}[p \mid \text{data}]
= \frac{\int_0^1 p \cdot p^s (1-p)^{n-s}\, dp}{\int_0^1 p^s (1-p)^{n-s}\, dp}
= \frac{s + 1}{n + 2} .
\tag{6.1}
That is exactly the add-one estimate. It is also the posterior predictive probability that the next game is a win, which is the quantity a classifier needs, so “Bayesian optimal” in the lecture means this: the posterior mean, the best guess under squared error. The generator integrates the posterior numerically for 0 wins in 4 and recovers 1/6 to six decimal places, then repeats the check for other counts.
14:22 For a variable with k possible values the rule adds one to each count and k to the denominator,
\hat p(x = j) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^m 1\{x^{(i)} = j\} + 1}{m + k} ,
\tag{6.2}
which still sums to one over the k values and never returns exactly 0 or 1. 15:14 For the binary word features of naive Bayes, k = 2:
\phi_{j \mid y=1} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^m 1\{x^{(i)}_j = 1,\; y^{(i)} = 1\} + 1}{\sum_{i=1}^m 1\{y^{(i)} = 1\} + 2} ,
and the same for y = 0. A word never seen in training now gets a small positive probability in both classes, the zero factor disappears, and the NIPS e-mail is classified on the strength of its other words. Ng’s assessment of the resulting filter is measured — “not a great spam classifier but it’s not terrible either” — and its virtue is that training is counting and prediction is multiplying.

title: 6  Support Vector Machines
text:
6.2 Discretising a continuous feature
17:58 Naive Bayes extends past binary features with no change to its structure. Ng’s example goes back to houses, now as a classification problem — will this house sell within 30 days? — with floor area as a feature. Cut the area into buckets (under 400 square feet, 400 to 800, 800 to 1,200, over 1,200), let x_j \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\} record which bucket a house falls in, and model p(x_j \mid y) as a multinomial over four values instead of a Bernoulli over two. The factorisation p(x \mid y) = \prod_j p(x_j \mid y) is unchanged, the estimates are still counts, and Laplace smoothing adds k = 4 to each denominator. 19:29 His rule of thumb when discretising is ten buckets; it “often seems to work well enough”, and the board had room for four.

title: 6  Support Vector Machines
text:
6.3 The multinomial event model
20:17 For text specifically there is a better variant, and Ng motivates it with what the binary representation throws away. Take the spam e-mail “drugs buy drugs now”, with “buy”, “drugs” and “now” at positions 800, 1600 and 6200 of the vocabulary. 21:40 Under the representation so far, x is a 10,000-dimensional binary vector with three ones. The word “drugs” appears twice, and the vector records it once; the e-mail “drugs buy now” maps to exactly the same x (Figure 6.1). A word that a spammer repeats is arguably stronger evidence than one that appears once, and the binary model cannot see the difference.






Figure 6.1: The e-mail “drugs buy drugs now” under the two event models. Above, one binary entry per dictionary word; below, one dictionary index per word of the e-mail, so the repeated word is represented twice.



22:34 The alternative represents an e-mail of n words as a vector of length n, whose jth entry x_j \in \{1, \dots, 10{,}000\} is the dictionary index of the jth word: here x = (1600, 800, 1600, 6200). The length now varies from e-mail to e-mail, n_i for the ith training example, which also answers a property of text Ng points out — e-mails can be five words long or a thousand, and the binary representation forces both into one fixed-length vector.
23:57 The names are, in Ng’s words, “very confusing, very horrible names”, but they are the ones the field uses. The binary model is the multivariate Bernoulli event model — 10,000 coin tosses, one per word, each deciding whether that word appears. The new one is the multinomial event model. 24:49 Ng credits the naming to his friend Andrew McCallum, and the paper that compares the two, by McCallum and Nigam, says it set out to clear up exactly this confusion.
25:12 The generative story is that the sender first decides spam or not, with probability \phi_y, and then draws each word of the e-mail independently from one distribution over the vocabulary that depends on the class. So

p(x, y) = p(y) \prod_{j=1}^{n} p(x_j \mid y) ,

which looks identical to lecture 5’s naive Bayes and means something different: the product now runs over the words of the e-mail rather than over the dictionary, and each factor is a multinomial over 10,000 outcomes rather than a coin toss. The parameters are \phi_y and \phi_{k \mid y=c} = p(x_j = k \mid y = c), the chance that a word in a class-c e-mail is word k. 28:05 Ng puts a question to the room — “the chance of word blank being blank” — and the answer, any position being word k, exposes the hidden assumption: the distribution does not depend on j. The first word of a spam e-mail is “drugs” with the same probability as the third, which is why j does not appear on the left-hand side.
29:41 The maximum likelihood estimates are again counts, now over word occurrences instead of e-mails, and with Laplace smoothing they are

\phi_{k \mid y=0} =
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} 1\{x^{(i)}_j = k,\; y^{(i)} = 0\} + 1}
     {\sum_{i=1}^m 1\{y^{(i)} = 0\}\, n_i + 10{,}000} .
\tag{6.3}
In English: pool every word of every non-spam e-mail, and ask what fraction of them are word k. If the non-spam e-mails contain 100,000 words in all and “drugs” is 200 of them, the unsmoothed estimate is 200/100{,}000. 31:59 Ng asks the room what to add to the denominator for smoothing, and the answer is the number of values x_j can take: the vocabulary size, 10,000, not two.
33:44 A student asks what to do with a word that is not in the dictionary at all. Either drop it, or map every out-of-vocabulary word to one special token, conventionally UNK, which then gets a probability like any other word. The second keeps the information that the e-mail contained rare words, which can itself be evidence.
The multinomial model is still a linear classifier, now in word counts. Taking the log of Bayes’ rule, the log-odds of spam is

\log \frac{p(y=1 \mid x)}{p(y=0 \mid x)}
= \log \frac{\phi_y}{1 - \phi_y} + \sum_{k=1}^{10{,}000} c_k \log \frac{\phi_{k \mid y=1}}{\phi_{k \mid y=0}} ,

where c_k is the number of times word k occurs in the e-mail. The generator confirms this against Bayes’ rule on 200 random e-mails. A repeated word now adds its weight once per occurrence, which is precisely the information the Bernoulli model discarded. McCallum and Nigam’s comparison on five corpora found the Bernoulli model competitive with small vocabularies and the multinomial model usually better with large ones, averaging a 27 percent reduction in error — “much better”, as the lecture puts it, for the typical text problem.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes2, section 2.1, gives Laplace smoothing for the binary naive Bayes model; section 2.2 writes out the multinomial event model’s likelihood and both smoothed estimates.

title: 6  Support Vector Machines
section: 6.4 Build something quick and dirty first
text:
6.4 Build something quick and dirty first
35:26 Naive Bayes is rarely the most accurate choice — logistic regression usually beats it — so the question is what it is for. Ng’s answer is a piece of working advice that appears in no PDF. 36:55 If your goal is to make a learning algorithm work for an application, rather than to invent a new algorithm, start by implementing something simple and fast, train it, look at how it fails, and let the failures decide what to build next. 38:11 His analogy is software: nobody writes 10,000 lines of code and compiles them for the first time at the end; you write a module, test it, and build up. A complicated learning system designed in full before any of it runs is the same mistake.
39:07 The spam filter shows why. Ng started a conference on e-mail and anti-spam, and his example list of promising ideas is long. Spammers misspell deliberately — “m0rtgage”, or the word broken up with slashes — so a filter keyed to words sees an unknown token where a person sees “mortgage”; one of his students published on mapping such spellings back to words. Spammers spoof headers to hide where mail came from. You could fetch the URLs in an e-mail and analyse the pages behind them. 40:59 Each of these is three to six months of work, and at the start you cannot know which one matters. So build the crude filter, then read the e-mails it gets wrong. If many of them are deliberate misspellings, you now have evidence that the misspelling problem is worth months; if few are, “don’t bother” — and you have saved the months. This is error analysis, which the course returns to later.
42:06 That is the niche for naive Bayes and GDA. Neither will give the best accuracy; logistic regression, SVMs and neural networks almost always do better. But both are non-iterative — counting, or computing means and covariances — and short to write, so they are a fast way to get the first system running. Ng’s advice for course projects follows: do not spend weeks designing; get a data set and apply something simple, logistic regression or naive Bayes rather than a neural network, and go from there.
44:26 A student points to a weakness of the word features themselves: “mother” and “father”, or “one” and “two”, are entirely unrelated indices to naive Bayes, which has no way to know that similar words should behave similarly. Ng agrees and names the fix from neural networks, word embeddings, which represent each word by a vector learned so that related words land close together. Because the embedding comes with that knowledge built in, a classifier built on it needs fewer labelled examples. The course leaves the topic to CS230 and CS224N.

title: 6  Support Vector Machines
text:
6.5 Why support vector machines
46:22 The SVM enters with a picture: two classes in the plane whose boundary is clearly curved. Logistic regression and GDA, as they stand, draw straight lines. 47:06 You can get a curve out of logistic regression by inventing features — map (x_1, x_2) to \phi(x) = (x_1, x_2, x_1^2, x_2^2, x_1 x_2, x_1^3, \dots) and fit the same linear model to \phi(x) — and with the quadratic terms the boundary can become an ellipse (Figure 6.2). The generator fits both models to the same data: on the raw features logistic regression misclassifies a third of the training set, with the quadratic terms 12 percent.






Figure 6.2: Logistic regression on the same data with and without hand-picked features. With x_1, x_2 alone the boundary must be a straight line and it gives up; with the squares and the product added, the boundary is an ellipse around the inner class.



48:05 The trouble is choosing the features. An ellipse needs quadratic terms; Ng admits he would not know which features produce the irregular boundary he drew, and nobody wants to guess between \sqrt{x_1} and (x_1 x_2)^{2/3}. The SVM’s promise is to map x into a much higher-dimensional feature space — 51:15 hundreds of thousands of dimensions, or infinitely many — and fit a linear classifier there, which is non-linear back in the original space, without anyone choosing the features by hand. That is the kernel idea of lecture 7.
48:48 Ng’s other reason is practical. The SVM is “turnkey”: mature software solves its optimisation problem reliably, without a learning rate to tune or a convergence to babysit. He is explicit that for many problems neural networks are now more effective, and equally explicit that practice uses a much wider set of tools than the press coverage of deep learning suggests.
49:57 The road map has three stages: the optimal margin classifier for data that a straight line can separate, which this lecture starts; kernels, which run it in huge feature spaces; and a modification for data that cannot be separated. The first stage needs two definitions of margin.

title: 6  Support Vector Machines
text:
6.6 The functional margin
54:50 Ng motivates the margin with logistic regression. The classifier predicts 1 when \theta^\top x \ge 0, but a correct prediction can be confident or marginal. If y^{(i)} = 1 we would like \theta^\top x^{(i)} \gg 0, so that g(\theta^\top x^{(i)}) is close to 1; if y^{(i)} = 0 we would like \theta^\top x^{(i)} \ll 0. A classifier for which both hold on every example is correct and confident.
1:00:02 The SVM changes notation to make the algebra cleaner. Labels are y \in \{-1, +1\}, the hypothesis outputs a hard \pm 1 instead of a probability, g(z) = 1 if z \ge 0 and -1 otherwise, and the intercept is pulled out of the parameter vector: h_{w,b}(x) = g(w^\top x + b), with b playing the role of \theta_0 and w of \theta_1, \dots, \theta_n, and no x_0 = 1 convention.
1:03:36 The functional margin of the hyperplane (w, b) with respect to the example (x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}) is

\hat\gamma^{(i)} = y^{(i)} \left( w^\top x^{(i)} + b \right) .
\tag{6.4}
The label folds the two hopes into one: if y^{(i)} = 1 we want w^\top x^{(i)} + b large and positive, if y^{(i)} = -1 large and negative, and either way we want \hat\gamma^{(i)} large. 1:06:30 Its sign alone already says something: \hat\gamma^{(i)} > 0 exactly when the example is classified correctly. 1:07:46 For the whole training set, the SVM takes the worst case, \hat\gamma = \min_i \hat\gamma^{(i)} — how well the classifier does on the example it does worst on. That is a harsh notion, and it makes sense for now only because this lecture assumes the data are linearly separable.
1:09:01 The functional margin has a flaw Ng calls cheating. Multiply w and b by 2, or 10, and every \hat\gamma^{(i)} multiplies by the same factor, yet the boundary w^\top x + b = 0 is the same line and every prediction is unchanged (the generator checks this for factors of 2, 10 and 1/17, Ng’s choices). So “make the functional margin large” is not a goal at all: any separating classifier achieves an arbitrarily large one. 1:10:00 The fix is to normalise — require \lVert w \rVert = 1, or equivalently divide w and b by \lVert w \rVert — and the freedom to rescale (w, b) without changing the classifier turns out to be useful later rather than only a nuisance.

title: 6  Support Vector Machines
text:
6.7 The geometric margin
1:11:29 The geometric margin is the normalised version, and it has a picture. The line w^\top x + b = 0 splits the plane into the half where the classifier predicts +1 and the half where it predicts -1, and the vector w is perpendicular to the line, pointing into the positive half. 1:12:33 For a correctly classified positive example A, the geometric margin \gamma^{(i)} is its Euclidean distance to the line: the length of the segment from A to the nearest point B on the boundary (Figure 6.3).






Figure 6.3: The geometric margin of one example. The boundary is w^\top x + b = 0 with w = (2, 1) and b = -2; w is perpendicular to it; the positive example A sits at distance \gamma^{(i)} from its foot B on the line.



1:13:49 Ng states the formula and leaves the derivation to the notes; it is short enough to give. B is A moved back along the unit normal by the distance \gamma^{(i)}, so B = x^{(i)} - \gamma^{(i)} w / \lVert w \rVert, and B lies on the line, so w^\top B + b = 0. Solving gives \gamma^{(i)} = (w^\top x^{(i)} + b)/\lVert w \rVert for a positive example, and including the label makes it hold for negative ones too:

\gamma^{(i)} = y^{(i)} \left( \frac{w^\top x^{(i)} + b}{\lVert w \rVert} \right)
= \frac{\hat\gamma^{(i)}}{\lVert w \rVert} .
\tag{6.5}
For the point A = (2, 1.6) in Figure 6.3, the functional margin is 3.6 and the geometric margin 3.6 / \sqrt 5 \approx 1.61; multiply w and b by ten and the functional margin becomes 36 while the geometric margin stays at 1.61. The geometric margin is the functional margin with the cheat removed. The generator checks Equation 6.5 against an explicit projection onto the hyperplane for 500 random hyperplanes and points in three dimensions. 1:15:23 As before, the training set’s geometric margin is the worst case, \gamma = \min_i \gamma^{(i)}.

title: 6  Support Vector Machines
text:
6.8 The optimal margin classifier
58:15 Ng drew the motivating picture well before the definitions. Two lines both separate a training set perfectly; one passes close to a few of the examples, the other keeps a wide berth from both classes, and the second “looks much better”. The geometric margin is what “looks better” means: the first line’s worst example is barely on the right side, the second line’s is far from it (Figure 6.4).






Figure 6.4: Two lines that both separate the training set. The dotted one passes within 0.10 of the closest example; the solid one, the maximum-margin separator, keeps a geometric margin of 0.77 from both classes. The dashed lines are where w^\top x + b = \pm 1, and the circled examples on them are the support vectors.



1:16:28 The optimal margin classifier chooses w and b to maximise the geometric margin of the training set. 1:17:59 Ng poses it as a problem in three unknowns, \gamma, w and b:

\max_{\gamma, w, b} \; \gamma
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
\frac{y^{(i)} (w^\top x^{(i)} + b)}{\lVert w \rVert} \ge \gamma ,
\quad i = 1, \dots, m .
\tag{6.6}
Every example must have geometric margin at least \gamma, and \gamma is pushed as high as the constraints allow, so at the optimum \gamma equals the worst example’s margin and that worst margin is as large as it can be.
1:19:03 In this form the problem is not convex, so there is no guarantee that a local method finds the global optimum. 1:19:13 Ng states, and leaves the steps to lecture 7 and the notes, that a few rewrites turn it into an equivalent convex problem: minimise \frac12 \lVert w \rVert^2 subject to every functional margin being at least 1. His one-line intuition is that the margin is the functional margin divided by \lVert w \rVert, so a smaller w means a smaller divisor and a larger geometric margin. Off-the-shelf solvers handle the convex form, and for separable data its solution is the optimal margin classifier — “really a baby SVM”, which kernels will grow up.
The solution has a property the picture already shows. In Figure 6.4 only two examples touch the dashed lines; they are the support vectors, and the separator depends on them alone. The generator finds this separator in two independent ways. It searches over directions for the one that leaves the widest gap between the classes, and then checks the result against the optimality conditions of the convex problem: every functional margin is at least 1, the two closest examples have functional margin exactly 1, and w = \sum_i \alpha_i y^{(i)} x^{(i)} over those two examples alone, with both \alpha_i > 0. That last fact — the solution is built from a few training examples — is where lecture 7 begins.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes3, sections 1–4, defines the functional and geometric margins with the same notation and gives the full chain of rewrites from Equation 6.6 to the convex quadratic program.

title: 7  Kernels
text:
7.1 From the largest margin to the smallest w
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
A support vector machine is the optimal margin classifier of lecture 6 run in a feature space of enormous, possibly infinite, dimension. That sounds impossible to compute, and the lecture’s argument is a chain of three observations that make it cheap. The optimal w is always a weighted sum of the training examples. Once w is written that way, the training problem and the prediction rule touch the data only through inner products \langle x^{(i)}, x^{(j)} \rangle. And for some very large feature maps \phi, the inner product \phi(x)^\top \phi(z) can be computed directly from x and z in time proportional to their own dimension — that shortcut is a kernel. Ng calls the SVM one of his favourite algorithms because it is “very turnkey”: the optimisation is convex and good packages solve it. The lecture ends by dropping the assumption that the data are separable and with kernels designed for inputs that are not vectors at all.
1:13 Lecture 6 posed the optimal margin classifier as: choose \gamma, w and b to maximise \gamma, subject to every example having geometric margin at least \gamma. 5:31 Ng spends a minute on why that maximises the worst margin. If three examples had geometric margins 17, 2 and 5, the set’s margin is 2, and the only way to raise \gamma under the constraints is to raise the margin of whichever example is lowest. Pushing \gamma up as far as it goes is the same as maximising \min_i \gamma^{(i)}.
6:33 The step to a tractable problem uses the freedom that made the functional margin useless in lecture 6. Take w = (2, 1) and b = -2: the boundary 2x_1 + x_2
= 2 crosses the axes at (1, 0) and (0, 2), and so does the boundary for 10w and 10b, or for w/10 and b/10. Because rescaling (w, b) changes nothing about the classifier, we may pick the scale, and 8:49 the convenient choice is the one that makes the worst functional margin exactly 1: \min_i y^{(i)}(w^\top x^{(i)} +
b) = 1. Then the geometric margin is \gamma = \hat\gamma / \lVert w \rVert = 1 /
\lVert w \rVert, maximising it is minimising \lVert w \rVert, and minimising the smooth \frac12 \lVert w \rVert^2 has the same solution:
\min_{w, b} \; \frac12 \lVert w \rVert^2
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
y^{(i)} \left( w^\top x^{(i)} + b \right) \ge 1 ,
\quad i = 1, \dots, m .
\tag{7.1}
This is a convex quadratic objective under linear constraints — a quadratic program, with one global optimum and reliable solvers. On lecture 6’s example set the solution has \lVert w \rVert = 1.293, so \gamma = 1/\lVert w \rVert = 0.773, the same margin lecture 6’s generator found by searching over directions; the two examples that touch the margin have functional margin exactly 1 and every other example more.

title: 7  Kernels
text:
7.2 The representer theorem
10:34 So far x has been two- or a hundred-dimensional. The goal is feature vectors with a hundred trillion dimensions, or infinitely many, where w cannot even be stored. 11:07 The way through is to assume that w is a linear combination of the training examples,

w = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i \, y^{(i)} x^{(i)} ,
\tag{7.2}
with the labels y^{(i)} = \pm 1 written in by convention because they make later algebra tidier. 11:57 Ng presents this as an assumption but stresses that it is not one: the representer theorem proves that the optimal w always has this form, so nothing is lost. He skips the proof as long and involved and gives two intuitions.
13:11 The first is from gradient descent. Run stochastic gradient descent for logistic regression from \theta = 0. Each update adds a multiple of one training example, \theta := \theta + \alpha \, (y^{(i)} - h_\theta(x^{(i)}))\, x^{(i)} (this \alpha is the learning rate, unrelated to the \alpha_i above). By induction, \theta is a linear combination of training examples after every step, however many steps you take; 15:22 batch gradient descent is the same, and so is gradient descent on the SVM’s own objective. The generator runs 300 SGD steps in five dimensions on three examples and finds \theta within 10^{-15} of the span of those three vectors.
16:09 The second is geometric. 16:50 The vector w is perpendicular to the decision boundary: it fixes the boundary’s orientation, and b slides the boundary along it. 18:39 Now suppose the inputs have three features but every training example has x_3 = 0, so the data lie in the x_1 x_2-plane. Then, Ng says, w_3 should be 0 — w should lie in the space the examples span.
That second intuition is worth sharpening, because as stated it is not true of every separator. With all x_3 = 0, the term w_3 x_3 is zero on every training example, so any value of w_3 classifies the training set identically: the generator takes the SVM’s w and sets w_3 = 5, and every margin constraint still holds. What forces w_3 = 0 is the objective. A non-zero w_3 adds w_3^2 to \lVert w \rVert^2 and buys nothing in the constraints, so the minimum-norm solution drops it. That is the real content of the representer theorem: among all the w that fit the data equally well, minimising \lVert w \rVert^2 (or, in general, any loss plus a squared-norm regulariser) picks one in the span of the data.

title: 7  Kernels
text:
7.3 Everything is an inner product
20:34 Substitute Equation 7.2 into Equation 7.1. Since \lVert w \rVert^2 = w^\top w, the objective becomes

\frac12 \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_i \alpha_j \, y^{(i)} y^{(j)}
\left\langle x^{(i)}, x^{(j)} \right\rangle ,

and the constraints become y^{(i)} \big( \sum_j \alpha_j y^{(j)} \langle x^{(j)},
x^{(i)} \rangle + b \big) \ge 1, where \langle x, z \rangle = x^\top z is the inner product. 24:13 The point is where the inputs now appear: nowhere except inside inner products. Whatever the dimension of x, the problem is stated in terms of the m \times m table of inner products between training examples.
25:14 The form actually solved in practice goes one step further. Ng skips the derivation, which uses Lagrange duality, and writes down the result, the dual optimisation problem:

\max_\alpha \; W(\alpha) = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i
- \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^m y^{(i)} y^{(j)} \alpha_i \alpha_j
\left\langle x^{(i)}, x^{(j)} \right\rangle
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
\alpha_i \ge 0, \quad \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i y^{(i)} = 0 .
\tag{7.3}
b has dropped out, to be recovered afterwards from any example with \alpha_i > 0. Two facts about Equation 7.3 go beyond the lecture and are worth having. First, it is not merely a simplification of the substituted problem: when there are more examples than dimensions, many different \alpha give the same w, and the dual picks out particular ones — non-negative, and zero for every example that is not on the margin. Those with \alpha_i > 0 are the support vectors. Second, its optimal value equals the primal’s: on lecture 6’s data the generator solves Equation 7.3 by sequential minimal optimisation, the algorithm in the official notes, and finds W(\alpha^*) = \frac12
\lVert w^* \rVert^2 = 0.8364, with only 2 of the 24 \alpha_i non-zero, and the resulting w and b agree with lecture 6’s direction search to five decimal places.
27:05 Prediction is an inner product too:

h(x) = g\!\left( w^\top x + b \right)
= g\!\left( \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i y^{(i)} \left\langle x^{(i)}, x \right\rangle + b \right) .
\tag{7.4}
28:20 Once the \alpha_i are stored, both training and prediction need nothing but inner products of inputs — and since most \alpha_i are zero, prediction sums only over the support vectors.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes3, section 5, derives Lagrange duality and the KKT conditions, and section 6 applies them to obtain Equation 7.3 and the formula for b. The representer theorem, with a proof for general losses, is in the supplementary notes on the representer theorem, section 2.

title: 7  Kernels
text:
7.4 The kernel trick
28:42 Ng gives the recipe in four steps. First, write the whole algorithm in terms of inner products \langle x, z \rangle. Second, choose a feature map \phi from the original inputs to a higher-dimensional space — 30:12 a house’s floor area x could become (x, x^2, x^3, x^4), or area and bedrooms (x_1, x_2) could become all their products up to some degree. Third, find a way to compute

K(x, z) = \phi(x)^\top \phi(z) ,
\tag{7.5}
the kernel function, cheaply. Fourth, replace every \langle x, z \rangle in the algorithm by K(x, z). 32:19 The algorithm is then running on \phi(x), in the high-dimensional space, without ever forming \phi(x). Forming it is what would be expensive: Ng has seen problems with a billion features, and even 100,000 makes every vector operation costly.
33:55 A student asks about the no-free-lunch theorem, and Ng’s answer frames why this works at all. The theorem — Wolpert’s form of it for supervised learning shows that, averaged over all possible target functions, no learning algorithm has lower off-training-set error than any other — says that in the worst case learning does not work. Ng finds it less useful than fascinating, because the problems we meet are not drawn adversarially: “the universe is not that hostile toward us”, and an inductive bias such as “the boundary is smooth in some feature space” tends to pay off.

title: 7  Kernels
text:
7.5 Polynomial kernels
34:42 The first example shows the saving. Let x \in \mathbb{R}^n and let \phi(x) list every product x_i x_j — for n = 3, the nine terms x_1 x_1, x_1
x_2, x_1 x_3, x_2 x_1, \dots, x_3 x_3, duplicates included. 35:38 So \phi(x)
\in \mathbb{R}^{n^2}: with n = 10{,}000 that is 10^8 features, and computing \phi(x)^\top \phi(z) explicitly takes order n^2 time. 37:18 But

\left( x^\top z \right)^2
= \Big( \sum_{i=1}^n x_i z_i \Big) \Big( \sum_{j=1}^n x_j z_j \Big)
= \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n (x_i x_j)(z_i z_j)
= \phi(x)^\top \phi(z) ,
\tag{7.6}
and the left-hand side takes order n time: one inner product of n-vectors, then one squaring. The middle expression is the explicit computation — march down both lists of products, multiply, add — and the identity says that the cheap computation gives the same number.
41:11 Adding a constant, K(x, z) = (x^\top z + c)^2, corresponds to appending the first-degree terms and a constant to the features: \phi(x) now also contains \sqrt{2c}\, x_1, \dots, \sqrt{2c}\, x_n and c. The constant c sets the relative weight of the linear terms against the quadratic ones. 42:29 More generally, K(x, z) = (x^\top z + c)^d is still order n to compute and corresponds to a \phi(x) containing every monomial of degree up to d — terms like x_1 x_2 x_5
x_{17} x_{29} or x_1 x_2^2 x_3 x_{18} when d = 5 — each with a weight that involves c and a multinomial coefficient. The generator builds these explicit feature vectors for d = 2 and 3 and confirms that their inner product equals the kernel on 200 random pairs.
42:56 Ng gives the number of distinct monomials as \binom{n+d}{d}, which the generator confirms by enumeration, and then glosses it as “roughly (n+d)^d, very roughly”. The binomial coefficient is the right count; the gloss is high by about a factor of d!. For n = 10{,}000 and d = 5, \binom{n+d}{d} \approx 8.3 \times
10^{17} while (n+d)^d \approx 1.0 \times 10^{20}, a ratio of 120 = 5!. The point survives — the feature space grows like n^d/d!, astronomically, while the kernel costs order n for every d.
44:23 This is what Ng means by the SVM: the optimal margin classifier plus the kernel trick. Choose a kernel, solve Equation 7.3 with K(x^{(i)}, x^{(j)}) in place of the inner products, and predict with Equation 7.4 likewise; the computation scales with the dimension of x, not of \phi(x). 45:51 A student asks whether a kernel belongs to one feature map. Essentially yes: up to trivial changes such as permuting the features, which leave every inner product unchanged, a different feature map needs a different kernel.

title: 7  Kernels
text:
7.6 Seeing the lift
47:09 To show what this does geometrically, Ng plays a short visualisation by Udi Aharoni. Red and blue points in the plane cannot be separated by a line; a feature map lifts them into three dimensions, where a plane separates them; and the plane, viewed back in the original plane, cuts out an ellipse. Figure 7.1 does the same thing one dimension lower, so it fits on a page. The positives sit between the negatives on a line, so no single threshold separates them. Map each x to \phi(x) = (x, x^2) and the points land on a parabola, where the SVM finds a straight line; pulled back to the original line, that straight line becomes the two thresholds x = -1.30 and x = 1.40.






Figure 7.1: A one-dimensional data set lifted by \phi(x) = (x, x^2). On the left no threshold separates the classes; on the right the SVM separates them with a straight line, and the four circled support vectors fix it. Pulled back to the line, the linear boundary is the pair of thresholds marked on the left.



49:10 The boundary is linear in a high-dimensional space and very non-linear in the original one. 49:27 A student asks whether the data must be linearly separable in that high-dimensional space; so far the derivation has pretended so, and the soft margin below removes the assumption.

title: 7  Kernels
text:
7.7 Which functions are kernels
50:02 Ng’s working intuition is that a kernel measures similarity. An inner product is large when two vectors point the same way and small when they point in unrelated directions, so K(x, z) should be large when x and z are alike and small when they are not. 51:19 By that standard, here is a function pulled “out of the air”:

K(x, z) = \exp\!\left( -\frac{\lVert x - z \rVert^2}{2\sigma^2} \right) ,
\tag{7.7}
close to 1 when x and z are near each other and close to 0 when they are far apart. 52:13 Can it be used? Only if some \phi makes K(x, z) = \phi(x)^\top
\phi(z); the whole derivation assumed so, and a K without such a \phi breaks it — the optimisation problem may no longer correspond to any classifier at all.
53:01 One necessary condition is immediate: K(x, x) = \phi(x)^\top \phi(x) \ge
0. 53:27 A stronger one comes from taking any m points x^{(1)}, \dots,
x^{(m)} and forming the kernel matrix (or Gram matrix) K_{ij} = K(x^{(i)},
x^{(j)}). For any vector z,

z^\top K z
= \sum_i \sum_j z_i \, \phi(x^{(i)})^\top \phi(x^{(j)}) \, z_j
= \sum_k \Big( \sum_i z_i \, \phi_k(x^{(i)}) \Big)^2
\ge 0 ,

so a valid kernel always produces a positive semidefinite kernel matrix (and a symmetric one, since inner products are). 57:21 Mercer’s theorem says the converse holds too: K is a valid kernel if and only if, for every finite set of points, the kernel matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite. Ng proves only the direction above and states the other.
The similarity intuition is a good guide but not a test, and the gap is easy to fall into. “Two points are similar if they are within 1.5 of each other” sounds like a reasonable similarity, K(x, z) = 1\{|x - z| < 1.5\}. At the three points 0, 1, 2 its kernel matrix has eigenvalues 1 + \sqrt 2, 1 and 1 - \sqrt 2 < 0; the vector z = (1, -\sqrt 2, 1) gives z^\top K z \approx -1.66. No feature map produces that matrix, so it is not a kernel, and the SVM built on it can fail to be a convex problem. The generator checks this alongside the Gaussian kernel, whose kernel matrix on 25 random points has every eigenvalue non-negative.
59:13 Equation 7.7 is valid, and it is called the Gaussian kernel. 59:36 The most widely used kernel is in fact the linear kernel, K(x, z) =
x^\top z with \phi(x) = x — the SVM with no feature map at all — and the Gaussian is next. 1:00:11 Its feature space is infinite-dimensional, and Ng describes it as containing every monomial, of every degree, with the high-degree ones given smaller weight. That can be made exact in one dimension:

e^{-\frac{(x - z)^2}{2\sigma^2}}
= e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{z^2}{2\sigma^2}} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{1}{k!}\left(\frac{xz}{\sigma^2}\right)^k
= \sum_{k=0}^\infty \phi_k(x) \phi_k(z) ,
\qquad
\phi_k(x) = e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}} \frac{x^k}{\sigma^k \sqrt{k!}} .

The weight on the degree-k feature falls like 1/\sqrt{k!}, which is the “smaller weighting” in concrete form. The generator truncates the sum: with \sigma = 1, on sixteen pairs of inputs drawn from [-1.5, 1.5], three features reproduce the kernel to within 0.26, twelve to within 3 \times 10^{-6}, and twenty to rounding error.
Figure 7.2 shows the Gaussian kernel at work on data no polynomial of low degree separates cleanly: a disc of one class inside a ring of the other. The decision function f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i y^{(i)} K(x^{(i)}, x) + b is a sum of bumps centred on the support vectors, 22 of the 110 examples, and its zero level set is the closed curve between the classes.






Figure 7.2: A Gaussian-kernel SVM (\sigma = 0.8, C = 10) on a disc of positives inside a ring of negatives. The solid curve is f(x) = 0, the dashed curves f(x) = \pm 1, and the circled points are the support vectors. Far from every training example f(x) falls back to b, which is why a dashed curve also appears near the corners.

title: 7  Kernels
text:
7.8 Kernelising other algorithms
1:01:20 The kernel trick is not specific to the SVM. Any algorithm that can be written in terms of inner products of inputs can be kernelised, and Ng lists linear regression, logistic regression, every generalised linear model, the perceptron (which the problem sets kernelise) and, later in the course, principal components analysis. Linear regression in an infinite-dimensional feature space is a perfectly well-defined computation. 1:03:07 In practice, though, the trick is applied overwhelmingly to SVMs and much less often elsewhere.
1:01:26 Ng credits the popularisation to Vladimir Vapnik and Corinna Cortes. The history is slightly split between two papers. The kernelised maximum-margin classifier was introduced by Boser, Guyon and Vapnik in 1992; Cortes and Vapnik’s “Support-vector networks” of 1995 added the soft margin of the next section.

title: 7  Kernels
text:
7.9 The soft margin
1:04:07 Mapping to a high-dimensional space makes data much more separable, but a separating boundary is not always wanted. If the data are slightly noisy, a boundary that classifies every training example correctly may be contorting itself around a few mislabelled ones. 1:05:17 The \ell_1-norm soft margin SVM relaxes the constraint that every functional margin be at least 1, allowing a slack \xi_i \ge 0 per example and charging for it:

\min_{w, b, \xi} \; \frac12 \lVert w \rVert^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^m \xi_i
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
y^{(i)} \left( w^\top x^{(i)} + b \right) \ge 1 - \xi_i ,
\quad \xi_i \ge 0 .
\tag{7.8}
1:06:49 Recall that a positive functional margin means a correct prediction; the hard-margin SVM demands more, a functional margin of at least 1. A slack of \xi_i = 0.5 lets example i get away with functional margin 0.5; a slack above 1 lets it be misclassified. At the optimum each slack is as small as its constraint allows, \xi_i = \max(0,\, 1 - y^{(i)}(w^\top x^{(i)} + b)), so Equation 7.8 is the same as minimising \frac12\lVert w \rVert^2 plus C times the hinge loss summed over the training set — a form worth recognising, since it puts the SVM beside logistic regression as a regularised loss. 1:07:55 The examples on the margin have functional margin exactly 1, Ng notes, because otherwise the line could be moved to widen the margin; examples further away have larger ones.
1:08:59 His second reason for the soft margin is robustness. The hard-margin classifier maximises the worst-case margin, so a single outlier — technically leaving the data separable — can swing the boundary dramatically. Figure 7.3 measures this on lecture 6’s data with one positive example added near the negatives. The hard-margin normal turns by 43^\circ to squeeze past the outlier and the margin shrinks from 0.77 to 0.30. With C = 0.1, adding the same outlier turns the soft-margin boundary by under 4^\circ; the outlier simply sits on the wrong side, with slack \xi = 1.21.






Figure 7.3: The same data with one positive outlier near the negatives. Left, the hard-margin SVM turns its boundary by 43^\circ to separate the outlier. Right, a soft margin with C = 0.1 barely moves: the dotted line is the solution with the same C and the outlier removed.



How much protection the soft margin gives depends on C, which is the part to take away from the figure. With C = 1 on the same data the outlier still turns the boundary by 27^\circ: the slack is so expensive that the solution prefers to move. C trades the width of the margin against the training errors it will tolerate, and 1:12:58 choosing it is a bias–variance question that lecture 8 takes up.
1:11:34 Repeating the dual derivation for Equation 7.8 changes exactly one thing: the constraint \alpha_i \ge 0 becomes the box 0 \le \alpha_i \le C. The generator checks the consequences on its solution, which are the optimality conditions in the notes: examples with 0 < \alpha_i < C sit exactly on the margin, every example with positive slack has \alpha_i = C, and examples beyond the margin have \alpha_i
= 0. 1:12:19 Ng’s practical remark is that in the early days of SVMs solving this problem was itself a research worry, much as matrix inversion once was; today’s packages solve it and you need not think about it. The generator’s solver is a version of sequential minimal optimisation, the coordinate method of the official notes, which updates two \alpha_i at a time so that \sum_i \alpha_i y^{(i)} = 0 stays satisfied.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes3, section 8, derives the dual of the soft-margin problem and its KKT conditions, and section 9 presents the SMO algorithm, including the closed-form update for a pair of \alpha_i under the box constraint.

title: 7  Kernels
section: 7.10 Kernels for inputs that are not vectors
text:
7.10 Kernels for inputs that are not vectors
1:13:39 In practice the polynomial kernel (x^\top z)^d works well, and Ng now calls the Gaussian kernel the one most used; earlier he gave that place to the linear kernel, and between them the two are the usual first choices. 1:14:05 One of the early proof points for SVMs was handwritten digit recognition: unroll an image into a vector of pixel intensities and train an SVM on it. On the classic MNIST benchmark this was, in Ng’s words, a very surprising result, and polynomial-kernel SVMs appear beside the convolutional networks of the time in the comparison of classifiers by LeCun et al. 1:15:07 Ng’s summary is that SVMs were for a time the best algorithm on it, with convolutional networks pulling ahead in more recent years.
1:15:25 Much of the inventive work on SVMs, Ng says, has gone into designing kernels, and his example is a protein classifier. A protein is a variable-length sequence of amino acids, of which there are 20 (Ng uses the letters A to Z on the board for convenience). 1:17:01 One feature vector for a sequence counts every possible run of four amino acids — how many times AAAA occurs, then AAAB, and so on to the end of the list — so that \phi(x) has 20^4 = 160{,}000 entries (with Ng’s 26 letters it would be 456,976). 1:18:20 Writing it out is expensive, but K(x, z) = \phi(x)^\top \phi(z) can be computed directly from the two sequences. Ng describes a dynamic programme reminiscent of Knuth–Morris–Pratt string matching; the kernel as published, the spectrum kernel of Leslie, Eskin and Noble, builds a suffix tree and computes it in time linear in the two sequences’ lengths. Only the four-letter runs that actually occur contribute, so a dictionary of counts per sequence is already enough, and the generator confirms that this gives the same number as the explicit 160,000-dimensional inner product.
1:19:35 If the inputs are histograms — the demographic make-up of two countries, say — one kernel sums the bin-by-bin minimum of the two histograms, K(h, g) = \sum_k \min(h_k, g_k), a direct measure of their overlap. It is a valid kernel on non-negative histograms, and the proof is one line: \min(a, b) =
\int_0^\infty 1\{t < a\}\, 1\{t < b\}\, dt, an inner product of two indicator functions. The generator’s kernel matrix on twenty random histograms has, as it must, no negative eigenvalue. The general lesson is the recipe of the kernel trick read backwards: for an unusual kind of input, ask what similarity you would want between two examples, then make sure it is an inner product in some space, and the SVM machinery applies unchanged.

title: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation
text:
8.1 Bias and variance
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Every learning algorithm so far has come with a knob — the degree of a polynomial, the bandwidth \tau of locally weighted regression, the constant C of the soft-margin SVM — and this lecture is about how to set it. The answer has two parts. The first is a diagnosis: a model that is too simple underfits, which Ng calls high bias, and a model that is too flexible overfits, which he calls high variance. The second is a procedure: never judge the knob by training error, because training error always prefers the most flexible model; judge it on data the model was not fitted to, held out once (a dev set) or in rotation (cross-validation). Between the two sits regularisation, the one-line change Ng says he uses more often than almost any other technique, which lets a large model behave like a small one.
Ng opens by saying that bias and variance is “easy to learn, hard to master”: former PhD students of his report that their understanding of it kept deepening for years after the course. The formal learning theory that used to accompany it — error decomposition, uniform convergence, VC dimension — has moved to the Friday discussion section, which has its own chapter. This lecture keeps the working concepts.
4:53 Ng draws the same six houses three times, size against price, with prices that rise and then level off. A straight line, h_\theta(x) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x, catches the trend but not the bend. A quadratic follows the data well. A fifth-order polynomial has six parameters for six points, so it passes through every one of them exactly — and is plainly a worse model of house prices than the quadratic, wiggling between the points and swinging off wildly beyond the outermost ones.
7:04 The line underfits, and Ng says it has high bias. The word has nothing to do with bias in the social sense; it means that the algorithm arrived with a strong preconception — that price is linear in size — and that the preconception is false, so no amount of data will talk it out of the wrong shape. 8:04 The fifth-order polynomial overfits, and has high variance. The name comes from a thought experiment Ng returns to several times: suppose a friend collects their own six houses, from the same market, with slightly different noise. The quadratic fitted to the friend’s data will look much like yours. The fifth-order polynomial will be some completely different curve, because it is fitting the noise, and the noise is what changed.
That thought experiment is easy to run, and Figure 8.2 runs it twelve times. The straight lines agree with one another and are all wrong in the same way; that shared error is the bias. The quintics agree only where the data pin them down and scatter everywhere else; that spread is the variance. Averaged over 4,000 friends, the linear fit at the middle of the range misses the true price by -0.081 (it sits below the bend) with a standard deviation across datasets of only 0.025; the quadratic is unbiased to three decimals with standard deviation 0.037. Near the small end of the range, at x = 0.02, the quintic is unbiased too, but its standard deviation is 0.35 — five times the quadratic’s 0.070 and larger than most house prices on the plot.
10:06 Classification has the same three regimes. Logistic regression on the raw features x_1, x_2 draws a straight boundary through data that clearly want a curve; with a handful of hand-chosen features such as x_1^2, x_2^2, x_1x_2 it draws a sensible curve; with a great many features, or an SVM with a rich kernel, it can draw a contorted boundary that classifies every training example correctly and generalises poorly.
9:30 The reason this matters is practical. Ng’s workflow is to train something quick and dirty first, because a learning algorithm “almost never works the first time”, and then to ask whether it is suffering from bias or from variance, since the remedies for the two are different and often opposite. The diagnostics come in lecture 12. Here the lecture turns to the most common remedy for variance.
27:40 A student asks whether “underfit” and “high bias”, “overfit” and “high variance”, are just synonyms. To a first approximation, Ng says, yes. The exception he flags is a model that has both problems at once: very complex, and still not fitting the data well — a contorted boundary that misses the obvious structure. It is rarer, but it happens.

title: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation
text:
Figure 8.1: The same six houses fitted three ways. The line misses the curvature; the quadratic is “just right”; the fifth-degree polynomial interpolates every point and makes absurd predictions between and beyond them. The data are synthetic: a concave quadratic plus Gaussian noise.











Figure 8.2: Twelve friends’ datasets, each of six houses drawn from the same curve (dashed). Degree-1 fits (left) cluster tightly around the wrong answer: high bias, low variance. Degree-5 fits (right) are right on average but disagree wildly, worst beyond the outermost houses, where several leave the plotted range: low bias, high variance.
crumbs: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation

title: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation
text:
8.2 Regularisation
13:56 Take the least-squares objective and add one term:

\min_\theta \; \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^{m} \bigl(y^{(i)} - \theta^\top x^{(i)}\bigr)^2 \;+\; \frac{\lambda}{2}\,\lVert\theta\rVert^2 .
\tag{8.1}
The second term is the regularisation term, and \lambda \ge 0 sets its strength; whether it is written \lambda or \lambda/2 is a matter of which derivations one wants to come out tidy. It gives the algorithm an incentive to keep the parameters small. That is all there is to implement, and Ng warns against underestimating it on that account: it is “deceptively simple” and one of the techniques he reaches for most.
15:17 Put the fifth-order polynomial back on the six houses. With \lambda = 0 we have the interpolating curve of Figure 8.1, whose wiggles need large coefficients of opposite sign. A moderate \lambda makes those coefficients expensive, and the fit relaxes into something like the quadratic — in Figure 8.3, \lambda = 0.1, which is what leave-one-out cross-validation (Section 8.5) picks for these six points. 16:47 At the other extreme, \lambda = 10^{100}, every parameter is crushed to zero and the hypothesis becomes h(x) = 0. Sweeping \lambda from huge to zero therefore interpolates smoothly between a function that is far too simple and one that is far too complex, and somewhere in between is the one we want.
One detail of the board version deserves a correction in the margin. h = 0 is the limit only if the intercept \theta_0 is penalised along with everything else, as \lVert\theta\rVert^2 written literally does. In practice \theta_0 is usually left out of the penalty — there is no reason to prefer prices near zero — and then the limit is the constant h(x) = \bar y, the mean price. The generator checks both limits, and Figure 8.3 draws both. The distinction will reappear in a moment with a probabilistic meaning.






Figure 8.3: A fifth-degree polynomial on the six houses with three penalties. λ = 0 interpolates. λ = 0.1, chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation, behaves like the quadratic. λ = 10¹⁰⁰ flattens everything: to the mean price if the intercept is left out of the penalty (solid), to zero if it is penalised too (dashed).



18:15 The same move regularises any model fitted by maximum likelihood. For logistic regression, or any generalised linear model, we were maximising the log-likelihood \ell(\theta), so the penalty is subtracted:

\max_\theta \; \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log p\bigl(y^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}; \theta\bigr) \;-\; \lambda \lVert\theta\rVert^2 .
\tag{8.2}
19:23 Ng then answers a question the kernels lecture left hanging. An SVM with a Gaussian kernel works in an infinite-dimensional feature space; why does it not overfit like crazy? Because its objective is to minimise \lVert w\rVert^2, which is a regularisation term in all but name. 26:10 Asked later whether the protection comes from the small number of support vectors or from the small norm, he says the formal argument rests on the norm: the class of functions that separate the data with a large margin has low complexity, in the precise sense of a low VC dimension that the discussion section defines. An algorithm could have many support vectors and still enjoy that protection.
21:08 His favourite illustration is text classification. Take 100 labelled emails and a 10,000-word vocabulary, one binary feature per word. Unregularised logistic regression has 10,000 parameters and 100 examples, and it will badly overfit; on data like this the training set is almost always linearly separable, and on separable data the likelihood has no maximum: scaling up any separating \theta always increases it, so \lVert\theta\rVert grows without bound. (On a toy with ten features and four examples, gradient ascent’s \lVert\theta\rVert is 3.9 after 100 steps, 5.2 after 1,000 and 6.7 after 10,000, and would keep going.) For least squares the same situation shows up as a singular X^\top X: with more features than examples it has rank at most m, and the normal equations have no unique solution. Adding \lambda I makes the matrix invertible for any \lambda > 0, which is the algebraic face of the same fix. Ng’s experience is that regularised logistic regression on such data “will usually outperform” naive Bayes.
22:50 He attaches a rule of thumb. Without regularisation, it is nice to have at least as many examples as parameters, and he is personally only comfortable with roughly ten times as many. With regularisation, 10,000 parameters on 100 examples can make a perfectly decent classifier.
23:36 Why one \lambda for every parameter rather than a separate \lambda_j for each, as a student asks? Because then there are 10,000 more numbers to choose, and choosing them is as hard as choosing the parameters in the first place; the selection procedures later in this lecture work for one or a few hyperparameters, not for thousands. 24:41 The student’s follow-up is the reason a single \lambda is reasonable at all: the penalty treats every \theta_j alike, so the features must be on comparable scales. Binary word indicators already are. Square feet (hundreds to thousands) and bedrooms (one to five) are not, and the standard preprocessing is to subtract each feature’s mean and divide by its standard deviation — which, as a bonus, also speeds up gradient descent.
