title: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation
section: 8.3 Regularisation as a prior on θ
text:
8.3 Regularisation as a prior on θ
29:07 Least squares turned out, in lecture 3, to be maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise. Regularised least squares has a matching story, and it requires treating \theta itself as random. Given the training set S, Bayes’ rule gives the posterior

p(\theta \mid S) = \frac{p(S \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}{p(S)},

and since p(S) does not depend on \theta, the most probable \theta after seeing the data is

\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}} = \arg\max_\theta \; \prod_{i=1}^{m} p\bigl(y^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}, \theta\bigr)\; p(\theta).
\tag{8.3}
This is the maximum a posteriori estimate. It is maximum likelihood with one extra factor, the prior. (The semicolon of p(y \mid x; \theta) has become a comma: once \theta is a random variable we may condition on it.)
31:12 Now choose the prior \theta \sim \mathcal N(0, \tau^2 I). Its log is -\lVert\theta\rVert^2 / (2\tau^2) plus a constant, so taking logs of Equation 8.3 adds exactly a squared-norm penalty to the log-likelihood. For logistic regression that is Equation 8.2 with \lambda = 1/(2\tau^2). For linear regression with noise variance \sigma^2, the log-likelihood is -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y^{(i)} -
\theta^\top x^{(i)})^2; multiplying through by -\sigma^2 turns the maximisation into Equation 8.1 with

\lambda = \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}.

The ratio reads sensibly: a tight prior (small \tau) or noisy data (large \sigma) both mean “trust the data less”, and both raise \lambda. The generator confirms both identities by two routes: gradient ascent on the log posterior lands on the ridge solution with \lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2 (for \sigma = 0.06, \tau = 0.5, that is \lambda = 0.0144), and on the penalised logistic solution with \lambda =
1/(2\tau^2), each to within 10^{-15}.
This also explains the intercept detail from Section 8.2. A prior \mathcal N(0, \tau^2 I) over the whole of \theta says that, before seeing any houses, we believe the price at the average size is probably near zero — which is why the \lambda \to \infty limit of the fully penalised fit is h = 0. Leaving \theta_0 out of the penalty is the same as giving it a flat prior, an admission that we have no idea of the overall price level, and the limit becomes \bar y.
32:18 Ng frames this in terms of the two schools of statistics. To a frequentist, there is a true \theta out in the world that generated the housing prices; it is unknown but not random, and the job is to devise a procedure, such as maximum likelihood, that estimates it well. To a Bayesian, \theta is unknown and therefore uncertain, and the uncertainty is expressed as a distribution p(\theta) before any data arrive. A Gaussian with mean zero is a reasonable default: we do not know whether each parameter is positive or negative, and we would bet against any of them being enormous. Problem set 2 asks for the equivalence above and for the penalty a Laplace prior produces instead.
36:19 A student asks whether “MLE versus MAP” is the same thing as “unregularised versus regularised”. Mechanically yes, Ng says; but frequentists regularise too. They simply present the penalty as part of an estimator they designed, rather than deriving it from a prior. He considers the debate largely philosophical: “I just like my stuff to work.”






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes5, section 3, goes one step past MAP to fully Bayesian prediction, which averages p(y \mid x, \theta) over the whole posterior rather than plugging in its mode, and explains why that integral is usually intractable.
crumbs: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation

title: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation
section: 8.4 Choosing a model: train, dev and test sets
text:
8.4 Choosing a model: train, dev and test sets
37:57 Plot error against model complexity. Training error falls monotonically: a fifth-order polynomial can always fit the training set at least as well as a fourth, because it contains the fourth as a special case. Error on new data falls at first, as the model becomes flexible enough to capture the trend, and then rises, as the extra flexibility goes into fitting noise. 39:42 The same U appears when the knob is \lambda instead of the degree, with large \lambda at the simple end. Figure 8.4 computes both curves for ten houses, averaged over 400 datasets: test error bottoms out at degree 2, at 0.0047 against a noise floor of \sigma^2 =
0.0036, and climbs to 0.042 at degree 8, while training error keeps falling.






Figure 8.4: Training error (indigo) and expected test error (teal) for polynomial fits to ten houses, averaged over 400 datasets. Left: against degree, without regularisation; test error is lowest at degree 2. Right: a ninth-degree polynomial as λ is relaxed from 10² to 10⁻⁶; test error is lowest near λ = 0.2. Both axes of error are logarithmic.



41:32 The task is to find the bottom of the U, and it is the same task whether the knob is the degree, \lambda, the bandwidth \tau of locally weighted regression or the C of the soft-margin SVM. 42:47 The procedure is to split the data. Fit each candidate model M_1, M_2, \dots on one part, S_{\text{train}}, to get hypotheses h_1, h_2, \dots; measure each one’s error on the other part, S_{\text{dev}}; and pick the model with the lowest dev error. “Dev” is short for development; the same set is also called the hold-out set or the cross-validation set, and Ng notes that the shorter name has won out mostly because it saves syllables. The procedure is hold-out cross-validation.
45:17 The tempting alternative, choosing the model with the lowest training error, does not work, and the left panel of Figure 8.4 shows why without further argument: the most complex model always wins on training error. Selecting on the training set would pick the fifth-order polynomial every time.
46:46 Choosing on the dev set has a cost of its own. The chosen model has now been tuned to the dev set — its parameters were fitted on S_{\text{train}} and its complexity on S_{\text{dev}} — so its dev error is no longer an unbiased estimate of how it will do on new data. Anyone who wants to report a number, in a paper especially, needs a third set, S_{\text{test}}, that played no part in any decision.
48:38 A student asks whether dev and test error usually differ by much, and Ng answers with numbers. Suppose polynomials of increasing degree score dev errors of 10, 5.1, 5.0, 4.9, 7 and 10. The winner reports 4.9; but perhaps the middle three are all really 5.0, and the one at 4.9 simply got lucky with the noise. Choosing the minimum of noisy scores systematically selects a lucky one. How lucky is computable: the expected minimum of k independent standard normals is about -1.27 for k = 6 (the generator gets -1.2672 by integration and -1.2665 by simulation), so six models of identical true error, scored with noise of standard deviation 0.1, report on average 4.87 for the winner. The bias grows with the number of models compared.
51:31 The same effect, Ng says, operates on a whole research field when everyone tunes against one public test set for years; he cites a then-recent study of CIFAR as arguing that some of the field’s apparent progress on it was overfitting to the benchmark. The study’s own conclusion is more specific (Recht et al., 2018). Its authors built a fresh CIFAR-10 test set and found that accuracy dropped by 4 to 10 percentage points across a broad range of models — but that newer models dropped less and kept their ranking, which they read as evidence against adaptive overfitting to the old test set; they attribute the drop to the models’ sensitivity to small shifts in the data distribution instead. The worry Ng describes is legitimate, but this paper is evidence for a different one.
52:29 When Ng is shipping a product rather than making a claim, he sometimes does without a test set altogether, knowing that the dev number he sees is optimistic. That is acceptable only because nobody outside the team is relying on the number. 1:00:22 The opposite case is also allowed: a team may evaluate on the test set every week and chart the result. What is not allowed is acting on it. Rolling back to last week’s model because this week’s scored lower on the test set is a decision made on the test set, and from that moment it is one more dev set.
53:33 How much data goes into each set? The historical rule of thumb is 70 % train and 30 % test, or 60/20/20 with a dev set, and Ng considers it fine for datasets of a hundred to a few thousand examples. 54:46 For very large datasets the fractions shrink: with 10 million examples, a 20 % dev set is 2 million examples, and the question is whether that many are needed. His criterion is that the dev and test sets should be large enough to detect the size of difference you care about, and no larger; the rest belongs in training. Splits of 90/5/5, or 98/1/1, are common at that scale.
55:40 His example is online advertising, where a team might ship ten projects that each raise the click-through rate by 0.01 %. To tell 90 % from 90.01 % accuracy, he says, a hundred examples cannot do it, and you need “at least 1,000 examples and maybe 10,000 or more”. That last figure is the size at which a single example is worth 0.01 % — the resolution of the measurement — but resolution is not detectability. The standard error of an accuracy near 90 % measured on m examples is \sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1 / m}:



Table 8.1: How the resolution of an accuracy and its sampling noise scale with the size of the dev set.

At 10,000 examples the noise is thirty times the difference being sought. Two independently measured accuracies 0.01 % apart are only two standard errors apart at around 4 \times 0.09 / 10^{-8} \approx 36 million examples. Comparing both classifiers on the same examples helps a great deal, because the noise then comes only from the examples on which they disagree; but even then a 0.01 % difference needs tens of thousands of examples at the very least. Ng’s broader point stands and is, if anything, understated: small improvements need very large evaluation sets. The same table shows that his other example, telling apart algorithms 1 % apart with 1,000 examples, is about one standard error — enough for a hint, not for a verdict.

title: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation
text:
8.5 k-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation
1:02:10 Hold-out validation is wasteful when data are scarce. Ng’s group has worked on medical datasets in which every example is a patient, collected, as he puts it, through “a lot of literal pain”. With 100 examples, a 70/30 split trains every candidate on only 70 of them and then judges it on only 30, which is a noisy judge.
1:04:09 k-fold cross-validation recycles the data. Split S into k disjoint pieces S_1, \dots, S_k of m/k examples each. For each candidate model, and for each j = 1, \dots, k, train on all the pieces except S_j and measure the error on S_j; the model’s score is the average of those k errors. Pick the model with the best score. Ng draws k = 5 to keep the board legible, but k = 10 is by far the most common choice. 1:13:51 The averaging is of the k held-out errors, which are just numbers — a squared error of 5.0 on one fold, 5.7 on the next, 2.8 on the next — not of the models.






Figure 8.5: Five-fold cross-validation of one model on 100 examples. Each fold of 20 is held out exactly once; the model is trained on the other 80 each time, and the five held-out errors are averaged into one score. The procedure is repeated for every candidate model.



1:07:41 At the end there are k trained copies of the winning model, each fitted on (k-1)/k of the data. One could keep all of them and average their predictions, but the more common final step is to refit the chosen model once on all of S. With k = 10 each round holds out 10 % of the data rather than 30 %, so the models being compared are trained on nearly as much data as the final one; the price is fitting every candidate ten times.
1:09:31 Taking k = m gives leave-one-out cross-validation: train on all but one example, test on that one, and repeat for every example. It is the most data-efficient version and the most expensive, m fits per model. Ng uses it only when m is roughly 100 or less, and would switch to k-fold somewhere between 20 and 50 examples. For linear models with a squared-error loss the expense is an illusion, because the leave-one-out residuals can be read off a single fit: if H = X(X^\top X +
\lambda D)^{-1}X^\top is the matrix that maps the targets to the fitted values (D is the identity with a zero for the intercept), then the error on example i when it is held out is (h(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)})/(1 - H_{ii}). The generator computes leave-one-out error both ways, by m refits and by this formula, and they agree to nine significant figures; it is how the \lambda = 0.1 of Figure 8.3 was chosen.
1:11:38 A student asks whether the spread of the ten fold errors gives a variance for the cross-validation estimate. It does not, quite, because the ten errors are correlated: any two of the ten training sets share eight-ninths of their examples. Ng recalls research by Michael Kearns on how correlated they are and says the theory does not settle it. The cleaner result came later: Bengio and Grandvalet (2004) proved that no unbiased estimator of the variance of k-fold cross-validation exists. The naive estimate errs low. On forty houses with a quadratic and k = 10, the actual variance of the cross-validation estimate across 1,500 datasets is 1.21 times the average of what the folds’ own spread suggests.
1:12:46 Cross-validation is rare in deep learning, Ng adds, because training a network ten times is expensive, and with only twenty examples a network needs other help anyway, such as transfer learning. 1:15:32 And how should examples be assigned to the sets? Shuffle at random, provided all the data come from one distribution. When training and deployment data differ, as when speech recorded on phones is used to build a smart speaker, splitting becomes more delicate; Ng defers that case to his book Machine Learning Yearning and to CS230.
crumbs: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation

title: 8  Data Splits, Models and Cross-Validation
text:
8.6 Feature selection
1:17:00 Feature selection is model selection where the models are subsets of features. It makes sense when there are many features and one suspects only a few matter: of 10,000 word indicators, stop words such as “the” and “of” say nothing about whether an email is spam; of the hundreds of sensor readings on a truck, perhaps a handful predict a breakdown. It does not make sense for images, where every pixel carries a little information. Ng stresses that deciding which regime one is in takes judgement.
With n features there are 2^n subsets, far too many to try, so the search is greedy. 1:19:09 Forward search starts from the empty set \mathcal F = \varnothing — the model h(x) = \theta_0, which predicts the average y — and repeats one step: for every feature not yet in \mathcal F, fit the model on \mathcal F plus that feature and evaluate it on the dev set (or by cross-validation); then add the feature whose addition helped most. 1:20:18 With five features, the first round fits five one-feature models; if x_2 wins, the second round fits four models of the form \{x_2, x_j\}; and so on, stopping when adding a feature no longer helps, or running to the end and returning the best subset seen. Backward search runs the other way, starting from all features and removing one at a time.
The generator runs forward search on five features of which only x_2 and x_4 matter. It adds x_2, then x_4, and after that dev error stops moving (0.320, 0.319, 0.322, 0.328 as the three irrelevant features are added). Run to the end, forward search makes n(n+1)/2 + 1 fits — 16 for five features, the count the generator verifies — which is quadratic rather than exponential in n. That is the sense in which it is affordable, and also the sense in which Ng calls it expensive: for 10,000 features it is fifty million fits.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes5, section 2, also covers filter feature selection, which scores each feature on its own — for instance by its mutual information with y — and keeps the top k, choosing k by cross-validation. It is much cheaper than forward search and is the usual choice for naive Bayes on text.

title: Learning Theory
text:
The learning algorithm as an estimator
Based on the Friday discussion section of CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018, taught by a member of the course staff.
Lecture 8 told you to choose models on held-out data because training error is optimistic. This section asks how optimistic, and answers with a theorem: if an algorithm picks the hypothesis with the lowest training error from a class of k hypotheses, then with probability at least 1 - \delta its true error is within
2\sqrt{\frac{1}{2m}\log\frac{2k}{\delta}}
of the best the class can do. Two facts are hiding in that expression. The number of examples needed grows only with the logarithm of the size of the class, and, once the class is infinite, the logarithm is replaced by a measure of the class’s expressiveness called the VC dimension. Getting there takes two elementary tools — the union bound and Hoeffding’s inequality — and a change of viewpoint about what a learning algorithm is.
Ng explained in lecture 8 that this material used to be part of the main lectures and moved to a Friday section because it matters less to making algorithms work than it once did. The section promises to state results rather than prove them, and the proofs are in cs229-notes4. What this chapter adds is the section’s own pictures, its answers to questions, and a computation behind every claim: the bounds are checked against exact probabilities and simulations, which also shows how loose they are.
1:15 Everything rests on two assumptions. There is a fixed data distribution \mathcal D over pairs (x, y), from which both the training set and every future test example are drawn; and the examples are drawn independently. Without the first, training data say nothing about test data, and the theory has nothing to work with. Lecture 8’s aside about training on phone recordings to deploy on a smart speaker is exactly a case where it fails.
3:15 A learning algorithm is then a box. In goes a training set S = \{(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^m of m samples from \mathcal D; out comes a hypothesis \hat h, or equivalently, for a parametric class such as logistic regression in n dimensions, a parameter vector \hat\theta. 4:43 The point the section makes first is that S is random, the box is a deterministic function, and so its output is random too. Run the box on a different sample from \mathcal D and you get a different \hat\theta. In statistics the box is called an estimator, and the distribution of \hat\theta over repeated draws of S is its sampling distribution.
6:22 Against this randomness stands a fixed target, a true parameter \theta^* (or true hypothesis h^*) that we would like the box to output. It is unknown, but it is not random: there is no distribution over it. That is the frequentist stance of lecture 8, and the notation follows it — hats for things estimated from data, stars for the true values we never see. Asked whether \theta must be a vector, the section answers that it can be anything we estimate, a scalar, a matrix, or a function with no parameters at all.

title: Learning Theory
section: Bias and variance as moments of the sampling distribution
text:
Bias and variance as moments of the sampling distribution
10:26 Lecture 8 pictured bias and variance in the data view: curves through points, underfitting and overfitting. The section redraws them in the parameter view, which makes them precise. Take a model with two parameters, so that each \hat\theta is a dot in the plane. Draw a training set of size m, run the algorithm, plot the dot; draw another training set of the same size, plot another dot; repeat. The cloud of dots is a sample from the sampling distribution. 13:51 Bias asks whether the cloud is centred on \theta^*: it is \mathbb E[\hat\theta] - \theta^*, a statement about the first moment. Variance asks how spread out the cloud is, the second moment. They are, in the section’s words, “just properties of the first and second moments of your sampling distribution”.
Figure 1 draws the clouds for two real estimators on one regression problem, y = \theta^{*\top} x + \varepsilon with \theta^* = (1, 0.5) and two features correlated at 0.9 — the situation of square footage and number of bedrooms. Least squares is unbiased, and at m = 10 its cloud is centred on \theta^* but enormous (total variance 1.47), stretched along the direction in which correlated features cannot be told apart: raising \theta_1 while lowering \theta_2 barely changes the fit. Ridge regression with \lambda = 10 on the same training sets is pulled towards the origin, a bias of length 0.52, and its variance is thirty times smaller, 0.045. That is lecture 8’s claim that regularisation trades a little bias for a lot of variance, seen directly.






Figure 1: Sampling distributions of θ̂ for least squares (teal) and ridge with λ = 10 (indigo), 300 training sets per panel, on a two-feature regression with correlated features. The cross marks θ, the ring the mean of θ̂. More data shrinks both clouds, and shrinks ridge’s offset from θ too.



15:58 With ten times the data, every cloud tightens: least squares’ variance falls from 1.47 to 0.110, roughly the factor of ten one expects from variance proportional to 1/m. As m \to \infty the variance goes to zero, and an estimator whose output converges to \theta^* is called consistent. 17:56 An estimator with \mathbb E[\hat\theta] = \theta^* at every m is called unbiased.
17:14 The rate at which variance falls with m the section calls statistical efficiency, a measure of how well an algorithm squeezes information from data, and it offers as examples one algorithm whose variance falls like 1/m^2 and another like e^{-m}. Those rates are not available to an unbiased estimator of a parameter in a regular model: the Cramér–Rao bound puts a floor of order 1/m under its variance. (Irregular models are different — the right endpoint of a uniform distribution can be estimated with variance of order 1/m^2 — but the models in this course are regular.) What efficiency usually measures is the constant in front of 1/m. The mean and the median of a Gaussian sample are both unbiased estimates of its centre, both with variance proportional to 1/m; but the median’s is larger by a factor of \pi/2. The generator measures m \cdot \operatorname{Var} at 1.01 for the mean and 1.575 for the median at m = 101, against \pi/2 = 1.571. Using the median wastes about a third of the data.
20:08 Informally, the section says, a high-bias algorithm is one that “no matter how much data or evidence you provide”, stays away from \theta^*. That runs two ideas together, and the bottom row of Figure 1 separates them. Bias is defined at a fixed m, as a student’s question prompts the section to confirm at 21:35; staying away forever is inconsistency. Ridge with a fixed \lambda is biased at every m and yet consistent, because the penalty stays the same size while the data term grows in proportion to m: its bias is 0.52 at m = 10, 0.18 at 100, 0.030 at 1{,}000 and 0.002 at 10{,}000. 58:09 The same point answers a later question that the section leaves open, whether adding regularisation destroys the consistency of maximum likelihood. With a fixed penalty, it does not.
20:58 Bias and variance are separate properties; any combination of the two can occur. 22:18 High variance has two standard remedies. More data shrinks the cloud directly. Regularisation shrinks it by restricting where \hat\theta can go, usually at the price of moving its centre — which is the trade Figure 1 shows.

title: Learning Theory
text:
Approximation error and estimation error
25:02 The second picture is drawn in the space of all hypotheses. Somewhere in it is g, the best possible hypothesis, with the lowest expected error under \mathcal D of any function whatsoever. 25:52 Our algorithm searches only a class \mathcal H — all logistic regression models, say, or all SVMs — drawn as a region that need not contain g. 26:27 Inside the region is h^*, the best hypothesis in the class. And what training on finite data actually produces is \hat h, a different point of \mathcal H for every training set.
27:51 For classification the error of a hypothesis is its probability of a mistake, and the training error is its frequency of mistakes on S:

\varepsilon(h) = P_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}\bigl(h(x) \neq y\bigr),
\qquad
\hat\varepsilon_S(h) = \frac1m \sum_{i=1}^m 1\bigl\{h(x^{(i)}) \neq y^{(i)}\bigr\}.
\tag{1}
The first is called the generalisation error or risk; the second the empirical risk. 30:30 \varepsilon(g) is the Bayes error, also called irreducible error: if the same x can come with different labels, no function gets all of them right. Then the error of what we learn splits into three:

\varepsilon(\hat h)
= \underbrace{\varepsilon(g)}_{\text{Bayes error}}
+ \underbrace{\varepsilon(h^*) - \varepsilon(g)}_{\text{approximation error}}
+ \underbrace{\varepsilon(\hat h) - \varepsilon(h^*)}_{\text{estimation error}} .
\tag{2}
31:35 The identity is a telescoping sum, but each term names a different cause. Approximation error is the price of restricting ourselves to \mathcal H, a property of the class alone. 32:20 Estimation error is the price of having only m examples, plus any quirks of the algorithm, and it shrinks as m grows.
34:49 The section then says this decomposition and the bias–variance decomposition are related but not the same: estimation error itself splits into a variance part and a bias part, and “bias” in the usual sense is approximation error plus that estimation bias. For 0–1 loss this is a picture rather than an equation — there is no clean additive bias–variance identity for classification error — but for squared error it is exact, and worth seeing. Let g(x) = \mathbb E[y \mid x], let \bar h = \mathbb E_S[\hat h] be the average learned hypothesis, and measure error by \varepsilon(h) = \mathbb E(y - h(x))^2. Then

\mathbb E_S\,\varepsilon(\hat h)
= \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{noise}}
+ \underbrace{\mathbb E_x\bigl(\bar h(x) - g(x)\bigr)^2}_{\text{bias}^2}
+ \underbrace{\mathbb E_{S,x}\bigl(\hat h(x) - \bar h(x)\bigr)^2}_{\text{variance}} ,
\tag{3}
and when \mathcal H is a linear space, such as all straight lines, g - h^* is orthogonal to it, so Pythagoras splits the bias: \text{bias}^2 = \text{approximation error} + \mathbb E_x(\bar h - h^*)^2, and the estimation error is the variance plus that same small term.
Figure 2 does this for straight lines fitted to eight points from a parabola, g(x) = 4(x - \frac12)^2, with noise \sigma = 0.3. The best line is flat, h^* = \frac13, and the approximation error is 0.0889. The expected test error of the fitted line is 0.2597, which splits as 0.0900 + 0.0889 + 0.0808 one way and 0.0900 + 0.0910 + 0.0786 the other. The difference between the two middle terms, 0.0021, is the estimation bias: the average fitted line, 0.290 - 0.006x, is not h^*, because least squares on a misspecified model is biased at small m. The generator asserts that both totals agree and that the Pythagorean identity holds.






Figure 2: Left: the hypothesis-space picture. The class H is a region; the best predictor g lies outside it; h* is the point of H closest to g; fitted hypotheses ĥ scatter inside H. Right: the expected test error of straight lines fitted to eight noisy points from a parabola, split into Bayes, approximation and estimation error, and into noise, squared bias and variance. The bars are to scale and their totals agree.



36:34 The picture also says how to fight each kind of error. To reduce bias, make \mathcal H bigger, so that it reaches closer to g; but a bigger class gives \hat h more room to wander, so variance tends to rise. 39:27 To reduce variance, make \mathcal H smaller — regularisation does this, by penalising hypotheses with large \theta — and unless the shrinking happens to move towards g, bias rises. 41:05 A student asks why not shrink the class towards h^*; because we do not know where h^* is, and if we did there would be nothing to learn.

title: Learning Theory
section: Empirical risk minimisation and two tools
text:
Empirical risk minimisation and two tools
44:56 Nothing so far depended on what happens inside the box. To prove something, the section now fixes the algorithm: empirical risk minimisation returns the hypothesis with the lowest training error,

\hat h = \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal H} \hat\varepsilon_S(h).
\tag{4}
47:36 This is “what we’ve been doing so far in the course”, with one honest caveat that the section mentions: logistic regression minimises the logistic loss, not the 0–1 training error of Equation 1, and SVMs minimise the hinge loss. Those losses are convex stand-ins for the count of mistakes, which is intractable to minimise directly. The theorems below are about the count of mistakes; they extend to the stand-ins with more work, which this section does not do.
49:25 Two questions organise the rest. How close is the training error of a hypothesis to its true error? And how close is the true error of the hypothesis ERM picks to that of the best in the class? 50:47 The first tool is the union bound: for any events A_1, \dots, A_k, independent or not,

P(A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_k) \le P(A_1) + \dots + P(A_k).

“If this looks trivial, it is trivial,” the section says. 52:00 The second is Hoeffding’s inequality, stated for the case needed here. Let Z_1, \dots, Z_m be independent Bernoulli(\phi) variables and \hat\phi = \frac1m\sum_i Z_i their mean. Then for any \gamma > 0,

P\bigl(|\hat\phi - \phi| > \gamma\bigr) \le 2\exp(-2\gamma^2 m).
\tag{5}
The probability that an average of coin flips misses its expectation by more than a margin \gamma falls exponentially in the number of flips. The general version holds for any bounded independent variables, and the bound on the range is essential.
The bound is easy to check, because the exact probability is a binomial tail. Figure 3 compares them for \gamma = 0.1. At m = 100 the exact probabilities are 0.035 for a fair coin and 0.0034 for \phi = 0.15, against a bound of 0.27. The bound holds at every m and \phi the generator tries, with the exact tail never more than 0.23 of it. It has the right exponential rate, and it is loosest for coins far from fair, whose averages vary less — a looseness that matters here, because error rates of good classifiers are far from one half.






Figure 3: The probability that the mean of m coin flips misses φ by more than 0.1: computed exactly for φ = 0.5 and φ = 0.15, and bounded by Hoeffding’s inequality. The bound is valid everywhere and loose by an order of magnitude or more. The φ = 0.15 curve leaves the plot below 10⁻⁶.

title: Learning Theory
section: Uniform convergence for a finite class
text:
Uniform convergence for a finite class
59:54 The section’s central picture puts every hypothesis in \mathcal H on a horizontal axis and plots two curves above it: the true error \varepsilon(h), a fixed curve, and the training error \hat\varepsilon_S(h), a random curve that changes with every training set. Figure 4 computes it for a class small enough that the true error of every member is a closed form. Inputs are uniform on [0,1], the label is 1\{x \ge 0.4\} flipped with probability 0.15, and \mathcal H contains ten threshold classifiers h_t(x) = 1\{x \ge t\} with t = 0.05, 0.15, \dots, 0.95. The Bayes error is 0.15. The class has no threshold at 0.4, so its best members, t = 0.35 and t = 0.45, have error 0.185, an approximation error of 0.035.






Figure 4: True error ε(h) (solid) and training error on three samples of sixty examples (dashed) for each of ten threshold classifiers. The training-error curves scatter around the true curve. ERM on the first sample picks the hypothesis circled, whose training error is well below its true error: choosing the minimum selects a hypothesis whose training error happened to come out low.



1:05:19 For one hypothesis h fixed in advance, the training error is an average of m independent Bernoulli variables 1\{h(x^{(i)}) \ne y^{(i)}\} whose mean is \varepsilon(h), so Hoeffding applies directly:

P\bigl(|\hat\varepsilon_S(h) - \varepsilon(h)| > \gamma\bigr) \le 2\exp(-2\gamma^2 m).

On average over training sets the dashed curve passes through the solid one at every h, and with more data it hugs it more tightly. 1:08:16 But this is useless as it stands, and the section is precise about why: ERM does not fix h in advance. It looks at the training set and picks the hypothesis whose dashed curve is lowest, so \hat h depends on S and its training error is no longer an unbiased average. It is the minimum of noisy scores, which lecture 8 showed is optimistic. The circled point in Figure 4 is exactly that.
1:09:32 The fix is to demand that the whole dashed curve be close to the solid one at once — uniform convergence. If no hypothesis deviates by more than \gamma, then neither does the one ERM picks, however it was chosen. 1:11:54 For a class of k hypotheses the union bound gives this cheaply: the event that some h deviates is the union of k events, each of probability at most 2\exp(-2\gamma^2 m), so

P\bigl(\exists\, h \in \mathcal H : |\hat\varepsilon_S(h) - \varepsilon(h)| > \gamma\bigr)
\le 2k\exp(-2\gamma^2 m).
\tag{6}
Equivalently, with probability at least 1 - \delta, where \delta = 2k
\exp(-2\gamma^2 m), every hypothesis has training error within \gamma of its true error.
The union bound is pessimistic, since it treats the k events as if they could not overlap, and nested thresholds overlap heavily. With m = 200 and \gamma = 0.1 the generator finds that some hypothesis among the ten deviates in 1.6\,\% of training sets. The bound for a single hypothesis is already 3.7\,\%, and the union bound is 37\,\%. The guarantees in learning theory are worst-case statements over every distribution, and they read best as statements about how quantities scale.
1:16:04 Three quantities are tied together — m, \gamma and \delta — and fixing any two gives the third. Fixing \gamma and \delta and solving for m gives the sample complexity: with probability at least 1 - \delta, every training error is within \gamma of the true error, provided

m \ge \frac{1}{2\gamma^2}\log\frac{2k}{\delta}.
\tag{7}
The striking feature is the logarithm. For \gamma = \delta = 0.05, ten hypotheses need 1{,}199 examples, a thousand need 2{,}120, and a million need only 3{,}501.

title: Learning Theory
section: How good is the hypothesis ERM picks?
text:
How good is the hypothesis ERM picks?
1:17:58 The second question compares \hat h with the best in class. On the event that uniform convergence holds, a three-step chain does it, each step either uniform convergence or the definition of ERM:

\varepsilon(\hat h)
\le \hat\varepsilon_S(\hat h) + \gamma
\le \hat\varepsilon_S(h^*) + \gamma
\le \varepsilon(h^*) + 2\gamma .

The first step drops from the solid curve to the dashed one at \hat h. The second uses the fact that \hat h has the lowest training error of any hypothesis, h^* included. The third climbs from the dashed curve back to the solid one at h^*. 1:22:29 Substituting \gamma from Equation 6 gives the theorem: with probability at least 1 - \delta,

\varepsilon(\hat h) \le \Bigl(\min_{h \in \mathcal H} \varepsilon(h)\Bigr)
+ 2\sqrt{\frac{1}{2m}\log\frac{2k}{\delta}} .
\tag{8}
This is bias and variance once more, in theorem form. The first term is the best the class can do, which can only fall as \mathcal H grows; the second, which grows with k, is the price of searching a larger class with the same data. cs229-notes4 makes the same reading. On the threshold class the guarantee holds in every one of 3,000 runs at each m the generator tries, but it is very loose: at m = 200 and \delta = 0.05, 2\gamma is 0.245, while ERM picks a best-in-class threshold in every run.

title: Learning Theory
section: Infinite classes and the VC dimension
text:
Infinite classes and the VC dimension
1:23:40 Most classes of interest, linear classifiers among them, are infinite, and Equation 8 with k = \infty says nothing. The section ran out of time here and only stated the result; cs229-notes4, section 4, gives more, and two pieces of it are worth having.
The first is a crude argument that gets the right answer. A class with d real parameters, stored as 64-bit floating-point numbers, has at most k = 2^{64d} members, and \log k = 64 d \log 2 is linear in d. So the sample complexity of ERM over a d-parameter class grows linearly in d. With \gamma = \delta = 0.05 the bound gives about 9{,}600 examples for d = 1 and 89{,}000 for d = 10, which is far too many in absolute terms and right in how it scales.
The second is the principled version. A class \mathcal H shatters a set of points if, for every one of the 2^n ways of labelling them, some h \in \mathcal H gets every label right. The Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension \mathrm{VC}(\mathcal
H) is the size of the largest set \mathcal H can shatter. For lines in the plane it is 3, and Figure 5 shows why: three points in general position can be split by a line under all eight labellings, while no four points can. Any four points in general position either form a convex quadrilateral, where the labelling that alternates around it defeats every line, or a triangle with a point inside, where labelling the inner point against the outer three does. The generator checks every labelling of each set by exhaustive search over line directions. The definition needs only one shattered set of size 3: three collinear points cannot be shattered, since no line puts the middle point on the other side from its two neighbours, and the VC dimension is still 3.






Figure 5: Shattering with lines. Left: three points in general position under all eight labellings, each separated by a line (the all-same labellings need none). Right: the two shapes four points in general position can take, each with a labelling no line separates. The VC dimension of lines in the plane is therefore 3.



1:24:52 Vapnik’s theorem then replaces \log k with the VC dimension d: with probability at least 1 - \delta,

\varepsilon(\hat h) \le \varepsilon(h^*) + O\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{d}{m}\log\frac{m}{d} + \frac1m\log\frac1\delta}\Bigr),

and the section’s take-away is that the number of examples needed is of the order of the VC dimension. For most classes with a reasonable parametrisation the VC dimension is roughly the number of parameters — linear classifiers in n dimensions have n + 1 — which is the formal version of Ng’s rule of thumb in lecture 8 that unregularised models want at least as many examples as parameters.
The VC dimension also answers the question from lecture 8 about why an SVM in an infinite-dimensional feature space does not overfit. The VC dimension of all linear separators in that space is infinite. But Ng’s answer was that the relevant class is the separators with a large margin, and for data inside a ball of radius R the VC dimension of separators with margin at least \gamma is bounded in terms of R^2/\gamma^2, however many dimensions the feature space has. That is the sense in which minimising \lVert w \rVert^2 is regularisation.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes4, sections 2 and 3, prove the finite-class results stated here, including the sample-complexity corollary; section 4 gives the 64-bit argument, the definition of shattering and Vapnik’s theorem. Hoeffding’s inequality is proved in the supplementary notes on Hoeffding’s inequality, via Chernoff bounds and moment generating functions.

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.1 A model that cuts the space into boxes
Based on the lecture by Raphael Townshend, head TA — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
A decision tree splits the input space into rectangles by asking one yes-or-no question about one feature at a time, and predicts a constant in each rectangle. It is the course’s first genuinely non-linear model, it is easy to explain to anyone, and on its own it is not very accurate: a fully grown tree has low bias and very high variance. The second half of the lecture is about the cure, which is to average many trees. Averaging cuts variance by an amount the correlation between the trees controls, and that single formula explains bagging, the extra randomness of random forests, and why boosting, which works on bias instead, uses deliberately weak trees.
The lecture is given by Raphael Townshend, one of the course’s head TAs, while Ng is travelling. It is almost entirely board work, built on one running example.
1:24 Townshend, who is Canadian and likes to ski, poses a classifier: given a month and a latitude, can you ski there? Plot month (1 for January to 12 for December) against latitude (+90° at the North Pole, -90° at the South). The positives sit in two separate blocks, the northern winter at high northern latitudes and the southern winter, mid-year, at high southern ones, with nothing near the equator. No line separates that, and while a kernel might lift it into a space where a hyperplane does, the structure is plainly a set of boxes, and it would be simpler to find the boxes directly.
3:38 Finding the best set of regions is intractable in general. A decision tree finds a good one greedily, top-down and recursively. It starts with the whole space and asks the single question that best separates the classes — “is the latitude above 30°?” — which cuts the plane in two. It then treats each half as a fresh problem and asks another question there, “is the month before March?”, and so on: a game of twenty questions with the data. Figure 9.1 shows the result on synthetic ski data. Seven leaves isolate both skiing seasons.
6:08 Formally, a split of a parent region R_p is a feature j and a threshold t, which divide it into two children:
R_1 = \{x \in R_p : x_j < t\}, \qquad R_2 = \{x \in R_p : x_j \ge t\}.
Each leaf predicts the most common class among the training examples that land in it. What remains is to say which (j, t) is “best”.
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text: Figure 9.1: Synthetic ski data: one can ski in the northern winter above 30° and in the southern winter below −30°. A tree grown greedily until its leaves are pure cuts the plane into axis-aligned rectangles; the shaded ones are those it labels “ski”.
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.2 Choosing a split
8:32 Define a loss L(R) for a region and choose the split that reduces it the most, from the loss of the parent to the combined loss of the children. Since the parent’s loss is fixed, this is the same as minimising the children’s loss. With \hat p_c the proportion of the region’s examples in class c, the obvious loss is the misclassification rate, L_{\text{mis}}(R) = 1 - \max_c \hat p_c: predict the majority class and count everything else as an error.
12:29 Townshend’s example shows why that loss is the wrong one. A region holds 900 positives and 100 negatives. One split sends 700 positives and 100 negatives one way and 200 positives the other; another sends 400 and 100 one way and 500 positives the other. The second split looks better — it isolates a pure region of 500 — but both children of both splits still predict “positive”, so each split makes exactly the 100 mistakes the parent made. Misclassification registers no gain for either, and a tree built on it would have no reason to prefer the split that obviously helps.
15:21 The fix is a loss that rewards purity even when it does not change any prediction. The standard choice is the cross-entropy,

L_{\text{cross}}(R) = -\sum_c \hat p_c \log_2 \hat p_c ,
\tag{9.1}
the number of bits needed, on average, to tell someone the class of an example when they already know the proportions: zero for a pure region, one bit for a 50/50 binary region. 51:56 Asked whether the logarithm must be base 2, Townshend is “pretty sure” it does not matter. It does not: changing the base multiplies every loss and every gain by the same constant, so the ranking of splits cannot change. The generator confirms the ratio is exactly \ln 2 for both splits.
One detail on the board needs care. The children’s loss must be weighted by their sizes,

\frac{|R_1|\,L(R_1) + |R_2|\,L(R_2)}{|R_1| + |R_2|},
\tag{9.2}
as cs229-notes-dt writes it. The board writes L(R_1) + L(R_2), which is correct for misclassification measured in counts, as in the example, but not for losses defined on proportions such as Equation 9.1. Unweighted, the sum can be made larger than the parent’s loss by peeling off a single positive and a single negative — a region of two with a full bit of entropy — even though such a split barely changes anything. With the weighting, cross-entropy gives the lecture’s two splits gains of 0.034 and 0.108 bits, preferring the second as intuition does.
21:44 The geometry explains why this works, and Figure 9.2 draws it. Plot a binary loss against \hat p, the share of positives. A parent’s \hat p is the size-weighted average of its children’s, so the parent sits on the curve at that average, while the children’s weighted loss sits on the chord between the children’s points. For a strictly concave curve such as cross-entropy, the chord lies strictly below the curve whenever the children differ, so every split that changes the class proportions gains something. Misclassification is a tent, linear on each side of \frac12. When both children fall on the same side as the parent, the chord lies on the curve and the gain is exactly zero, which is what happened in the example. Over random splits of random regions the generator finds this case — positive cross-entropy gain, zero misclassification gain — in about half of all splits.






Figure 9.2: Three impurities against the share of positives. The 900/100 parent sits at 0.9; the 400/100 and 500/0 children sit at 0.8 and 1.0, and their average loss is the midpoint of the dashed chord. The gain is the vertical gap between the parent’s point (teal) and the midpoint (ring): zero for misclassification, positive for cross-entropy and Gini.



29:36 The Gini impurity \sum_c \hat p_c (1 - \hat p_c) has the same shape and is the other common choice. It is tempting to treat the two as interchangeable, and usually they are; but the generator, offering both the same ten random candidate splits of a 60/40 region 2,000 times, finds that they choose different splits in 5.8\,\% of cases. The family resemblance is the concavity, and that, Townshend says, is what the losses that work in practice have in common.
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.3 Regression trees and categorical features
31:03 Nothing above depends on the labels being classes. To predict snowfall instead of “can ski”, let each leaf R_m predict the mean of its targets, \hat y_m = \frac{1}{|R_m|}\sum_{i \in R_m} y^{(i)}, and measure the region by squared error, L_{\text{sq}}(R_m) = \frac{1}{|R_m|}\sum_{i \in R_m} (y^{(i)} - \hat y_m)^2. These are regression trees, and splitting proceeds exactly as before. 34:34 Asked how the best split is actually found, Townshend says it is found by brute force, efficiently: sort the examples along each feature, and every distinct gap between consecutive values is a candidate threshold that can be scored with running sums in one pass.
35:06 Trees also take categorical features naturally. If location is one of north, equator or south, a split is a question such as “is the location in the northern hemisphere?” — in general, “is the category in subset A?”. 36:27 The catch is the number of subsets. The lecture counts 2^q for q categories; the number of distinct binary splits is 2^{q-1} - 1, since a subset and its complement define the same split and the empty set defines none. Either way it is exponential. 37:01 For binary classification there is a well-known escape, which the lecture mentions without proof: sort the categories by their proportion of positives, and the best split is always one of the q - 1 splits of that sorted list into a prefix and a suffix. The generator checks this against brute force over all subsets for 500 random six-category problems under cross-entropy, and the two always agree.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes-dt, sections 2 to 4.1, give the recursive partitioning algorithm, the size-weighted split criterion and the treatment of categorical variables.
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.4 Regularising a tree
37:39 Grown until every leaf is pure, a tree can put each training example in a region of its own. That overfits, and trees are in this sense high-variance models. 38:24 The usual controls are heuristics: stop splitting a node with fewer than a minimum number of examples, cap the depth, or cap the number of nodes.
39:07 A fourth heuristic, stopping when the best split decreases the loss by less than some threshold, is one Townshend calls “very tempting” and advises against. Interactions between features can make the first question worthless on its own and the second one decisive. In the ski data the latitude question alone helps little; the latitude question followed by the month question nails it. The extreme case is XOR: label a point positive when exactly one of its two coordinates exceeds a threshold. The generator builds a balanced XOR set of 64 points, on which every single split leaves the cross-entropy exactly where it was, so a tree that splits only on positive gain stops at the root, with 32 mistakes. Taking the zero-gain split anyway, the two children are each solved by one more split, with no mistakes at depth 2.
40:07 The better approach is to grow the tree fully and then prune it backwards: remove a split if doing so does not hurt the misclassification error on a held-out validation set — the dev set of lecture 8, used to choose the size of the tree.
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.5 Runtime
42:54 Let n be the number of examples, f the number of features and d the depth of the tree. Prediction walks one path from root to leaf, so it costs O(d), and for a reasonably balanced tree d is about \log_2 n. Training is the surprise. 44:46 Each example lands in exactly one node per level, so it takes part in at most d split searches, and in each it is scanned once per feature. The total is O(nfd). Since nf is the size of the data matrix, training a tree costs about as much as reading the data d times. (For continuous features the scan needs the examples sorted along each feature; the sort is done once up front, or the bound picks up a logarithmic factor.)
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.6 What trees cannot do
47:58 The main weakness is additive structure. Label points positive above the line x_2 = x_1. Logistic regression represents that boundary exactly with one weight per feature. A tree can only approximate it with a staircase of axis-aligned steps, and every step costs leaves. On 400 training points, a depth-1 tree reaches 75.8\,\% test accuracy, depth 3 reaches 89.0\,\%, and a tree grown until its leaves are pure stops at 18 leaves and 96.9\,\%, the staircase being as fine as the training data allow (Figure 9.3).






Figure 9.3: Points above the dashed diagonal are positive. Trees of depth 1 and 3, and one grown until every leaf is pure, each trained on 400 points, shade the region they call positive. The boundary is always a staircase, and following the diagonal more closely takes more leaves and more data.



49:36 The scorecard, then. Trees are easy to explain — twenty questions — and short ones can be read directly. They handle categorical features and they are fast. Against that, they have high variance, they are bad at additive structure, and, mostly for those two reasons, their predictive accuracy is low. 51:09 “I know what you guys are thinking,” Townshend says: why spend half a lecture on a model that, on its own, is not very good? Because trees are the ideal raw material for ensembles, which (as of 2018) underpin many of the methods winning Kaggle competitions.
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.7 Why averaging helps
53:11 Let X_1, \dots, X_n be independent random variables with variance \sigma^2. Their average has variance \sigma^2 / n: each independent source divides the variance further. 55:00 Models trained on related data are not independent, though. If the X_i are identically distributed with pairwise correlation \rho, then

\operatorname{Var}\Bigl(\frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\Bigr) = \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{n}\,\sigma^2 .
\tag{9.3}
The second term vanishes as n grows; the first does not. With \rho = 1 averaging does nothing at all, and in general the variance can never fall below \rho\sigma^2 (Figure 9.4). 57:01 So the game has two moves: average many models to shrink the second term, and make them as decorrelated as possible to shrink the first. The generator checks Equation 9.3 by simulation for \rho = 0, 0.3, 0.6.






Figure 9.4: The variance of an average of n equally correlated models, relative to one model’s. Independent models (ρ = 0) average away to nothing; correlated ones level off at ρ, the dotted lines. Rings are simulated averages.



57:48 The most decorrelated ensembles come from different algorithms — averaging a neural network, a random forest and an SVM is a common Kaggle tactic that works well — or from different training sets, which is rarely an option, since collecting one was hard enough. Bagging approximates the second; boosting does something else.
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.8 Bagging
1:00:20 Bagging stands for bootstrap aggregation. The bootstrap is a statistician’s device for measuring the uncertainty of an estimate. The training set S was sampled from a population P; ideally we would draw fresh training sets from P, but we cannot. So pretend S is the population, and draw new training sets Z from it: n examples sampled from S with replacement, which is what sampling from a population means. 1:03:25 Bagging takes M bootstrap samples Z_1, \dots, Z_M, trains a model G_m on each, and averages:

G(x) = \frac1M \sum_{m=1}^M G_m(x).

1:05:06 In the terms of Equation 9.3, the bootstrap lowers \rho (the models see different data) and M controls the second term. A consequence Townshend stresses is that more bootstrap models cannot make the ensemble overfit more: they only shrink the second term, so the usual practice is to keep adding models until the error stops falling. Figure 9.5 shows exactly that.
1:07:33 Asked how far bootstrapping can push \rho down, he has no formula, only the reason there is a floor: every bootstrap sample is drawn from the same S, and each contains about two-thirds of it. The exact fraction of distinct examples is 1 - (1 - 1/n)^n \to 1 - 1/e \approx 0.632, which the generator confirms by sampling. 1:08:29 That missing third is also the price: each model trains on fewer distinct examples, so bagging slightly raises bias. In Figure 9.5 a single tree on a bootstrap sample has test error 1.52 against 1.08 for one tree on the full data, but by three or four trees the average has overtaken the full-data tree, and a hundred bagged trees reach 0.75.
1:11:23 This is why trees and bagging belong together. A deep tree has low bias and high variance; bagging trades a little bias for a large cut in variance; and so a model whose error is mostly variance gains the most. Bagging a high-bias model would gain little.






Figure 9.5: Test error of an average of M regression trees grown on bootstrap samples, for plain bagging and for a random forest that considers three of eight features at each split. Both fall steeply and then flatten; neither rises as trees are added. One full tree on all the data is far worse; the dotted line is the noise floor.



The method is due to Breiman (1996).
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.9 Random forests
1:12:29 A random forest is bagged trees with one more source of randomness: at each split, the tree may only consider a random subset of the features. 1:13:56 Townshend gives two reasons this helps, which are the same reason. It lowers \rho. And concretely, if one feature is a very strong predictor, every bagged tree will split on it first whatever its bootstrap sample, so the trees are alike from the root down; forbidding it at some splits forces them apart.
The decorrelation is real and easy to measure. On the problem of Figure 9.5 — eight noisy measurements, five of one latent variable and three of another — the correlation between two bagged trees’ predictions across training sets is about 0.18; letting each split see only three features drops it to 0.07, with each tree’s own variance roughly unchanged, so \rho\sigma^2 falls from about 0.14 to 0.05. The test error of 100 trees falls from 0.738 with all features to about 0.70 with two to four.
But the argument above is only about variance, and the lecture does not mention the other side. Forbidding a feature can also make a tree worse. On a second problem where one feature carries most of the signal and the others are weak, restricting each split to two of six features roughly doubles each tree’s variance — many splits must make do with weak features — and the forest’s test error rises from 0.44 to 0.51; with one feature per split it reaches 0.74. Random feature selection pays when the features it forces the trees to use are nearly as good as the ones it hides, as with redundant or correlated measurements. The number of features per split is a hyperparameter to tune like any other, which is how Breiman (2001) treated it.
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
text:
9.10 Boosting
1:15:16 Bagging fights variance. Boosting works in the opposite direction: it reduces bias, by building an ensemble additively, each new model trained to fix what the previous ones got wrong. It starts from deliberately weak models — typically decision stumps, trees of depth one that ask a single question. A stump has high bias and low variance, which is the right raw material for a method that lowers bias. (The lecture’s sentence at 1:16:44 runs these two the wrong way round, saying that restricting to depth one decreases bias before saying it increases it; the second is right.)
1:16:59 The first stump draws its line and misclassifies some examples. Boosting increases the weight of those examples and trains the next stump on the reweighted set, which pushes it to get the hard ones right; and so on, each example’s weight reflecting how often the ensemble so far has got it wrong. Figure 9.6 runs it on the diagonal boundary that defeats a single tree. 1:18:17 Each stump G_m also gets a vote \alpha_m, larger for more accurate stumps, and the final classifier is the weighted vote G(x) = \operatorname{sign}\bigl(\sum_m \alpha_m G_m(x)\bigr). The algorithm is AdaBoost, due to Freund and Schapire (1997). In the form the official notes give, with labels y \in \{-1, +1\} and weights starting at w_i = 1/n, each round:

fits a stump G_m to the weighted data;
computes its weighted error \operatorname{err}_m = \sum_i w_i\, 1\{y_i \ne G_m(x_i)\} / \sum_i w_i;
sets its vote to the log-odds \alpha_m = \log\bigl((1 - \operatorname{err}_m)/\operatorname{err}_m\bigr);
multiplies the weight of every misclassified example by e^{\alpha_m}.







Figure 9.6: AdaBoost with decision stumps on 60 points labelled by the diagonal. Left: the first stump, with its nine mistakes ringed. Middle: point areas show the weights before round 2, the mistakes now heavy, and the second stump that responds to them. Right: the region the weighted vote of 40 stumps calls positive, an additive staircase that classifies every training point correctly.



The weights look arbitrary, and the notes justify them: AdaBoost is forward stagewise additive modelling under the exponential loss e^{-y f(x)}, adding one stump at a time and choosing each stump’s coefficient to minimise that loss with the earlier ones fixed. That derivation gives a coefficient of \frac12 \log\bigl((1 - \operatorname{err}_m)/
\operatorname{err}_m\bigr) — half the vote above. The generator runs both versions side by side for 40 rounds: they choose the same stump every round, their coefficients differ by a factor of exactly 2, and since doubling every vote does not change the sign of the sum, they make the same prediction everywhere on a fine grid.
On the diagonal data the first stump has weighted error 0.15 and the second 0.18. Training error is 15\,\% after two rounds, 5\,\% after five, 1.7\,\% after ten, and zero from round twenty, each stump being only a little better than chance — by round 40 the newest stump’s weighted error is 0.35. Freund and Schapire’s bound guarantees this kind of progress: training error is at most \prod_m 2\sqrt{\operatorname{err}_m(1 - \operatorname{err}_m)}, which shrinks geometrically as long as every stump beats chance by some margin. The generator asserts the bound at every round; it is 0.068 at round 20 and 0.023 at round 40.
The additive structure that trees lack (Section 9.6) is exactly what boosting adds, since the ensemble is a sum. That cuts both ways, and the notes say so where the lecture does not: because each new model depends on the earlier ones, adding rounds raises the risk of overfitting, unlike adding trees to a bagged ensemble. The number of rounds is chosen on held-out data. 1:20:08 The same stagewise idea with other losses gives gradient boosting, and with engineering on top, XGBoost.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes-ensemble, section 1, covers the bootstrap, aggregation and their combination with trees; section 2 gives AdaBoost, states that it is forward stagewise additive modelling under the exponential loss (leaving the derivation to The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 10.4), and sketches gradient boosting.
crumbs: 9  Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods

title: 10  Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
10.1 Logistic regression as one neuron
Based on the lecture by Kian Katanforoosh — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
A neural network is logistic regression repeated and stacked. One neuron computes a linear function of its inputs and passes the result through a non-linearity; a layer is several neurons reading the same inputs; a network is layers feeding one another. This lecture builds that up one step at a time from a classifier the course already has, and at each step asks the same three questions: what the output means, what the loss must therefore be, and how many parameters there are. It ends with the forward pass written in matrices, for one example and for a whole batch, and with the reason gradients are computed from the last layer backwards, which the next chapter works out in full.
The two deep-learning lectures are given by Kian Katanforoosh, who teaches CS230, the Stanford deep-learning course. 1:02 He opens with the usual account of why the methods took off when they did: GPUs made the computation affordable, the digitised world made large datasets available, and these models are flexible enough to keep improving as the data grows, which older methods mostly stop doing.
3:05 The running task is to say whether an image contains a cat: output a number close to 1 if it does and close to 0 if it does not. A colour image of 64 \times 64 pixels is three such grids, one per red, green and blue channel, so it is 64 \cdot 64 \cdot 3 = 12{,}288 numbers. Logistic regression needs a vector, so the first step is simply to flatten the image into a column vector x \in \mathbb{R}^{12288}, and then
\hat y = \sigma(wx + b), \qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}.
\tag{10.1}
This is the model of Section 3.6 with the intercept split out: \theta^\top x with a constant feature becomes wx + b, where b plays the role of \theta_0 and w holds the rest. 6:03 Since \hat y is a scalar and x is 12{,}288 \times 1, w must be a row vector, 1 \times 12{,}288. The lecture asks for that shape before anything else, and the habit of checking shapes first carries the whole of the next chapter.
Training is the familiar loop: initialise w and b, minimise the logistic loss
L(\hat y, y) = -\bigl[\,y \log \hat y + (1 - y)\log(1 - \hat y)\,\bigr]
\tag{10.2}
by gradient descent, then predict with the fitted parameters. The loss is the negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli model, so minimising it is maximum likelihood. What Katanforoosh stresses is its role: the function we actually want, the one that recognises cats, has parameters we cannot write down, and the loss is the proxy we can optimise in their place.
10:26 The model has 12{,}288 weights and one bias. There is a quicker way to count that the lecture uses from here on: draw the model with one edge from each input to the neuron, and there is one weight per edge and one bias per neuron. It also shows something unwelcome, that the parameter count grows with the size of the input. A larger image means a larger w, and the lecture flags this as something to change later; convolutional networks, which share weights across the image, are the change.
11:34 Two slogans come out of this. The first is that a neuron is a linear part plus an activation: z = wx + b, then a = g(z), with the sigmoid as one choice of g among several. The second is that a model is an architecture plus parameters. When a team says it has shipped a model, it has shipped two files, one describing the computation and one holding the numbers that computation uses. The rest of the lecture changes the architecture and lets the parameters, still called W and b, grow.

title: 10  Introduction to Neural Networks
text: Figure 10.1: Logistic regression drawn as a neuron. The image is flattened into x, every entry reaches the neuron along its own weighted edge, and the neuron computes a linear part z followed by the activation \sigma.

title: 10  Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
10.2 Three animals, three neurons
13:42 Now the task is to detect a cat, a lion and an iguana. The obvious extension is to put three neurons side by side, each connected to every pixel, each computing its own logistic regression:

\hat y_k = a^{[1]}_k = \sigma\bigl(w^{[1]}_k x + b^{[1]}_k\bigr), \qquad k = 1, 2, 3.

The square-bracket superscript names the layer and the subscript the neuron within it. This network has one layer, whose neurons do not talk to one another, and its output \hat y is now a vector of three numbers. 17:08 Each neuron has its own weights, so the parameter count triples, to 3n + 3 = 36{,}867 for n = 12{,}288.
The labels must change with the output. 18:42 An image of a cat gets (1, 0, 0), a lion (0, 1, 0), an iguana (0, 0, 1), and the loss is the sum of three logistic losses, one per entry. Which neuron ends up detecting cats is decided by nothing more than this labelling convention: the first neuron is only ever compared with the first entry, so it becomes the cat detector, and had the convention put cats second, the second neuron would have.
20:37 The same observation answers the question of an image showing a cat and a lion. Label it (1, 1, 0) and nothing breaks, because the three neurons are trained independently; each sigmoid depends only on its own weights, and nothing forces the outputs to add up to anything. 22:32 As a student points out, the network is not yet a network in any interesting sense: it is three logistic regressions that happen to share an input.
23:49 The case where this design is the wrong one is when the classes exclude each other: a cell image showing exactly one of many diseases, say. The lecture’s argument is that a very rare class, the one iguana in a zoo of thousands of lions and cats, leaves its neuron almost untrained. That needs one qualification. The iguana neuron does receive a gradient on every image: the derivative of its logistic loss with respect to its logit is \sigma(z_3) - y_3, which on an image without an iguana is \sigma(z_3) > 0 and pushes the neuron towards saying “no iguana”. What the neuron lacks is positive examples, and a softmax does not create those either. The real reason to prefer a softmax for exclusive classes is that it builds the exclusivity into the model, which is the subject of the next section.

title: 10  Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
10.3 Softmax: one class per image
25:10 Add the constraint that each image shows exactly one of the three animals. Write the linear part of neuron k as z^{[1]}_k = w^{[1]}_k x + b^{[1]}_k, drop the three sigmoids, and replace them by a single function of all three logits:

\hat y_k = \frac{e^{z^{[1]}_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{3} e^{z^{[1]}_j}}.
\tag{10.3}
This is the softmax of softmax regression, derived as a generalised linear model in Section 4.7. 28:27 Its outputs are positive and sum to one, so they form a probability distribution over the classes. It can no longer say “probably a cat and probably a lion”: raising one output lowers the others. Labels are one-hot, (1,0,0), (0,1,0) or (0,0,1), and the prediction is the class with the largest output. 30:03 The constraint also bakes in an assumption that one of the three animals is always present; if images with none of them can occur, a fourth class for “no animal” has to be added. The parameter count does not change, since the softmax has no parameters of its own: still 3n + 3.






Figure 10.2: The same logits, z = (2.0, 1.5, -1.0), through three independent sigmoids and through a softmax. The sigmoids can report two animals at once and their outputs need not sum to anything; the softmax shares one unit of probability among the classes.



33:17 A student asks what happens if this network is trained on the multi-hot label (1, 1, 0) anyway. The lecture’s guess is that it will settle near (\tfrac12, \tfrac12,
0), and that is exactly right: with the cross-entropy loss below, the best a distribution can do against two targets of 1 is split its mass equally between them, and the generator, training a softmax on that label by gradient descent, ends at (0.5000, 0.5000, 0.0000). The fit can never be exact, because the outputs sum to 1 and the label sums to 2.
34:07 The loss has to change too. For the three independent sigmoids the derivative of the summed loss with respect to w^{[1]}_2 involves only the second term, since the other two do not depend on w^{[1]}_2. Under a softmax every output depends on every logit through the denominator, so the loss is the softmax cross-entropy

L(\hat y, y) = -\sum_{k=1}^{3} y_k \log \hat y_k,
\tag{10.4}
which for a one-hot y is just -\log of the probability given to the right class. The lecture leaves its derivative as an exercise and suggests it is harder than the sigmoid case. It looks harder and is not. The coupling through the denominator cancels, and for a one-hot label the gradient with respect to the logits is

\frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{[1]}_k} = \hat y_k - y_k,
\tag{10.5}
the same form as the logistic loss of one sigmoid neuron, \sigma(z) - y. The generator checks both against finite differences on 500 random logit vectors. This shared form is not a coincidence: both are canonical-link GLMs (Section 4.4), and it is the reason the next chapter’s backpropagation starts from “prediction minus label” at the output whichever of the two is used.

title: 10  Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
10.4 Predicting a number
37:17 Suppose instead the network has to estimate the cat’s age. One answer, from the room, is to treat each age as a class and use a softmax, since a cat has exactly one age. The other is to make it a regression, and that changes two things. The sigmoid at the output has to go, since it confines \hat y to (0, 1). With the identity in its place, the one-neuron model is linear regression. 39:29 A better choice here is the rectified linear unit,

\operatorname{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z),

which is linear for positive inputs and zero for negative ones, a natural fit for a quantity that cannot be negative. The loss changes as well, to the absolute or squared error between \hat y and y. The lecture’s reason is that these are easier to optimise for regression than the logistic loss would be; the reason from the earlier chapters is that squared error is the log-likelihood of a Gaussian output, just as the logistic loss is the log-likelihood of a Bernoulli one, and a student’s suggestion of a Poisson output for counts would pick the matching loss in the same way.

title: 10  Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
10.5 Hidden layers
41:16 Back to cat or no cat, but with more neurons: a layer of three, feeding a layer of two, feeding one output neuron. 43:00 The only hard constraint on the architecture is at the end, where the output layer must have one neuron per number to be predicted. The parameter count follows from one weight per edge and one bias per neuron:

\underbrace{3n + 3}_{\text{layer 1}} + \underbrace{2 \cdot 3 + 2}_{\text{layer 2}} + \underbrace{2 + 1}_{\text{layer 3}} = 3n + 14 = 36{,}878.

Adding two layers cost eleven parameters; 99.97\,\% of the network is still the first layer, because that is the layer that touches all 12{,}288 pixels.
44:31 Some vocabulary. A layer is a set of neurons that are not connected to one another. Katanforoosh calls the first layer of neurons the input layer, the last the output layer, and the one between a hidden layer; the official notes, and this book, instead treat the input x as layer 0 and count only layers of neurons, which gives the same three. His reason for “hidden” is that the layer sees neither the input nor the label, only what the previous layer hands it. The more common reading is about the training data: it supplies values for the inputs and the outputs and never for these units, so what they compute is not specified by anyone.
45:31 What they do compute, in a network trained on enough cat images, is usually described as a hierarchy: neurons early on respond to edges, later ones combine edges into ears and eyes, and the output combines those into a face. 1:03:48 A student later asks why the first layer should find edges, and the lecture’s answer is that those neurons see only pixels, which is too granular to see more. For the network on the board that argument does not hold. Each neuron of a fully connected first layer is a weighted sum of all 12{,}288 pixels, a template the size of the whole image, and nothing prevents that template from looking like a face. The edge story comes from convolutional networks, whose first-layer neurons each look at a small patch of the image; for them a local pattern such as an edge is about all a single neuron can represent, and there the argument is right.
46:44 The second example makes the point about hidden units from the other side. Predict a house’s price from its size, number of bedrooms, zip code and the wealth of the neighbourhood. An engineer wiring the network by hand would give each hidden neuron a job: size and bedrooms say how large a family fits, the zip code says how walkable the area is, the zip code and wealth say how good the nearby school is, and those three predict the price better than the raw inputs. 48:51 A fully connected layer instead links every input to every neuron of the next layer and lets training decide what each hidden neuron computes. It often finds better features than the hand-designed ones, at the price of not saying what they are, which is why neural networks get called black boxes. Training only from input to label, with nothing constrained in between, is what end-to-end learning means.






Figure 10.3: Four inputs, three hidden neurons and a price. Left: the edges chosen from domain knowledge, so that each hidden neuron computes a named quantity. Right: a fully connected layer, where every hidden neuron sees every input and its meaning is left to training.

title: 10  Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
10.6 Forward propagation and shapes
51:31 For the three-layer cat network, pushing one example from input to output is six lines, each layer a linear part and an activation:

\begin{aligned}
z^{[1]} &= W^{[1]} x + b^{[1]}, & a^{[1]} &= \sigma\bigl(z^{[1]}\bigr),\\
z^{[2]} &= W^{[2]} a^{[1]} + b^{[2]}, & a^{[2]} &= \sigma\bigl(z^{[2]}\bigr),\\
z^{[3]} &= W^{[3]} a^{[2]} + b^{[3]}, & \hat y = a^{[3]} &= \sigma\bigl(z^{[3]}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.6}
This is forward propagation. Where Section 10.2 wrote one equation per neuron, these write one per layer: W^{[1]} stacks the three neurons’ weight rows into a matrix, and the sigmoid is applied entry by entry.
53:13 The shapes follow from two facts, that z^{[l]} has one entry per neuron in layer l and that W^{[l]} must turn the previous layer’s activations into it. So z^{[1]} is 3 \times 1 and x is n \times 1, which forces W^{[1]} to be 3 \times n; a^{[1]} is 3 \times 1 and z^{[2]} is 2 \times 1, so W^{[2]} is 2 \times 3, one entry per edge between the layers; and W^{[3]} is 1 \times 2. In general W^{[l]} is n_l \times n_{l-1} and b^{[l]} is n_l \times 1, where n_l is the width of layer l. Katanforoosh’s advice is to know every shape in the network before writing a line of code, and it is the tool that makes the next chapter’s derivatives come out right.






Figure 10.4: The 3-2-1 network with the shape of every parameter and activation. Each weight matrix has one row per neuron in its layer and one column per neuron, or input, in the layer before.

title: 10  Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
10.7 Vectorising over a batch
54:59 Recall the two ends of gradient descent from Section 2.6: stochastic gradient descent updates after every example, with a noisy direction; batch gradient descent updates after seeing all of them, with an accurate one. Either way, a network with many layers does a lot of arithmetic per example, and the way to make that fast is to process many examples in one set of matrix operations rather than in a loop.
55:59 Stack m examples as the columns of an n \times m matrix X = [x^{(1)} \cdots
x^{(m)}], using round-bracket superscripts for the example and square brackets for the layer. Then the first layer for the whole batch is

Z^{[1]} = W^{[1]} X + b^{[1]},
\tag{10.7}
and Z^{[1]} is 3 \times m, its i-th column the z^{[1]} of example i. W^{[1]} is still 3 \times n: 59:21 feeding the network a thousand images does not give it more parameters. 59:36 But that leaves Equation 10.7 adding a 3 \times m matrix to a 3
\times 1 vector, which is not defined. The fix is broadcasting: read b^{[1]} as the 3 \times m matrix whose columns are all b^{[1]}, so the same bias is added to every example. NumPy does this automatically when the shapes are compatible. The generator checks that the broadcast batch computation gives column for column what the per-example loop gives. The remaining lines of Equation 10.6 become capital-letter versions in the same way; the lecture leaves writing them out, with their shapes, as an exercise.
Two student questions in this stretch are worth keeping. 1:03:05 One asks how this differs from principal component analysis, which also builds new features from the inputs.
