PCA is unsupervised: it finds the directions along which the inputs vary most and never looks at a label. The hidden layer is trained to predict y, and a direction of large input variance that does not help with that is of no interest to it.
1:05:53 The other asks how to choose the number of layers and neurons. Nobody knows in advance, so the honest answer is to train several architectures and compare them on the validation set, as in Section 8.4. Experience narrows the search: a harder problem needs more data and a deeper network, and judging which problem is harder is a skill. Telling cats from non-cats seems harder than telling day from night, since cats come in many breeds and nights do not, though even day or night has its trap, a photo taken indoors next to a small window.

title: 10  Introduction to Neural Networks
section: 10.8 The cost, and why backpropagation starts at the end
text:
10.8 The cost, and why backpropagation starts at the end
1:09:06 With the architecture fixed, what is left is to find its parameters W^{[1]}, b^{[1]}, \dots, W^{[3]}, b^{[3]}. The objective over a batch is the average loss,

J(\hat Y, Y) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} L\bigl(\hat y^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\bigr),
\tag{10.8}
with L the logistic loss of Equation 10.2. The lecture keeps the words apart: the loss is the error on one example, the cost the average over a batch. 1:11:13 Differentiation is linear, so the gradient of J is the average of the gradients of the per-example losses, and it is enough to work out derivatives of L and average at the end. The generator confirms this numerically.
1:12:55 Gradient descent then updates every layer,

W^{[l]} \leftarrow W^{[l]} - \alpha \frac{\partial J}{\partial W^{[l]}}, \qquad
b^{[l]} \leftarrow b^{[l]} - \alpha \frac{\partial J}{\partial b^{[l]}}, \qquad l = 1, 2, 3,
\tag{10.9}
which needs six derivatives. 1:14:13 Asked which to compute first, the room suggests W^{[1]}, and Katanforoosh argues for W^{[3]}. It is the closest to the loss, so its effect on J passes through the fewest functions, while W^{[1]} affects J through every layer above it. Splitting the derivative along the chain of the forward pass,

\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[3]}} =
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{[3]}}\,
\frac{\partial a^{[3]}}{\partial z^{[3]}}\,
\frac{\partial z^{[3]}}{\partial W^{[3]}},

every factor is easy, and the first two together are \partial L / \partial z^{[3]}. 1:17:33 The next layer down needs exactly that quantity again:

\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[2]}} =
\frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{[3]}}\,
\frac{\partial z^{[3]}}{\partial a^{[2]}}\,
\frac{\partial a^{[2]}}{\partial z^{[2]}}\,
\frac{\partial z^{[2]}}{\partial W^{[2]}},

so it is computed once and reused, and the same happens one layer further down with \partial L / \partial z^{[2]}. That is the whole idea of backpropagation: start at the loss, apply the chain rule one layer at a time, and carry the error backwards instead of recomputing it. 1:18:42 The forward equations say which path the chain must take. z^{[3]} depends on W^{[2]} only through a^{[2]}, so the chain for W^{[2]} runs through a^{[2]} and not through W^{[3]}, which is a dead end. The derivation, with the shapes that make the products well defined, is the first half of Section 11.1 in the next chapter.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes-deep_learning, section 1, builds the network from the housing example; section 2 vectorises the output computation and the computation over training examples; section 3.1 counts the parameters of the three-layer network (3n + 14) and explains why they cannot all start at zero. The backpropagation derivation is in section 3 and in the separate cs229-notes-backprop.

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
text:
11.1 The gradient at the output
Based on the lecture by Kian Katanforoosh — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Backpropagation is the chain rule applied one layer at a time from the loss downwards, with each layer’s intermediate result handed to the layer below instead of being recomputed. For the three-layer network of the previous chapter it comes down to one recurrence: the error at the output is prediction minus label, and each layer’s error is the next layer’s error carried back through the transposed weights and multiplied entry by entry by the slope of the activation. The first third of the lecture derives that by hand. The rest is about why a network that computes its gradients correctly can still fail to train, and the standard remedies: the choice of activation, normalised inputs, initial weights of the right size, mini-batches and momentum.
The lecture continues the previous one, again given by Kian Katanforoosh, on the same running example: a 64 \times 64 colour image flattened into x \in \mathbb{R}^n, a layer of three sigmoid neurons, a layer of two, and one sigmoid output that says whether the image shows a cat (Section 10.6).
5:41 The cost is the average of the per-example logistic losses, and since differentiation is linear it is enough to differentiate one loss and average at the end (Section 10.8). Write the loss for one example with the output layer spelled out,
L = -\Bigl[\,y \log \sigma\bigl(W^{[3]} a^{[2]} + b^{[3]}\bigr) + (1 - y)\log\Bigl(1 - \sigma\bigl(W^{[3]} a^{[2]} + b^{[3]}\bigr)\Bigr)\Bigr],
and differentiate with respect to W^{[3]}, the parameter closest to it. Each term is a logarithm of a sigmoid of a linear function, so the chain rule gives three factors: 1/a^{[3]} from the logarithm, a^{[3]}(1 - a^{[3]}) from the sigmoid, whose derivative is \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr), and the derivative of W^{[3]} a^{[2]} + b^{[3]} with respect to W^{[3]}. The second term is the same with 1/(1 - a^{[3]}) and a minus sign. 15:46 The sigmoid factors cancel against the logarithm’s, the cross terms cancel against each other, and what is left is
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[3]}} = \bigl(a^{[3]} - y\bigr)\, a^{[2]\top}.
\tag{11.1}
The result “doesn’t look that bad,” as Katanforoosh puts it, and it is the same prediction-minus-label form as logistic regression (Equation 10.5), with the activations of the layer below standing in for the input.
12:05 A student asks where the transpose comes from. The answer is a shape argument, and it is the tool for the rest of the derivation. L is a scalar and W^{[3]} is 1 \times 2, so the derivative of one with respect to the other has one entry per entry of W^{[3]} and must be 1 \times 2 as well. In scalar calculus the derivative of wa with respect to w is a; here a^{[2]} is 2 \times 1, which is the wrong shape, so the answer has to be a^{[2]\top}. Either learn the matrix-calculus identities by heart, or learn to check shapes. The bias works the same way and gives \partial L / \partial b^{[3]} = a^{[3]} - y. Averaging over a batch, the cost’s gradient is \frac1m \sum_i (a^{[3](i)} - y^{(i)})\, a^{[2](i)\top}, which in the matrix notation of Section 10.7 is the single product \frac1m (A^{[3]} - Y) A^{[2]\top}: the sum over examples is done by the matrix multiplication.
crumbs: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
section: 11.2 The chain rule, one layer down
text:
11.2 The chain rule, one layer down
19:05 For W^{[2]} the lecture does not start over. It decomposes the derivative along the path that connects W^{[2]} to the loss in the forward equations:

\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[2]}} =
\underbrace{\frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{[3]}}\,\frac{\partial a^{[3]}}{\partial z^{[3]}}}_{\partial L/\partial z^{[3]}}\,
\frac{\partial z^{[3]}}{\partial a^{[2]}}\,
\frac{\partial a^{[2]}}{\partial z^{[2]}}\,
\frac{\partial z^{[2]}}{\partial W^{[2]}}.

20:24 The path has to go through a^{[2]}. z^{[3]} = W^{[3]} a^{[2]} + b^{[3]} also depends on W^{[3]} and b^{[3]}, but differentiating with respect to those leads nowhere: they do not depend on W^{[2]}, and the error has to travel through variables that do. 22:04 Asked which part of this is already known, a student says the first three factors and then corrects it to two, which is right: since \partial L / \partial W^{[3]} = (\partial L / \partial z^{[3]})\, a^{[2]\top}, Equation 11.1 says \partial L / \partial z^{[3]} = a^{[3]} - y. The remaining factors are each one step of the forward pass. \partial a^{[2]}/\partial z^{[2]} is the sigmoid’s derivative, a^{[2]} \circ (1 - a^{[2]}); \partial z^{[2]} / \partial W^{[2]} brings in a^{[1]\top} as before; and 25:24 \partial z^{[3]}/\partial a^{[2]} is W^{[3]} or its transpose, which the shapes decide: z^{[3]} is a scalar and a^{[2]} is 2 \times 1, so the factor is the 2 \times 1 vector W^{[3]\top}.
28:01 Written in the order the chain rule produced them, the factors are 1 \times 1, 2 \times 1, 2 \times 1 and 1 \times 3, and they do not multiply. The derivation so far was a bookkeeping of which quantities appear, not of how they combine. Two facts put them together. The sigmoid acts on each entry of z^{[2]} separately, so its derivative enters as an entry-by-entry product, written \circ, and that is true of every activation. And the result must have the shape of W^{[2]}, 2 \times 3, which fixes the order of the rest:

\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[2]}} = \Bigl(W^{[3]\top}\bigl(a^{[3]} - y\bigr) \circ a^{[2]} \circ \bigl(1 - a^{[2]}\bigr)\Bigr)\, a^{[1]\top}.
\tag{11.2}
Inside the parentheses is a 2 \times 1 vector, \partial L/\partial z^{[2]}, and the outer product with the 1 \times 3 vector a^{[1]\top} gives 2 \times 3. The lecture leaves W^{[1]} as an exercise; it comes out the same way, and the pattern is worth stating once in general. Write \delta^{[l]} = \partial L / \partial z^{[l]} for the error at layer l of an N-layer network with activation g. Then

\delta^{[N]} = a^{[N]} - y, \qquad
\delta^{[l]} = \bigl(W^{[l+1]\top} \delta^{[l+1]}\bigr) \circ g'\bigl(z^{[l]}\bigr), \qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[l]}} = \delta^{[l]}\, a^{[l-1]\top}, \qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{[l]}} = \delta^{[l]},
\tag{11.3}
with a^{[0]} = x. The first equation holds for a sigmoid output with the logistic loss and for a softmax with cross-entropy alike. The generator implements exactly these four lines for the 3-2-1 sigmoid network and compares every one of its parameters’ gradients with finite differences on fifty random networks; the worst disagreement is 4 \times
10^{-10}.
31:21 Katanforoosh’s view is that hardly anyone derives these by hand any more, since programming frameworks differentiate automatically, but that it is worth having done once, both to understand what the framework is doing and to read papers that write gradients out. For the rigorous version he points to the lecture notes.
crumbs: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
section: 11.3 What the forward pass must keep
text:
11.3 What the forward pass must keep
32:04 Every factor in Equation 11.3 other than \delta itself is something the forward pass already computed: the activations a^{[1]}, a^{[2]}, a^{[3]}, the values g'(z^{[l]}) depend on, and the weights. Discard them and the backward pass would have to re-run the forward pass from x each time it needed one, going forwards again to reach a^{[2]}, then again to reach a^{[1]}. So the forward pass caches what it computes and the backward pass reads it. This is a trade of memory for computation, and the memory is not small: every activation of every layer for every example in the batch is held until the backward pass reaches it.






Figure 11.1: Forward pass on top, left to right, caching each value. Backward pass below, right to left: the output error \delta^{[3]} = a^{[3]} - y is carried down by W^{[l+1]\top} and the activation’s slope, and each layer’s weight gradient is its \delta times the cached activation that fed it.
crumbs: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
text:
11.4 Activation functions
34:44 Getting the gradients right is necessary and nowhere near sufficient; a network built and differentiated correctly usually still trains badly, and the rest of the lecture is the set of practical fixes. The first is the choice of activation. There are three in common use:

\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, \qquad
\tanh(z) = \frac{e^{z} - e^{-z}}{e^{z} + e^{-z}}, \qquad
\operatorname{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z),

with derivatives \sigma(1 - \sigma), 1 - \tanh^2, and the indicator \mathbb{1}\{z > 0\}. 37:08 The sigmoid’s strength is that its output reads as a probability. Its weakness, which a student names, is saturation: for large positive or negative z the curve is flat, its derivative is nearly zero, and since that derivative is a factor in every \delta below it, layers early in the network get almost no gradient and barely move. The derivative is small even at its best. Its maximum is \tfrac14, at z = 0, so every sigmoid layer shrinks the gradient passing through it by at least a factor of four, and ten of them shrink it by at least 4^{10}, about a million. tanh saturates in the same way at both ends, but its slope at the centre is 1 and its output is centred on zero.
38:52 ReLU does not saturate for positive inputs: its slope there is exactly 1, so it passes the gradient through unchanged rather than scaling it down. Its slope for negative inputs is exactly 0, which has its own cost the lecture does not get to: a ReLU neuron whose input is negative for every example receives no gradient at all and stops learning. That trade has worked out well enough that ReLU is the usual choice for hidden layers.






Figure 11.2: Sigmoid, tanh and ReLU (solid) with their derivatives (dashed). Only ReLU keeps a slope of 1 for large inputs; the sigmoid’s slope never exceeds 0.25.



39:53 For the output layer the choice is made by the range of what is predicted, not by trainability: a sigmoid for a probability in (0, 1), tanh for values in (-1, 1) such as the rewards of reinforcement learning, a ReLU for a non-negative quantity such as a house price, the identity for an unrestricted one. 45:18 Within a hidden layer the convention is one activation for every neuron, so that a layer is described as, say, a fully connected ReLU layer. People have tried mixing activations inside a layer without finding a reason to, and the choice is treated as a hyperparameter like any other, settled by experiment rather than by theory.
crumbs: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
section: 11.5 Why the network needs a non-linearity
crumbs: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
text:
11.6 Normalising the inputs
48:16 If the inputs are large, z = Wx + b is large and the sigmoids saturate before training starts. The simple remedy is to standardise the inputs using the training set: compute the mean and variance of each feature,

\mu = \frac1m \sum_{i=1}^{m} x^{(i)}, \qquad
\sigma^2 = \frac1m \sum_{i=1}^{m} \bigl(x^{(i)} - \mu\bigr)^2,

entry by entry, and replace every x by (x - \mu)/\sigma. Subtracting \mu centres the cloud of points on the origin; dividing by \sigma gives every feature the same spread.
51:18 The second reason is the shape of the cost. When features have very different scales, or sit far from zero, the cost is a long narrow valley in parameter space, and gradient descent, which moves perpendicular to the contours, crosses the valley again and again while making slow progress along it. After standardising, the contours are closer to circles, the gradient points nearly at the minimum, and descent goes almost straight there. Figure 11.3 makes the comparison on a least-squares problem with two features, one centred at 2 and the other on a small scale. The ratio of the cost’s curvatures along its two axes is 29 with the raw inputs and 1 after standardising, and gradient descent, each run at its best fixed learning rate, needs 100 steps against 2. Standardising equalises scales, not correlations: afterwards the curvature matrix of a least-squares cost is the features’ correlation matrix, so two strongly correlated features still leave a long valley, tilted at 45°, which decorrelating transforms such as the PCA of a later chapter address.






Figure 11.3: Contours of a least-squares cost in its two weights and the path of gradient descent, with raw inputs (left) and the same inputs standardised (right). Each run uses its best fixed learning rate.



53:03 One rule matters more than the formulas: \mu and \sigma are computed on the training set and then reused, unchanged, on the dev and test sets. The network has learned to expect inputs transformed in one particular way, and normalising the test set by its own statistics would feed it a differently transformed input.
crumbs: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
text:
11.7 Vanishing and exploding gradients
54:19 To see why depth makes all of this harder, take a network of ten layers with two neurons each, identity activations and zero biases. The output is then the input multiplied by every weight matrix in turn,

\hat y = W^{[N]} W^{[N-1]} \cdots W^{[1]} x.

56:05 If every W^{[l]} is a little larger than the identity, say 1.5\,I, the product is 1.5^{N} I, which for N = 10 is about 58; if every one is 0.5\,I, it is 0.5^{10}
\approx 0.001. Small departures from 1 compound geometrically. 57:16 The same products appear in the backward pass, because Equation 11.3 multiplies by W^{[l+1]\top} and by g' once per layer, so the gradients reaching the early layers either explode or vanish. With sigmoids the g' factors alone contribute at most \tfrac14 each (Section 11.4). Nothing in the gradient computation is wrong; the arithmetic is simply unforgiving over many layers.
crumbs: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
text:
11.8 Initialising the weights
58:24 The lecture’s goal is to keep each layer’s multiplier “close to 1”, which needs a little care, because that is a statement about the layer and not about individual weights. A neuron computes z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i, a sum of n terms, and the more inputs it has, the larger z gets unless the weights shrink to compensate. Make that precise: if the weights and inputs are independent with mean zero, then

\operatorname{Var}(z) = n \operatorname{Var}(w)\operatorname{Var}(x),

so z has the same variance as its inputs when \operatorname{Var}(w) = 1/n, or standard deviation 1/\sqrt{n}. The lecture’s code multiplies standard normal draws by \sqrt{1/n^{[l-1]}}, where n^{[l-1]} is the number of inputs to layer l. The generator checks the variance identity by simulation, getting 0.96 against 1.
1:02:07 Katanforoosh reports, as an empirical observation, that a ReLU network trains better with 2 in place of 1. There is a clean reason, given by He et al. (2015): a ReLU zeroes the negative half of a symmetric input, which halves the mean square of what it passes on, so the variance needs to start twice as large to come out the same. Figure 11.4 shows how quickly this matters. In a 30-layer ReLU network with weights of variance 1/n, the signal loses half its mean square at every layer and ends about 2^{-15} of its starting size; with 4/n it grows by the same factor; with 2/n it stays level.






Figure 11.4: The root-mean-square size of the pre-activations at each layer of a 30-layer ReLU network, 64 units wide, for three weight variances. Only 2/n holds the signal steady.



1:02:38 The lecture then presents “Xavier initialisation” and “Glorot initialisation” as two different schemes. They are one person’s name: the method is from Glorot and Bengio (2010), whose first author is Xavier Glorot. The paper asks for two things at once, that activations keep their variance going forwards, which needs n_{\text{in}} \operatorname{Var}(w) = 1, and that gradients keep theirs going backwards, which needs n_{\text{out}} \operatorname{Var}(w) = 1. Both cannot hold unless the layer is square, and the compromise it proposes is

\operatorname{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{\text{in}} + n_{\text{out}}},

the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the fan-in and fan-out (the lecture says a geometric average). This is the formula the official notes give, under the name “Xavier/He”, though He’s 2/n is a different rule for a different activation. Glorot and Bengio derived theirs for tanh-like units; for ReLU networks, He’s is the one that holds the variance.
1:04:02 Finally, the initial weights must be random, and not merely small. If all the weights of a layer start equal, every neuron in it computes the same function, receives the same gradient, and is updated identically, forever: the layer behaves as a single neuron, however wide it is. The generator trains the 3-2-1 network from equal weights for 6,000 steps of stochastic gradient descent, and the three hidden neurons’ weights end up identical to the last bit. Starting from zero is the extreme case, and the official notes work it through. Random initial values break the symmetry, so that the neurons start in different places and can learn different things; biases have no such problem and can start at zero.
crumbs: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
crumbs: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks

title: 11  Backprop and Improving Neural Networks
text:
11.10 Momentum
1:11:24 Return to the long narrow valley of Section 11.6. Gradient descent zig-zags across it because the steep direction dominates every gradient, and the useful step would be large along the valley and small across it. Momentum gets there by looking at the history of updates. 1:13:27 Averaged over a few steps, the components across the valley alternate in sign and cancel, while the components along it all point the same way and add up. Stepping along the average rather than the latest gradient damps the zig-zag and builds up speed along the floor. In the lecture’s form,

v \leftarrow \beta v + (1 - \beta)\,\frac{\partial J}{\partial W}, \qquad
W \leftarrow W - \alpha v,
\tag{11.5}
where v, the velocity, is an exponentially weighted average of past gradients, and \beta, often around 0.9, sets how long a memory it has. 1:15:42 It costs one more line of code and one more variable per parameter. The physical picture is a heavy ball rolling downhill: its velocity cannot reverse at every bump, and 1 - \beta plays the part of friction.
A computation sharpens the picture in a way the lecture does not. In this form, at the same learning rate as gradient descent, momentum helps only modestly: on a quadratic 100 times steeper across the valley than along it, gradient descent at its best fixed rate takes 346 steps to converge and momentum with \beta = 0.9 at that rate takes 272. The large gain comes from what momentum makes possible. Gradient descent diverges as soon as \alpha exceeds 2/\lambda_{\max}, here 0.02, while the averaging raises the limit to 2(1 + \beta) / \bigl((1 - \beta)\lambda_{\max}\bigr), here 0.38. At \alpha = 0.06, three times the rate that makes gradient descent blow up, momentum converges in 90 steps.






Figure 11.5: The first 60 steps of gradient descent (at its best fixed rate) and of momentum (at a rate three times past gradient descent’s stability limit) on a quadratic 100 times steeper vertically than horizontally.



1:15:58 The optimisers used most in practice, RMSProp and Adam, go further and give every parameter its own effective learning rate, scaled by a running average of its squared gradients. Adam combines that scaling with momentum. The lecture’s closing point about them is a sociological one: a new optimiser has to prove itself across a wide range of problems before people adopt it, which is why so few are in common use.






NoteIn the official notes



cs229-notes-backprop derives the backward recurrence for a network of any depth, with the matrix calculus the lecture replaces by shape analysis. cs229-notes-deep_learning, section 3, covers backpropagation for the three-layer network; section 3.1 the parameter count, why zero and equal initialisations fail, and the variance-scaled initialisation; section 3.2 stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent and momentum; and section 3.3, which the lecture did not reach, L2 regularisation and parameter sharing.

title: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis
text:
12.1 What to try next
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
A learning algorithm that does not work can be fixed in a dozen ways, and most teams pick one at random. This lecture is about picking on evidence. Each diagnostic in it makes the same move: state a hypothesis about what is wrong, then find a measurement that comes out differently depending on whether the hypothesis holds. Learning curves separate an algorithm that overfits from one that underfits. Comparing two parameter vectors on the training objective tells a failing optimiser apart from an objective that is the wrong thing to optimise. Error analysis works out which stage of a pipeline is costing the most accuracy, and ablative analysis works out which component is actually earning its keep.
Ng is explicit that this is advice for building systems that work, not for writing research papers, and that it compresses what is otherwise learned from years of projects into a handful of worked scenarios. The chapter keeps his scenarios: a spam filter, an autonomous helicopter and a face-recognition door lock.
4:42 The running example is a spam filter. You have hand-picked a hundred words as features, trained logistic regression with a penalty on \lVert\theta\rVert^2 (which Ng also calls Bayesian logistic regression, since the penalty is a Gaussian prior on \theta; see Section 8.3), and it has 20 per cent test error. That is one mistake in every five emails, which is not good enough.
The list of things a team might try writes itself. Get more training examples. Use fewer features, since some of the hundred are probably irrelevant, or more features, since a hundred may be too few. Add features from the email header, including the routing information that records which servers the message passed through on its way to you. Run gradient descent for more iterations, or switch to Newton’s method. Change \lambda. Abandon logistic regression for an SVM or a neural network.
8:25 Ng’s observation is that teams usually pick one of these almost at random, going on what someone read the night before or what worked on the last project, and then spend days or weeks finding out whether it helped. Just writing the list down and weighing the options already puts a team ahead of most. The real fix is to work out first what kind of problem you have, because each item on the list treats only one kind. More data never hurts, but in some situations it barely helps, and finding that out by collecting it is expensive.
He also notes that he says “test error” in what follows but means error on a dev set, since decisions made by looking at the test set use it up (Section 8.4).
crumbs: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis

title: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis
text:
12.2 Learning curves
12:00 The diagnostic Ng says he uses on nearly every project is bias against variance (Section 8.1). An algorithm with high variance does much better on its training set than on the dev set. An algorithm with high bias does badly on both. The tool that tells these apart is the learning curve: training error and dev error against the number of training examples m, with a horizontal line at the error you need to reach for the application to be useful. The earlier bias–variance plots had model complexity on the horizontal axis. This one holds the model fixed and varies the amount of data.
Two facts set the shape. Dev error usually falls as m grows. Training error usually rises, because a small training set is easy to fit: logistic regression fits one email perfectly and five almost certainly, and a straight line passes through any two points. Only with many examples does the model start to miss some of them. Since training error is normally below dev error, the two curves approach each other from opposite sides.
Figure 12.1 draws both regimes for least-squares regression, where the expected curves have closed forms. With p Gaussian features, noise variance \sigma^2 and m > p + 1 examples, the expected training and test mean squared errors are

\mathbb{E}[\text{train}] = \sigma^2\Bigl(1 - \frac{p}{m}\Bigr), \qquad
\mathbb{E}[\text{test}] = \sigma^2\Bigl(1 + \frac{p}{m - p - 1}\Bigr).
\tag{12.1}
Any signal the model cannot represent acts as extra noise, so in an underfitting model \sigma^2 is replaced by the noise plus the variance it leaves unexplained. The generator checks both formulas against least squares fitted to simulated data.






Figure 12.1: Expected training and test error of least squares against training-set size, computed from Equation 12.1. Left: 20 features, of which 5 matter. Right: 2 features when the target needs more.



The left panel shows high variance: twenty features of which only five matter, so the fit chases noise. Ng reads two signals from a plot like this. The weaker one is that the dev error is still falling at the right edge, which suggests more data would help, but extrapolating a curve by eye is unreliable. The stronger one is the large gap between the curves. Training error sits near the target while dev error is well above it, and as the curves have to close that gap, more data will bring the dev error down. In this example it reaches the target at 155 examples.
The right panel shows high bias: two features when more are needed. Here the training error is already above the target, and since training error rises with m and dev error sits above training error, no amount of data brings the dev error below the target. The curves have nearly met and both have levelled off. Collecting more data in this situation might help slightly but can never get you where you need to go.
21:12 A student asks whether these shapes depend on the data. Ng’s answer is that they assume the training, dev and test sets come from one distribution, that learning theory suggests the dev error falls roughly as 1/\sqrt m, and that it need not fall to zero, because some examples are ambiguous even to an expert: a blurry X-ray, or a medical record that does not say whether the patient will survive the year.
The 1/\sqrt m is worth qualifying. It is the rate in the uniform convergence bound of the learning-theory chapter, which is a worst-case guarantee across a whole hypothesis class. A particular algorithm can approach its limit faster. For least squares, Equation 12.1 puts the test error’s excess over the noise at \sigma^2 p/(m-p-1), which falls as 1/m. Doubling the training set from 200 to 400 examples cuts the excess in the left panel from 0.112 to 0.053, a factor of 0.47, where 1/\sqrt m would predict 0.71. The practical effect is that a learning curve can flatten sooner than the bound suggests, which makes Ng’s warning against extrapolating curves by eye even more apt.
crumbs: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis

title: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis
section: 12.3 Matching the fix to the diagnosis
text:
12.3 Matching the fix to the diagnosis
19:08 With the diagnosis in hand, the first four items on the spam list sort themselves out. More training examples fix high variance: they are what moves the left panel’s dev curve down, and they do nothing much for the right panel. A smaller set of features also fixes high variance. Ng’s picture is a tenth-order polynomial that wiggles through every point, where dropping the high-order terms removes the wiggle. A larger set of features fixes high bias, as when a straight line is not doing well and you add a quadratic term. Header features are another way of adding information, so they are something to try against bias.
24:16 He adds advice on how to start, which the earlier chapter on Naive Bayes already raised (Section 6.4). On a new application it is very hard to know in advance what will go wrong, so implement something quick and dirty, such as plain logistic regression, run the bias–variance diagnosis on it, and let the result decide whether the next step is a bigger model or more data. The exception is a domain where you already have experience. Ng has done enough speech recognition to know roughly how much data a system needs, and someone who has read the face-recognition literature can build on it. Without that experience, the diagnosis on a simple system is the cheapest way to learn where the difficulty lies. His slides call the alternative, a careful up-front design of exactly the right features and architecture, a risk of “premature statistical optimisation”. The term parallels premature optimisation in software: effort spent on a part of the system that turns out not to be the bottleneck.
crumbs: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis

title: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis
text:
12.4 Optimisation algorithm or objective
26:30 The second diagnostic addresses the last four items on the list. Change the spam example: logistic regression now has 2 per cent error on spam and 2 per cent on non-spam. The first is tolerable, since you read the occasional spam message. The second is not, because it loses one important email in fifty. A teammate’s linear SVM gets 10 per cent error on spam but 0.01 per cent on non-spam, which is acceptable. You would still rather ship logistic regression, because it is cheaper to run and easier to update as new email arrives. What should you do?
Two quantities are in play. What you care about is a weighted accuracy on the dev set,

a(\theta) = \frac{\sum_i w^{(i)} \, 1\{h_\theta(x^{(i)}) = y^{(i)}\}}{\sum_i w^{(i)}},

with a larger weight w^{(i)} on the non-spam emails. What logistic regression maximises is something else, the regularised log-likelihood

J(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^m \log p\bigl(y^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}; \theta\bigr) - \lambda \lVert\theta\rVert^2 .

34:09 A student asks the natural question: why not maximise a(\theta) directly? Because it is a sum of indicator functions. As \theta moves, a stays constant until some example crosses the decision boundary and then jumps, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere and gradient ascent has nothing to follow. The generator confirms this: at random parameter vectors, a finite-difference gradient of the weighted accuracy is exactly zero. Ng adds that maximising it exactly is NP-hard. In the learning-theory literature this is the hardness of agnostically learning halfspaces: even finding a halfspace that classifies slightly better than chance on data that some halfspace classifies almost perfectly is intractable (Guruswami and Raghavendra, 2009). So we optimise J as a proxy, and the question is whether the proxy or its optimisation is letting us down.
Write \theta_{\text{SVM}} for the SVM’s parameters, put in the same (\theta, x) form as logistic regression, and \theta_{\text{BLR}} for logistic regression’s. We know that a(\theta_{\text{SVM}}) > a(\theta_{\text{BLR}}). Two hypotheses could explain this. Either the optimiser has not found the maximum of J, or J is the wrong function to maximise. 34:40 The diagnostic is to evaluate logistic regression’s own objective at both parameter vectors and see which is higher.
Case 1: J(\theta_{\text{SVM}}) > J(\theta_{\text{BLR}}). Logistic regression was trying to maximise J, yet the SVM, which was not even trying, found a point where J is higher. So \theta_{\text{BLR}} is not the maximiser, and the problem is the optimisation algorithm.
Case 2: J(\theta_{\text{SVM}}) \le J(\theta_{\text{BLR}}). Logistic regression did better on J, yet the SVM did better on a. A higher value of J therefore does not mean a higher weighted accuracy, so maximising J is not the right thing to do. The problem is the objective.
40:09 The remaining fixes on the list now sort the same way. Running gradient descent longer and switching to Newton’s method fix the optimisation algorithm, since Newton’s method maximises the same J, often much faster. Changing \lambda changes the objective, although Ng notes that in practice it is usually tuned for bias and variance instead. Switching to an SVM replaces the objective altogether. A student asks what to do once the objective is known to be wrong, and the honest answer is that nothing is automatic: you brainstorm objectives. In this example one obvious candidate is to put the weights w^{(i)} into the log-likelihood, but the diagnostic only says which category of fix to look in.
The two cases are not symmetric, and the slides claim more for case 2 than the inequality delivers. Case 1 is a proof: \theta_{\text{SVM}} is a point where J is higher than where the optimiser stopped, so the optimiser has not finished. Case 2 proves that the objective is wrong, but the slides go further and read it as “BLR succeeded at maximizing J”. The inequality says only that logistic regression beat one particular point, and nothing forces that point to be anywhere near the maximum. Figure 12.2 runs the test along a training run on a toy spam problem. An SVM with errors on non-spam weighted ten times wins on weighted accuracy, 0.927 against 0.855. Logistic regression starts from \theta = 0, and after a single gradient step its J already exceeds the SVM’s, -159.6 against -160.0, so case 2 fires. Gradient ascent then needs another 31 steps to get within one per cent of the optimum at -86.5.






Figure 12.2: Logistic regression’s objective along gradient ascent on a toy spam problem (log step axis), against its value at the SVM’s parameters. The SVM wins on weighted accuracy at every step.



The SVM’s J is low in this example partly because its parameters were never chosen to make good probabilities. Scaling \theta_{\text{SVM}} leaves every prediction, and hence a, unchanged but changes J. Here the best rescaling only lifts J(\theta_{\text{SVM}}) from -160.0 to -158.8, which is still nowhere near the optimum. So read case 2 as “the objective is wrong”, which it shows, and not as “the optimiser is fine”, which it does not. Both can be true at once. Ng’s own practice in the helicopter story below, re-running the diagnostics after each fix, covers exactly that.
crumbs: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis

title: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis
text:
12.5 The helicopter
43:17 The more complex example is the autonomous helicopter from Ng’s group, built in three steps. First build a simulator, because a simulated helicopter can crash a thousand times for free. Then choose a cost function. Ng keeps it simple for now: the squared distance \lVert x - x_{\text{desired}}\rVert^2 between where the helicopter is and where it should be, summed over the flight. Finally run a reinforcement-learning algorithm, which the course covers in its last lectures, to find controller parameters \theta_{\text{RL}} that minimise the expected cost J(\theta) in the simulator.
The resulting controller flies much worse than a human pilot. Each of the three steps suggests a fix, and 48:10 each fix could absorb a PhD. Simulators can always be made more accurate: airflow around a helicopter is complicated enough that parts of it are still not fully understood, so there is almost unlimited room to improve one. The cost function may be wrong. A hovering helicopter is not level, for example: the tail rotor pushes the body sideways and the pilot tilts against it, so penalising position alone may not capture what good flight is. And the reinforcement-learning algorithm may not be finding the minimum of J. Ng knows of a PhD thesis spent on helicopter simulation. That is a fine outcome if the goal is the thesis, and a poor one if the goal is a helicopter that flies.
49:50 The reasoning that cuts this down is the same as in the spam example. Suppose all three steps were sound: the simulator is accurate, the RL algorithm minimises J in it, and minimising J means flying well. Then \theta_{\text{RL}} would fly well on the real helicopter. It does not, so at least one of the three is false. The job is to find which, much as one isolates a bug in a large program by bisecting it instead of reading the whole code base. Figure 12.3 lays out the two tests.






Figure 12.3: The helicopter diagnostics. First check the controller in simulation, then compare the human pilot with the controller on the cost the RL algorithm minimises.



51:48 First, fly \theta_{\text{RL}} in the simulator. If it flies well there and badly in reality, the RL algorithm did its job on the problem it was given, and the simulator is what differs from the real world. A student asks whether the reverse can happen, flying badly in simulation and well in reality. Ng says it is rare, and when it happens he still works on the simulator. His group deliberately adds noise to its simulators so that a controller robust to the simulated noise is more likely to be robust to real disturbances, and a controller that does well in reality but not in simulation can mean that too much noise was added.
54:40 If the controller also flies badly in simulation, compare it with the human on the RL algorithm’s own cost: record the human pilot’s flight and evaluate the same squared error. If J(\theta_{\text{human}}) < J(\theta_{\text{RL}}), the human achieved a lower cost than the algorithm found, so the algorithm is not minimising J, and that is the part to improve. If J(\theta_{\text{human}}) \ge J(\theta_{\text{RL}}), the algorithm reached a cost at least as low as the human’s while flying worse, so a low J does not mean good flight, and the cost function is wrong. The same asymmetry as in the previous section applies here, now with the human as the witness point.
58:10 In the actual project, Ng says, the bottleneck moved around. For a few weeks the diagnostics pointed at the simulator; once it was good enough they pointed at the RL algorithm, and later at the cost function. Running them again after each round of work is what kept the team on the part that mattered. The cost function turned out to be the hard one, because it is not obvious how to write down mathematically what a good banked turn is. His student Adam Coates found a way through learning the target trajectory from several imperfect expert demonstrations, work published as Learning for Control from Multiple Demonstrations (Coates, Abbeel and Ng), which was presented in the award-paper session of ICML 2008.
crumbs: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis

title: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis
text:
12.6 Error analysis
1:01:24 Many applications are not one learning algorithm but a pipeline of them. Ng’s example is a camera by a door that unlocks for authorised people. The image goes through background removal, which with a fixed camera can be as simple as keeping the pixels that changed. Then a face detector finds the face, separate components segment the eyes, nose and mouth (the eyes being a particularly strong cue for identity), and logistic regression on those features decides whether to open the door. Ng adds that pipelines like this are what small data sets call for. His teams often get good results from a hundred examples, but only through more careful design than a single end-to-end model needs.
When such a system reaches 85 per cent accuracy, which component should you work on? 1:06:04 Ng tells the story of someone who chose background removal, which can be made almost arbitrarily sophisticated by modelling the trees and bushes moving behind the subject, and wrote a whole PhD thesis on it, without improving the face recognition he set out to build.
1:07:50 Error analysis answers the question by substituting ground truth. On the dev set, replace the output of background removal with a perfect one, labelled by hand, and measure the system’s accuracy. Then also give it perfect face locations, then perfect eye, nose and mouth segmentations, and finally perfect labels, which must give 100 per cent. Figure 12.4 shows the lecture’s numbers.






Figure 12.4: The face-recognition pipeline (top) and the system’s accuracy as each component, from left to right, is cumulatively replaced by ground truth (bottom). The lecture’s illustrative numbers.



Perfect background removal is worth 0.1 points, so a thesis on it can change the door lock’s accuracy by at most that much. Perfect face detection is worth almost six points and perfect eye segmentation another four, so those are the components to work on, in parallel if the team is big enough. The fifteen points between 85 and 100 per cent are divided among the stages, and each stage’s share bounds what improving it could gain.
Two student questions sharpen this. 1:11:13 Should the substitution be cumulative, as in the figure, or one component at a time? Ng’s answer is that either will do, that they usually agree, and that if you suspect they will not, you should run both. Ablation, below, gives a concrete case where they do not. 1:13:21 What if giving a component perfect output makes the system worse? That should be rare, and Ng’s advice is not to gloss over it. Treat it like a button that misbehaves only when the mouse hovers over it: an anomaly to understand, not one to dismiss because users will not notice. He also notes that the numbers are a guide to prioritisation, to be combined with a judgement of how hard each component would be to improve. They do not settle the decision by formula.
crumbs: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis

title: 12  Debugging ML Models and Error Analysis
text:
12.7 Ablative analysis
1:14:35 Error analysis explains the gap between where a system is and perfection. Ablative analysis explains the gap between where it is and a much worse baseline. Back to spam: suppose a good classifier has been built by adding clever components to plain logistic regression. These are spelling correction (spammers misspell words to get them past the tokeniser), features of the sending host, email header features, a parser for the email text, a JavaScript parser and features from images. Plain logistic regression gets 94 per cent and the full system 99.9. What accounts for the difference?
Remove components one at a time, cumulatively, and record the accuracy after each removal:



Table 12.1: The lecture’s ablation, cumulative from the top.

The text-parser features account for most of the gain. For a paper or a project report this is the result to state: the report then explains why the system works, not just that it does. If you are going to work on spam for years, it tells you where to invest. 1:18:21 The last question of the lecture asks how to choose the order of removal. There is no systematic way, Ng says, so if in doubt use the non-cumulative version: remove one component, put it back, remove the next.
1:17:03 He says that the two versions usually give similar insight. Usually they do, but there is a common case where they cannot, and Table 12.1 hints at it. Removing the header features costs nothing after the sender-host features are gone, which is what happens when two components carry largely the same information. The generator builds this case exactly. Two classes are Gaussian with a shared covariance, and there are four features: “sender host” and “email header” are separate measurements of the same signal (correlation 0.95), “text parser” is a strong independent feature and “JavaScript” a weak one. For this model the best classifier on any subset of features has accuracy \Phi(\Delta/2), where \Delta is the Mahalanobis distance between the class means on that subset, so every ablation can be computed in closed form.



Table 12.2: Accuracy lost when a feature is removed, on a toy with two redundant features. The full model gets 0.788; with no features, 0.5.

Leave-one-out says the sender-host and header features are each worth a tenth of a point, since either one can stand in for the other. Yet removing both together costs 5.6 points. Cumulative removal hands the whole 5.5 to whichever of the two is removed second, so the conclusion depends on an order that was chosen arbitrarily. The final column, the drop averaged over every removal order (the Shapley value from cooperative game theory), splits the credit evenly. Its entries add up to the full 28.8 points, as any single removal order’s do. Leave-one-out’s add up to only 9.4, because the credit the two redundant features share is counted for neither.
Order also matters for weak features: JavaScript looks worthless with everything else present and worth six points once the stronger features are gone. None of this makes ablation less useful. It means that when two components could plausibly duplicate each other, you should remove them together as well as separately before concluding either is dead weight. Error analysis has the same problem in reverse when stages interact: giving one stage perfect input may help little until another stage is fixed too.
