title: 13  Expectation-Maximization Algorithms
text:
13.1 k-means
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
In unsupervised learning the training set is \{x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(m)}\} with no labels, and the job is to find structure in it. This lecture builds two algorithms that alternate between a guess about hidden structure and a fit given that guess. k-means guesses which cluster each point belongs to and moves each cluster’s centre to the mean of its points. The EM algorithm for a mixture of Gaussians does the same with probabilities instead of hard assignments. The second half derives EM in general. Each E-step builds a lower bound on the log-likelihood that touches it at the current parameters, and each M-step maximises that bound, so the likelihood can never decrease. Jensen’s inequality is the tool that makes the bound.
The same derivation carries the next lecture’s factor analysis, which is why Ng gives it in full rather than stopping at the intuitive version.
2:19 Ng opens with an animation (Figure 13.1). Given unlabelled points that seem to form two groups, place two cluster centroids at random. Then repeat two steps: colour every point by the centroid it is closer to, and move each centroid to the mean of the points of its colour. After a few rounds the colours stop changing and the centroids stop moving, and the algorithm has converged.
5:42 Written out, the algorithm is:
The first inner step assigns each example to its nearest centroid. The second moves each centroid to the average of the examples assigned to it. 6:23 The animation drops the initial centroids at arbitrary positions, but Ng points out that the usual practice is to set them to k training examples chosen at random. In two dimensions this hardly matters, but in high dimensions a random vector tends to land far from all the data and capture no points.
The most common use Ng names is market segmentation: group a website’s users into types that can be targeted differently, without anyone having labelled what the types are. The Google News clustering of stories from the first lecture is another.

title: 13  Expectation-Maximization Algorithms
text:
Figure 13.1: k-means on 60 unlabelled points: two centroids placed badly, the first assignment, the first update, and the converged state.





Initialise the cluster centroids \mu_1, \dots, \mu_k \in \mathbb{R}^n.
Repeat until convergence:

for every i, set c^{(i)} := \arg\min_j \lVert x^{(i)} - \mu_j \rVert^2;
for every j, set \mu_j := \dfrac{\sum_{i} 1\{c^{(i)} = j\}\, x^{(i)}}{\sum_i 1\{c^{(i)} = j\}}.

title: 13  Expectation-Maximization Algorithms
text:
13.2 The cost k-means descends
11:45 k-means is guaranteed to converge, and the proof is a cost function. Define the distortion

J(c, \mu) = \sum_{i=1}^m \bigl\lVert x^{(i)} - \mu_{c^{(i)}} \bigr\rVert^2 ,
\tag{13.1}
the total squared distance from each point to the centroid it is assigned to. The assignment step minimises J over c with \mu fixed, since each term is minimised separately by choosing the nearest centroid. The update step minimises J over \mu with c fixed, because the point that minimises a sum of squared distances to a set of points is their mean. So k-means is coordinate descent on J, and J never increases. Since it is bounded below by zero, it must converge. The generator tracks J after every half-step of every run and confirms it never rises. In Figure 13.1 it falls from 476.9 to 31.3 in three rounds. On very large data sets, Ng adds, people often stop once the decrease in J has become small, without waiting for convergence.
8:49 A student asks whether the norm in the circulated notes is an L_1 norm. Ng says it is L_2, the default whenever a norm is written without a subscript, and adds that with or without the square “the algorithm is the same either way”. For the assignment step that is right. Squaring is monotone on non-negative numbers, so the nearest centroid is the same under \lVert\cdot\rVert and \lVert\cdot\rVert^2, and the generator confirms identical assignments for 200 random sets of centroids. For the update step it is not. The mean minimises the sum of squared distances. The point that minimises the sum of plain distances is a different one, the geometric median, so the convergence argument above only works for the squared cost. The generator finds random starts where moving to the means raises the unsquared cost: 26 of 2,000. So k-means does descend a cost, but it is the squared one, Equation 13.1.
13:33 Ng is most often asked how to choose k. He usually chooses it by hand, for two reasons. Unsupervised data is often genuinely ambiguous: the same picture can look like two clusters to one person and four to another. And criteria that pick k automatically, such as AIC and BIC, answer a question the application did not ask. The better guide is what the clusters are for. If the marketing team can run four campaigns but not a hundred, use four clusters. In image compression, choose k by how much compression you want.
15:41 k-means can stop at a local minimum of J, since coordinate descent only guarantees that J stops decreasing. The fix Ng gives is to run it many times from different random initialisations and keep the run with the lowest J. On three well-separated clusters, the generator’s 100 restarts, each initialised at three random training examples, ended at seven different final costs, from 92.6 to 378.2, and the best was reached 92 times. Taking the lowest cost over a handful of restarts is therefore cheap insurance.

title: 13  Expectation-Maximization Algorithms
text:
13.3 Density estimation and anomalies
16:18 A related but different problem is density estimation: model p(x) from unlabelled data. Ng’s example comes from friends who worked on aircraft engines. As each engine comes off the assembly line, measure its vibration and the heat it produces. If a new engine’s measurements fall where p(x) is very small, flag it and send it for inspection before it is fitted to a plane. The same scheme finds cell towers whose network traffic has turned strange, and computers sending unusual traffic.
19:46 The interesting anomaly in his sketch is one where neither feature is unusual on its own. Many engines vibrate that much, and many run that hot, but few do both. Only a joint model of p(x) catches it. And the data he draws are L-shaped, which no single textbook distribution fits. They look instead like two Gaussian blobs, perhaps engines from two production processes, which is the idea of the next section.

title: 13  Expectation-Maximization Algorithms
text:
13.4 The mixture of Gaussians
24:23 The model introduces a latent random variable z, meaning one that exists but is never observed. For each example,

z^{(i)} \sim \operatorname{Multinomial}(\phi), \qquad
x^{(i)} \mid z^{(i)} = j \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_j, \Sigma_j),
\tag{13.2}
where \phi_j = p(z^{(i)} = j), \phi_j \ge 0, \sum_j \phi_j = 1. In words: pick one of k Gaussians with probabilities \phi, then draw x from it. The density of x is the mixture p(x) = \sum_j \phi_j \, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_j, \Sigma_j), which with enough components can take almost any shape, such as an L, or a narrow peak beside a wide hump (Figure 13.2, left).
This is Gaussian discriminant analysis (Section 5.3) with two cosmetic differences: z takes k values instead of two, and each component has its own covariance \Sigma_j by convention, where GDA shared one. The real difference is that GDA’s labels y^{(i)} were observed and z^{(i)} are not. 28:12 If the z^{(i)} were observed, maximum likelihood would give GDA’s closed-form estimates, \phi_j = \frac1m \sum_i 1\{z^{(i)}=j\} and \mu_j the mean of the examples with z^{(i)} = j, and \Sigma_j their covariance. Not knowing which Gaussian each example came from is the whole difficulty.

title: 13  Expectation-Maximization Algorithms
section: 13.5 EM for the mixture: soft k-means
text:
13.5 EM for the mixture: soft k-means
30:54 EM resolves the difficulty with the same bootstrap as k-means. Guess the z^{(i)}, fit the parameters as if the guesses were labels, and repeat. The guesses are probabilities rather than hard labels.
E-step. For each i and j, compute the posterior probability that example i came from component j,

w^{(i)}_j := p\bigl(z^{(i)} = j \mid x^{(i)}; \phi, \mu, \Sigma\bigr)
= \frac{\phi_j \, \mathcal{N}(x^{(i)}; \mu_j, \Sigma_j)}{\sum_{l=1}^k \phi_l \, \mathcal{N}(x^{(i)}; \mu_l, \Sigma_l)},
\tag{13.3}
which is Bayes’ rule, exactly as GDA used it to classify.
M-step. Re-estimate the parameters with the GDA formulas, with each indicator 1\{z^{(i)} = j\} replaced by w^{(i)}_j:

\phi_j := \frac1m \sum_i w^{(i)}_j, \qquad
\mu_j := \frac{\sum_i w^{(i)}_j x^{(i)}}{\sum_i w^{(i)}_j}, \qquad
\Sigma_j := \frac{\sum_i w^{(i)}_j (x^{(i)} - \mu_j)(x^{(i)} - \mu_j)^\top}{\sum_i w^{(i)}_j}.
\tag{13.4}
36:30 The replacement is principled: w^{(i)}_j is the expected value of the indicator under the current posterior, since the expectation of an indicator is the probability of its event. 37:10 Ng’s intuition is that this is k-means with soft assignment. k-means gives each point entirely to the nearest centroid, even when it is only slightly nearer. EM gives it, say, 0.8 to one Gaussian and 0.2 to the other, and each mean becomes a weighted average in which each point counts with that strength. A student asks how to think about the weights. Ng’s reading is that each point is assigned with total strength one, split across the components. In the engine story, a point with a 10 per cent chance of coming from process one contributes a tenth of an engine to process one’s Gaussian.
The analogy can be made exact. Give all components the same fixed covariance \sigma^2 I and equal \phi_j, and let \sigma^2 \to 0. Then the posterior in Equation 13.3 goes to 1 for the nearest mean and 0 for the others, and the mean update becomes k-means’ update. In the generator’s one-dimensional example, the largest gap between EM’s soft assignments and k-means’ hard ones is 3 \times 10^{-11} once \sigma^2 = 0.01.
34:06 Ng describes the E-step for two classes as a sigmoid: the probability of the left Gaussian falls smoothly from one to zero across the gap between the means. That is GDA’s result (Section 5.4), and it holds when the components share a covariance. With equal variances the posterior is exactly 1/(1 + e^{-(ax+b)}), which the generator checks to 10^{-12}. With separate covariances, the convention the model was just given, \log(w_1/w_2) is quadratic in x rather than linear, and the posterior need not be monotone. In Figure 13.2 the left component is narrow and the right one wide. The posterior of the left component rises to 0.955 near x = -2.1 and falls back to 0.003 at x = -5, because far out on either side the wide Gaussian is the likelier source. EM handles this without any change. It only means “points on the left go to the left cluster” is not what the E-step computes.






Figure 13.2: A mixture of a narrow and a wide Gaussian: the components (dashed) and p(x) (left), and the E-step posterior of the left component (right) with the variances shared and separate.



38:56 Once fitted, the mixture gives p(x) = \sum_j p(x, z = j) for any new engine, and a low value flags an anomaly. Ng closes the section with a memory from a summer at AT&T Bell Labs, of a colleague who had just run EM on a mixture of three Gaussians for the first time and could not stop showing people what it did.

title: 13  Expectation-Maximization Algorithms
text:
13.6 Jensen’s inequality
48:07 The argument so far was heuristic: guess the latent variables, then pretend they were observed. To show that EM really is maximum-likelihood estimation, Ng needs Jensen’s inequality. Let f be convex, meaning f''(x) \ge 0, and X a random variable. Then

f\bigl(\mathbb{E}[X]\bigr) \le \mathbb{E}\bigl[f(X)\bigr].
\tag{13.5}
His example takes X = 1 or X = 5, each with probability one half. Then \mathbb{E}[X] = 3, and \mathbb{E}[f(X)] is the average of f(1) and f(5), which is the midpoint of the chord joining those two points of the curve (Figure 13.3). A convex function lies below its chords, so the chord’s midpoint is above f(3). Ng admits that he and his friends do not remember which way the inequality goes. They redraw this picture every time.






Figure 13.3: Jensen’s inequality: the chord’s midpoint, \mathbb{E}[f(X)], lies above the curve at the mean, f(\mathbb{E}[X]).



53:23 EM also needs the equality case. If f is strictly convex, f'' > 0, then equality holds only if X is constant, i.e. X = \mathbb{E}[X] with probability one, which is the measure theorist’s way of saying it. A straight line is convex but not strictly, and for it equality holds for any X. 54:47 A student asks about a curve with f(1) = f(3). Equal end values alone change nothing: the chord is then flat, and a strictly convex curve still dips below it in between. Equality for a non-constant X needs the function to be straight between the values X takes, for instance flat between 1 and 3, and such a function is not strictly convex. The strictness is the hypothesis that rules this out.
For EM the inequality is used upside down. A concave function is the negative of a convex one (f'' \le 0), and for concave f, f(\mathbb{E}[X]) \ge \mathbb{E}[f(X)], with equality for strictly concave f only when X is constant. The function it is applied to is \log, which is strictly concave.

title: 13  Expectation-Maximization Algorithms
section: 13.7 EM as maximising a lower bound
text:
13.7 EM as maximising a lower bound
57:30 Take any model p(x, z; \theta) with z latent and \theta all the parameters (for the mixture, \phi, \mu, \Sigma). The log-likelihood of the data marginalises z out:

\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^m \log p\bigl(x^{(i)}; \theta\bigr)
= \sum_{i=1}^m \log \sum_{z^{(i)}} p\bigl(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta\bigr).

The sum inside the logarithm is what makes this hard. 1:19:12 A student asks at the end why we do not just maximise \ell directly. Setting its derivatives to zero gives equations with no closed-form solution for the mixture, or for factor analysis next time, whereas each step of EM is in closed form. Gradient ascent on \ell is possible, but it needs a learning rate, and EM needs none.
59:58 Ng gives the picture first (Figure 13.4). The E-step builds a lower bound on \ell that has two properties: it lies below \ell everywhere, and it equals \ell at the current parameters \theta^{(t)}. The M-step jumps to the maximum of the bound. At that point \ell is at least as high as the bound, which is at least as high as it was at \theta^{(t)}, where it equalled \ell(\theta^{(t)}). Repeat, and \ell climbs until EM reaches a local optimum. As with k-means, which local optimum it finds depends on the starting point.






Figure 13.4: EM on a one-parameter mixture: the log-likelihood \ell(\theta) and the lower bounds built at the first three iterates. Each touches \ell at the current iterate; the M-step moves to its peak.



1:04:21 To build the bound, pick for each example any distribution Q_i over the values of z^{(i)}, multiply and divide by it, and read the inner sum as an expectation over z^{(i)} \sim Q_i:

\begin{aligned}
\ell(\theta)
&= \sum_i \log \sum_{z^{(i)}} Q_i(z^{(i)}) \, \frac{p(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta)}{Q_i(z^{(i)})}
= \sum_i \log \mathbb{E}_{z^{(i)} \sim Q_i}\!\left[\frac{p(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta)}{Q_i(z^{(i)})}\right] \\
&\ge \sum_i \mathbb{E}_{z^{(i)} \sim Q_i}\!\left[\log \frac{p(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta)}{Q_i(z^{(i)})}\right]
= \sum_i \sum_{z^{(i)}} Q_i(z^{(i)}) \log \frac{p(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta)}{Q_i(z^{(i)})} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{13.6}
The inequality is Jensen’s for the concave \log: the log of an expectation is at least the expectation of the log. The right-hand side, viewed as a function of \theta with the x^{(i)} fixed and the z^{(i)} summed out, is the green curve of Ng’s picture. Today it is usually called the evidence lower bound, or ELBO.
1:11:54 The bound holds for every choice of Q_i. The E-step chooses the Q_i that make it tight at the current \theta. By the equality case of Jensen’s inequality, that requires the random variable inside to be constant, so p(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta) / Q_i(z^{(i)}) must not depend on z^{(i)}. In other words, Q_i(z^{(i)}) \propto p(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta). Normalising to sum to one gives

Q_i(z^{(i)}) = \frac{p(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta)}{\sum_{z} p(x^{(i)}, z; \theta)} = p\bigl(z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}; \theta\bigr),

the posterior of the latent variable given the data, which is exactly the w^{(i)}_j of Equation 13.3. The general algorithm is then:

E-step: for each i, set Q_i(z^{(i)}) := p(z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}; \theta).
M-step: set \theta := \arg\max_\theta \sum_i \sum_{z^{(i)}} Q_i(z^{(i)}) \log \dfrac{p(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta)}{Q_i(z^{(i)})}.

For the mixture of Gaussians, the M-step’s maximisation is the weighted GDA fit of Equation 13.4, so the heuristic of the previous section was EM all along.
The generator checks each step of this argument on the one-parameter model of Figure 13.4, a mixture of \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and \mathcal{N}(\theta, 1) with equal weights, where only the second mean is unknown. At each of the first four iterates, the bound equals \ell to 10^{-9}, has the same slope (so the curves are tangent rather than merely touching), and lies below \ell at every point of a fine grid. Its maximiser found by grid search agrees with the closed-form M-step. From \theta^{(0)} = -1 the iterates run -0.20, 0.98, 2.03, 2.47 and converge to 2.72, and \ell rises at every step, from -138.4 to -73.5.
There is a caveat about “maximum likelihood” for mixtures. When each component has its own variance, the likelihood has no maximum at all. Centre one component exactly on a training point and shrink its variance. That point’s density grows without bound while the other components keep the remaining points’ densities finite, so \ell \to \infty. The generator shows \ell rising without limit as the variance falls through 10^{-8}, 10^{-16}, … 10^{-128}. EM does not usually find these degenerate solutions, because it climbs from where it starts, but a component that captures a single point can drift into one. In practice this is guarded against by restarting, or by putting a floor or a small prior under the covariances. “Converges to a local optimum” is the accurate claim, and for mixtures the global optimum is not a useful target.






NoteIn the official notes



k-means and its convergence as coordinate descent are in cs229-notes7a. The mixture of Gaussians and its EM updates, including the \Sigma_j step the lecture skipped, are in cs229-notes7b. Jensen’s inequality, the general derivation, the proof that \ell increases monotonically, and the view of EM as coordinate ascent on the lower bound are in cs229-notes8, sections 1 to 3. The original general treatment is Dempster, Laird and Rubin (1977), and the k-means iteration is Lloyd’s (1982).

title: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis
text:
14.1 From the general algorithm to the mixture updates
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Factor analysis is a density model for data with many more dimensions than examples. For example, a hundred temperature sensors give a hundred-dimensional reading, but you may have only thirty days of data. An ordinary Gaussian cannot be fitted to such data, because its maximum-likelihood covariance is singular. The model assumes that each observation is a low-dimensional hidden cause z, mapped linearly into the high-dimensional space, plus independent noise in every coordinate. Because z is hidden, the model is fitted with EM, and doing so means working out the conditional distributions of a joint Gaussian.
The lecture first closes off the previous one. It shows how the abstract E- and M-steps of Section 13.7 become code for the mixture of Gaussians, and it recasts EM as coordinate ascent. It then spends the rest of the hour on factor analysis.
3:00 The general M-step says to maximise the lower bound over \theta with the Q_i held fixed. For the mixture of Gaussians, Q_i(z^{(i)} = j) is the responsibility w^{(i)}_j = p(z^{(i)} = j \mid x^{(i)}; \phi, \mu, \Sigma) that the E-step computes and stores. The joint density factorises as p(x^{(i)} \mid z^{(i)} = j)\,p(z^{(i)} = j) = \mathcal{N}(x^{(i)}; \mu_j, \Sigma_j)\,\phi_j. So the quantity the M-step maximises is a double sum that can be written out in full:
J(\phi, \mu, \Sigma) = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^k w^{(i)}_j
\log \frac{\dfrac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2} |\Sigma_j|^{1/2}}
\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac12 (x^{(i)} - \mu_j)^\top \Sigma_j^{-1} (x^{(i)} - \mu_j)\Bigr)\,\phi_j}{w^{(i)}_j} .
\tag{14.1}
Ng’s point is that this objective is what gives you the updates. The rule “move each mean to the weighted average of the points” was an intuition in the last lecture, and here it is derived. Differentiating Equation 14.1 with respect to \mu_j and setting the result to zero gives
\mu_j = \frac{\sum_i w^{(i)}_j x^{(i)}}{\sum_i w^{(i)}_j},
and the same procedure gives \Sigma_j.
For \phi, “differentiate and set to zero” does not quite work, and the board skips over why. The only terms in \phi are \sum_i \sum_j w^{(i)}_j \log \phi_j, whose derivative with respect to \phi_j is \sum_i w^{(i)}_j / \phi_j. That derivative is positive for every value of \phi_j, so it never vanishes. Taken alone, the objective wants every \phi_j to be infinite. What stops it is the constraint \sum_j \phi_j = 1, so the step needs a Lagrange multiplier. With the multiplier, the solution is \phi_j = \frac1m \sum_i w^{(i)}_j. The generator confirms this on a three-component one-dimensional mixture. At the closed-form M-step, the unconstrained derivative equals exactly m = 200 for all three components (the multiplier), and none of 300 random perturbations of (\phi, \mu, \sigma^2) that stay on the simplex raises J.
14:11 Ng then gives a second view of EM that the factor-analysis derivation leans on. Treat the lower bound as a function of both arguments,
J(\theta, Q) = \sum_i \sum_{z^{(i)}} Q_i(z^{(i)}) \log \frac{p(x^{(i)}, z^{(i)}; \theta)}{Q_i(z^{(i)})}
\;\le\; \ell(\theta) \quad \text{for every } \theta \text{ and } Q .
The E-step maximises J over Q with \theta fixed, and the maximum is the choice that makes J = \ell. The M-step maximises J over \theta with Q fixed. EM is therefore coordinate ascent on J: it maximises over one block of variables, then the other, and alternates. This view also tells you how to check that an implementation is working. J cannot decrease in either step, and since it equals \ell(\theta) after every E-step, the log-likelihood you print at each iteration must not decrease either. If it ever goes down, there is a bug. On the mixture above, the generator asserts that J = \ell after each E-step to 10^{-8}, and that \ell never falls over 40 iterations: from -544.2 it reaches -388.9 after three iterations and -358.1 at the end.
When z is continuous, as it will be in factor analysis, every step of the derivation in Section 13.7 goes through with the sum over z^{(i)} replaced by an integral. Jensen’s inequality does not care which kind of expectation it is applied to.
crumbs: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis

title: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis
text:
14.2 Fewer examples than dimensions
17:46 A mixture of Gaussians suits data like Ng’s two-dimensional picture with a hundred points: m \gg n, and each cluster has plenty of points to estimate its covariance. Factor analysis is for the opposite regime, where m \approx n or m \ll n. Ng’s running example is a Stanford PhD student’s project with temperature sensors placed around campus buildings: a hundred sensors and thirty days of readings, so n = 100 and m = 30. The goal was anomaly detection by density estimation, as in Section 13.3. A window left open on a winter day produces a reading with low p(x), and in practice the point was saving energy rather than detecting fires. To do this you need a joint density over all hundred sensors, because neighbouring sensors are strongly correlated, and you have thirty examples to fit it with.
22:01 The obvious model is a single Gaussian with its maximum-likelihood estimates \mu = \frac1m \sum_i x^{(i)} and \Sigma = \frac1m \sum_i (x^{(i)} - \mu)(x^{(i)} - \mu)^\top. If m \le n, this \Sigma is singular. The reason is that it is a sum of m rank-one matrices whose vectors x^{(i)} - \mu sum to zero, so its rank is at most m - 1. The generator checks the exact statement on random data for n = 2, 5, 10 and every m from 2 to n + 2: the rank is \min(m - 1, n), so the estimate is invertible exactly when m \ge n + 1. A singular \Sigma breaks the density in two ways. The normaliser contains |\Sigma|^{1/2} = 0 and the exponent contains \Sigma^{-1}, which does not exist, so evaluating p(x) gives 0/0 at best. Ng’s picture with m = n = 2 shows the second problem (Figure 14.1, first panel). The fitted Gaussian has its contours squashed to zero width along the segment joining the two points. All of its probability mass lies on that line, so any test point slightly off the line gets density zero. That is a numerical failure, and it is also a bad model of the data.






Figure 14.1: Maximum-likelihood Gaussians on two-dimensional data, with the one- and two-standard-deviation contours. With two points (left) the full covariance is singular and the Gaussian collapses onto the line through them. With twelve strongly correlated points (sample correlation 0.93) the full covariance follows the tilt of the data, the diagonal covariance gives axis-aligned ellipses that miss it, and the spherical covariance gives circles.



26:53 Ng adds that one of the earliest applications of factor analysis had the same shape: psychological testing, with a hundred questionnaire items and thirty subjects, where the question is how attributes like verbal and mathematical ability are correlated.
crumbs: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis

title: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis
text:
14.3 Restricting the covariance
28:15 One way out is to fit fewer parameters. If \Sigma is constrained to be diagonal, the maximum-likelihood estimate is what you would guess: each feature gets its own sample variance, \Sigma_{jj} = \frac1m \sum_i (x^{(i)}_j - \mu_j)^2. That makes n parameters in place of about n^2/2, and they can be fitted from any m \ge 2. The contours are axis-aligned ellipses. The price is that the model assumes the features are uncorrelated, and for a hundred sensors in one room that is plainly false (Figure 14.1, third panel).
31:36 A stronger restriction is \Sigma = \sigma^2 I, with one parameter and circular contours. Its estimate is the average squared deviation over every coordinate of every example, which is the mean of the diagonal model’s n variances. A student asks why anyone would bother with a model that is worse still. Ng’s answer is that it is a building block: factor analysis uses a diagonal covariance for its noise, not for the data.
34:38 Another student asks about the standard fix, a Wishart prior on \Sigma. In practice this means adding a constant \lambda to the diagonal of the maximum-likelihood estimate. Ng’s verdict is that it removes the singularity “in a technical way” but is not the best model for many data sets. The generator puts that verdict to a test at the end of the chapter (Section 14.6). What Ng wants instead is a model that captures the main correlations, such as the room warming and cooling as a whole or one side heating up under the lamps, without paying for a full covariance matrix.
He follows this with an aside about small data that is worth keeping. The large technology companies, he says, all work on the same few big-data problems (translation, speech, face recognition), while many real applications in healthcare and manufacturing have a hundred or a thousand examples. The best algorithm for a thousand examples is often not the best for a million, and the field does not yet know how to make one algorithm work along the whole range. He mentions using a modified factor analysis on a manufacturing problem that same week.
crumbs: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis

title: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis
text:
14.4 The factor analysis model
40:32 Like the mixture of Gaussians, the model is a joint density p(x, z) = p(x \mid z)\,p(z) with z hidden. This time z is continuous and of lower dimension than x:

\begin{aligned}
z &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), \qquad z \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ d < n, \\
x &= \mu + \Lambda z + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Psi),
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.2}
with z and \varepsilon independent. The parameters are the mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^n, the factor loading matrix \Lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}, and a diagonal \Psi \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}. Equivalently, x \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu + \Lambda z, \Psi).
43:30 Ng’s reading of the model uses the room. Suppose three strong forces drive the temperatures in the room: the temperature outside, the lights on the left side, and the lights on the right. Then d = 3, and z holds those three numbers. Each sensor reads a linear combination of the three, weighted by where it sits, so a sensor near the door leans on the outdoor term. On top of that each sensor adds noise of its own, such as a gust of wind or a bad thermistor. The assumption that \Psi is diagonal says that this noise is independent across sensors once the shared factors are accounted for. All correlation between sensors has to come through \Lambda z.
46:21 The lecture’s example makes this concrete with d = 1, n = 2, m = 7, \Lambda = (2, 1)^\top, \mu = 0 and \Psi = \operatorname{diag}(1, 2) (Figure 14.2). Seven draws of z fall on the real line. Multiplying by \Lambda places them on the line x_2 = x_1 / 2 in the plane. Around each of these points, the noise \varepsilon has axis-aligned elliptical contours, taller than wide in the ratio \sqrt2 : 1. Drawing one sample from each gives the observed points. Only those crosses are data. The z values, and the points on the line, are latent.






Figure 14.2: The factor-analysis model as a generative process, with the lecture’s parameters. Seven draws of z (left) map through \Lambda z + \mu onto a line in the plane (centre). Independent axis-aligned noise with covariance \Psi moves each one to the observed x, the crosses (right). The thin lines join each latent point to its observation.



51:05 Ng repeats the construction with d = 2 and n = 3, carrying the five sampled z points on a sheet of cardboard and holding it up into three-dimensional space. The data then lie close to a two-dimensional “pancake” in \mathbb{R}^3, with some fuzz off it. Factor analysis takes data in a hundred dimensions and models it as lying near a three-dimensional subspace, plus independent noise in each coordinate. 54:57 Asked what happens when the data do not lie near a subspace, he concedes that the model is then not the best one. He adds that in a hundred dimensions you rarely know, because you cannot look.
crumbs: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis

title: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis
text:
14.5 Marginals and conditionals of Gaussians
56:43 Fitting the model needs two facts about multivariate Gaussians. Partition a Gaussian vector into blocks x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^r and x_2 \in \mathbb{R}^s:

\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} \sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left( \begin{bmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \mu_2 \end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix} \Sigma_{11} & \Sigma_{12} \\ \Sigma_{21} & \Sigma_{22} \end{bmatrix} \right).

The first fact is that the marginal of x_1 is \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \Sigma_{11}). You can prove it by integrating x_2 out of the joint density, but the result is the obvious one: the mean and covariance of x_1 are the corresponding blocks. The second fact is that the conditional is also Gaussian,

x_1 \mid x_2 \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu_{1|2}, \Sigma_{1|2}\bigr), \qquad
\mu_{1|2} = \mu_1 + \Sigma_{12} \Sigma_{22}^{-1} (x_2 - \mu_2), \qquad
\Sigma_{1|2} = \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12} \Sigma_{22}^{-1} \Sigma_{21} .
\tag{14.3}
This one is less obvious, and the lecture states it without proof. The conditional mean is a linear regression of x_1 on x_2. The conditional covariance does not depend on the value of x_2 that was observed.
1:02:32 Applying this to factor analysis starts with the observation that (z, x) is jointly Gaussian, since x is a linear function of the Gaussians z and \varepsilon. Its mean is (0, \mu). Ng derives the lower-right block of the covariance and leaves the others to the notes. Expanding

\mathbb{E}\bigl[(x - \mu)(x - \mu)^\top\bigr]
= \mathbb{E}\bigl[(\Lambda z + \varepsilon)(\Lambda z + \varepsilon)^\top\bigr]
= \Lambda\,\mathbb{E}[z z^\top]\,\Lambda^\top + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \varepsilon^\top]
= \Lambda \Lambda^\top + \Psi .

Here the cross terms vanish because z and \varepsilon are independent with mean zero. The same expansion gives \mathbb{E}[z (x - \mu)^\top] = \Lambda^\top, so

\begin{bmatrix} z \\ x \end{bmatrix} \sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left( \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \mu \end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix} I & \Lambda^\top \\ \Lambda & \Lambda\Lambda^\top + \Psi \end{bmatrix} \right).
\tag{14.4}
For the lecture’s example, Equation 14.4 gives the covariance of (z, x_1, x_2) as rows (1, 2, 1), (2, 5, 2) and (1, 2, 3). A Monte Carlo estimate from 200,000 samples in the generator agrees to within 0.015 in every entry.
By the marginal rule, x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Lambda\Lambda^\top + \Psi). This explains why the model escapes the singularity: \Psi is diagonal with positive entries, so \Lambda\Lambda^\top + \Psi is positive definite however small m is. The covariance has nd + n free parameters: a rank-d part that carries the correlations, plus a diagonal part. 1:10:09 The log-likelihood \sum_i \log \mathcal{N}(x^{(i)}; \mu, \Lambda\Lambda^\top + \Psi) is perfectly well defined, but setting its gradient to zero has no closed-form solution in \Lambda and \Psi. That is why the lecture turns to EM.
crumbs: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis

title: 14  EM Algorithm and Factor Analysis
text:
14.6 EM for factor analysis
1:11:03 In the mixture of Gaussians, Q_i was a list of k numbers. Here z^{(i)} is continuous, so the question is how to represent Q_i in a computer. The answer is that Q_i(z^{(i)}) = p(z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}) is Gaussian, by Equation 14.3 applied to Equation 14.4, so it is stored as a mean vector and a covariance matrix:

\mu_{z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}} = \Lambda^\top (\Lambda\Lambda^\top + \Psi)^{-1} (x^{(i)} - \mu),
\qquad
\Sigma_{z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}} = I - \Lambda^\top (\Lambda\Lambda^\top + \Psi)^{-1} \Lambda .
\tag{14.5}
The generator checks Equation 14.5 against Bayes’ rule applied directly, multiplying the prior on z by the likelihood of x on a grid of 12,000 points. For three different observations in the lecture’s example, the two agree to 10^{-6} in mean and variance. As the formula says, the posterior variance is the same for every observation: 1/(1 + 4 + \tfrac12) = 0.1818. In code, the n \times n inverse is avoided with the matrix-inversion lemma, \Sigma_{z \mid x} = (I + \Lambda^\top \Psi^{-1} \Lambda)^{-1}, which is d \times d.
1:13:39 The M-step derivation is long, and Ng gives only its two tricks. The first is to recognise expectations instead of expanding integrals. The objective contains terms like \int Q_i(z^{(i)})\, z^{(i)}\, dz^{(i)}. Substituting the Gaussian formula for Q_i and integrating is the wrong approach. The integral is \mathbb{E}_{z^{(i)} \sim Q_i}[z^{(i)}], which is \mu_{z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}}, already computed in the E-step. 1:18:13 The second is to expand a Gaussian density when a logarithm sits in front of it. Then the log cancels the exponential and leaves a quadratic in the parameters, whose expectation under Q_i is again a quadratic that can be maximised in closed form. The resulting update for \Lambda is

\Lambda = \left( \sum_{i=1}^m (x^{(i)} - \mu)\, \mu_{z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}}^\top \right)
\left( \sum_{i=1}^m \Bigl[ \mu_{z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}} \mu_{z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}}^\top + \Sigma_{z^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)}} \Bigr] \right)^{-1},
\tag{14.6}
with \mu the sample mean. \Psi is the diagonal of a similar expression, given in the official notes. Equation 14.6 has the form of the normal equations for regressing x on z, except that the unknown z^{(i)} are replaced by their posterior moments. The bracket in the second factor is \mathbb{E}[z^{(i)} z^{(i)\top}] under Q_i. That is the mean’s outer product plus the posterior covariance, because \mathbb{E}[zz^\top] is not \mathbb{E}[z]\,\mathbb{E}[z]^\top.
The official notes warn that dropping \Sigma_{z \mid x} here is a common mistake, which treats the posterior mean as if it were the true z. They do not say what the mistake costs, so the generator runs both versions (Figure 14.3). The data are 30 examples in n = 100 dimensions, drawn from a three-factor model; the sample covariance has rank 29, as Section 14.2 says it must. Correct EM increases \ell on every one of 200 iterations, from -5744.2 at the start to -3254.7 after 10 iterations and -3203.0 at 200. Over the last 50 iterations it is still gaining 1.3 nats. The shortcut version is deceptive. It climbs faster at first and reaches -3221.0 at iteration 4, ahead of the correct algorithm. Then the likelihood falls on every remaining iteration, 196 of 200 in all. Correct EM overtakes it at iteration 38, and the shortcut finishes at -3235.3. The shortcut is not coordinate ascent on any bound, so the monitoring rule of Section 14.1 is exactly what catches it: an implementation whose log-likelihood ever decreases has a bug, even if its first few iterations look better than the correct one.






Figure 14.3: EM for factor analysis with n = 100, m = 30, d = 3. Left: training log-likelihood per iteration for the correct M-step and for the shortcut that uses \mathbb{E}[z]\mathbb{E}[z]^\top in place of \mathbb{E}[zz^\top]. The first few iterations climb from far below and are clipped. The shortcut leads early, then declines on every iteration. Right: average log-likelihood of 300 held-out examples under factor analysis, a full Gaussian with \lambda I added to its covariance (with \lambda chosen on the test set itself, which favours it), and a diagonal Gaussian.



The same run tests Ng’s remark about the Wishart fix from Section 14.3. On 300 held-out examples, factor analysis scores an average log-likelihood of -129.0 per example. The full Gaussian with \lambda I added scores -138.5, even though \lambda was chosen from a grid using the test set itself, which is an unfair advantage. The diagonal Gaussian scores -198.8. The comparison does favour factor analysis, because the data were generated from a factor model. What it shows is narrower than “factor analysis is better” in general. When the correlations really are low-rank, adding \lambda I makes the covariance invertible without capturing that structure, and the diagonal model throws the correlations away entirely.






NoteIn the official notes



Restrictions on \Sigma, the marginal and conditional formulas with a derivation of the conditional, the joint distribution of (z, x), and the full M-step for \mu, \Lambda and \Psi are in cs229-notes9, sections 1 to 4. The mixture-of-Gaussians M-step with the Lagrange multiplier for \phi, and the coordinate-ascent view of EM, are in cs229-notes8, sections 2 and 3. The EM algorithm for factor analysis was given by Rubin and Thayer (1982).

title: 15  PCA and ICA
text:
15.1 One-dimensional data living in two dimensions
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Principal components analysis (PCA) reduces n-dimensional data to k \ll n dimensions by projecting it onto the k directions along which it varies most. Those directions are the top k eigenvectors of the data’s covariance matrix. Like factor analysis in the previous lecture, PCA assumes the data lie near a low-dimensional subspace. Unlike factor analysis it has no probabilistic model: it does not define p(x), it just finds the subspace. Ng spends as long on when not to use PCA as on how it works. The last quarter of the lecture sets up independent components analysis (ICA), which looks for statistically independent directions instead of high-variance ones. The algorithm itself is in lecture 16.
2:09 Ng’s first example is a school that measured its children’s heights twice in the same month, once in centimetres and once in inches, with each value rounded to a whole unit. Plotted against each other, the two numbers lie almost exactly on a line. The data have n = 2, but they are really one-dimensional: a child’s height plus a little rounding noise perpendicular to the line. PCA’s job is to find that line, the principal axis of variation, and replace each point by its position along it.
Because centimetres and inches measure the same thing, he offers two less contrived examples. In the first, two vibration sensors made by different manufacturers sit on different parts of a factory machine. Both measure how hard the machine is shaking, which is useful for preventive maintenance, since the vibration pattern changes before a machine fails. 5:50 In the second, from his autonomous-helicopter work, each pilot is scored on skill and on enjoyment of flying. The two might both reflect one underlying aptitude. Going from two dimensions to one is only for the whiteboard. In practice, Ng says, PCA takes something like 10,000 dimensions to 100 or 1,000.
7:29 Before running PCA, the data are standardised. Subtract the mean of each feature, then divide each feature by its standard deviation, so that every feature has mean 0 and variance 1. Section 15.4 explains why both steps matter.

title: 15  PCA and ICA
section: 15.2 Two definitions of the best direction
text:
15.2 Two definitions of the best direction
10:00 Ng draws two candidate lines through the standardised height data: the 45-degree line, which is clearly right, and the perpendicular line, which is clearly wrong. He then gives two ways to say what makes the first one right (Figure 15.1). Project every point orthogonally onto a line. For the good line, the projection segments are short, so the sum of squared distances from the points to their projections is small. The projected points are also spread out along the line, while on the bad line they bunch together near the origin. So PCA could be defined as minimising the squared projection distance or as maximising the variance of the projections.






Figure 15.1: Sixty standardised height measurements (crosses) projected orthogonally onto the first principal direction u_1 (left) and onto the perpendicular direction u_2 (right). The projections are the dots, joined to their points by thin segments. On u_1 the projections spread out and the segments are short; on u_2 the projections collapse onto the origin and the segments are long.



12:00 The two definitions are the same, and the reason is Pythagoras. For a unit vector u and a centred point x^{(i)}, the squared length of the point splits into the squared length of its projection plus the squared distance to it:

\lVert x^{(i)} \rVert^2 = \bigl(u^\top x^{(i)}\bigr)^2 + \bigl\lVert x^{(i)} - (u^\top x^{(i)})\,u \bigr\rVert^2 .

The left side does not depend on u. Averaging over the data, projected variance plus mean squared distance is a constant, so maximising one minimises the other. The generator checks this at 3,600 directions around the half-circle. The two terms sum to the same constant to 10^{-12}, and the direction with the largest variance is exactly the direction with the smallest distance. On the height data that direction is 45.0°. The projected variance there is 1.9986 and the mean squared distance is 0.0014, out of a total of 2, because the correlation between the two measurements is 0.9986. Ng leaves the proof to the homework and recalls a paper that collected many equivalent derivations of PCA. Historically these two are the founding pair: Pearson (1901) posed the problem as fitting the closest line or plane to a set of points, and Hotelling (1933) posed it as finding components that account for as much of the variance as possible.

title: 15  PCA and ICA
section: 15.3 The principal direction is an eigenvector
text:
15.3 The principal direction is an eigenvector
13:14 Ng derives PCA from the variance definition. For a unit vector u, the projection of x^{(i)} onto it has length u^\top x^{(i)}, so the problem is

\max_{u:\ \lVert u \rVert = 1}\ \frac1m \sum_{i=1}^m \bigl(u^\top x^{(i)}\bigr)^2
= \max_{u:\ \lVert u \rVert = 1}\ u^\top \Bigl( \frac1m \sum_{i=1}^m x^{(i)} x^{(i)\top} \Bigr) u
= \max_{u:\ \lVert u \rVert = 1}\ u^\top \Sigma\, u ,
\tag{15.1}
where \Sigma is the covariance matrix of the standardised data. Ng apologises that the symbol is the same as the one for summation. 19:13 The maximiser is the principal eigenvector of \Sigma, the one with the largest eigenvalue. The argument uses a Lagrangian, \mathcal{L}(u, \lambda) = u^\top \Sigma u - \lambda(u^\top u - 1). Setting its gradient in u to zero gives \Sigma u = \lambda u, so any stationary point of the constrained problem is an eigenvector. At such a point the objective equals u^\top \Sigma u = \lambda u^\top u = \lambda, so the best eigenvector is the one with the largest eigenvalue, and that eigenvalue is the variance captured. The generator checks this on a random 2 \times 2 covariance by finding every stationary point of u^\top \Sigma u around the half-circle of directions. It finds two, each lies along an eigenvector to within 0.02°, and the value of the objective there matches the eigenvalue to 10^{-6}.
22:11 To keep k dimensions, take the top k eigenvectors u_1, \dots, u_k. The new representation of x^{(i)} is the vector of its projections onto them:

y^{(i)} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1^\top x^{(i)} \\ \vdots \\ u_k^\top x^{(i)} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^k,
\qquad
x^{(i)} \approx y^{(i)}_1 u_1 + \dots + y^{(i)}_k u_k \in \mathbb{R}^n .
\tag{15.2}
The second formula decompresses: it maps the k numbers back to a point in \mathbb{R}^n on the k-dimensional subspace. For the heights, y^{(i)} is a single cleaned-up estimate of each child’s height, and mapping it back puts every child exactly on the line. Because \Sigma is symmetric, its eigenvectors can always be chosen orthogonal, so u_1, \dots, u_k is an orthonormal basis of the subspace. 47:11 A student asks whether the test set needs its own eigenvectors. It does not. The u_j are computed once, on the training set, and the same ones are used to map every future example.

title: 15  PCA and ICA
section: 15.4 Pre-processing and the choice of k
text:
15.4 Pre-processing and the choice of k
28:07 A student asks why the pre-processing matters, and Figure 15.2 shows both cases. If the data are not centred, \frac1m \sum_i x^{(i)} x^{(i)\top} is a second moment about the origin, not a covariance. Its top eigenvector points from the origin towards the cloud, not along it. In the generator it lies within 2° of the direction of the data’s mean. If the features are not scaled, a feature measured in small units has numerically large variance and dominates. Ng’s example is centimetres against kilometres. The heights show the effect in a milder form. Centimetre values are 2.54 times the inch values, so the unstandardised principal direction lies at 21.4°, close to \arctan(1/2.54) = 21.5°. That is the line x_2 = x_1/2.54, which is a statement about units, not about the data. After standardising, the principal direction is at exactly 45°.






Figure 15.2: What PCA returns without the pre-processing. Left: a cloud away from the origin; the top eigenvector of the uncentred second-moment matrix points at the cloud (purple), while PCA on centred data follows the cloud’s own axis (teal). Right: heights in centimetres against inches, centred but not scaled, on equal axes. The unscaled first direction (purple) follows the centimetre axis at 21°, while after standardising it is 45° (teal).



58:57 To choose k, look at the eigenvalues. Since the eigenvalue \lambda_j is the variance along u_j, the fraction

\frac{\sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j}{\sum_{j=1}^n \lambda_j}

is the share of the total variance kept by the first k directions. Practitioners report choosing k to “retain 90%” (or 95, 98, or 99%) of the variance. Ng adds that compressing very high-dimensional data tenfold while keeping 95% of its variance is common. The same quantity measures reconstruction quality. The mean squared error of the decompression in Equation 15.2 equals the sum of the discarded eigenvalues, \sum_{j > k} \lambda_j, so “variance retained” is one minus the relative reconstruction error. The generator asserts this equality for every k from 0 to 10 on a ten-dimensional data set.

title: 15  PCA and ICA
section: 15.5 When to use PCA, and when not to
text:
15.5 When to use PCA, and when not to
31:54 The use Ng endorses most is visualisation: projecting data from n dimensions down to 2 or 3 so that it can be plotted. His example is from Krishna Shenoy’s neuroscience lab at Stanford. Monkeys were trained to tap a square on a touch screen when it appeared, in exchange for juice, while about 50 electrodes recorded activity in their brains. A 50-dimensional time series cannot be looked at directly. A former CS229 student in the lab projected it with PCA and could watch the brain’s state move through two or three dimensions: waiting, preparing once the target appeared, holding, and then moving off at the go signal. 36:15 The second endorsed use is compression for efficiency. High-dimensional data usually lie close to a much smaller subspace. Ng calls it “just a fact of life”. Feeding a learning algorithm a 1,000-dimensional y^{(i)} in place of a 10,000-dimensional x^{(i)} saves memory, bandwidth and compute.
38:23 He calls two other uses questionable. The first is reducing overfitting by shrinking the number of features before, say, logistic regression. In his experience this works about half the time. The half that works gets published and the half that fails does not, so the literature makes it look more reliable than it is. He uses regularisation for this instead. 40:16 The second is measuring similarity in a reduced space. In early face recognition, two 100 \times 100 images were compared by Euclidean distance after PCA rather than in raw pixel space, in the hope that the projection would remove noise. Sometimes it helps a little, but not reliably. 42:11 This was the era of eigenfaces. Researchers ran PCA on face images and plotted each eigenvector as a picture. Then they read meaning into individual eigenvectors: one is the lighting direction, another is a beard. Ng’s judgement is that such readings were “at least as much a product of the researcher’s imagination” as of the data. The reason is that individual eigenvectors are unstable, which the next section quantifies.
44:35 His rule of thumb follows: before putting PCA into a system, try the system on the original x^{(i)}. Class project proposals often include a PCA step by default. Unless you need the speed or the memory, the step adds a component to debug without a reason. Asked whether there is a minimum dimension below which PCA is pointless, he says no. Even going from two dimensions to one is justified if halving memory really matters.

title: 15  PCA and ICA
section: 15.6 Why individual eigenvectors should not be interpreted
text:
15.6 Why individual eigenvectors should not be interpreted
54:49 A student asks why k-means centroids are treated as interpretable and principal components are not. Ng’s answer is that individual eigenvectors are numerically unstable, while the subspace spanned by the first k of them is stable. His picture is three-dimensional data lying close to the plane of the whiteboard. u_1 and u_2 are two directions in that plane, and u_3 points out of the board. A small change to the data can spin u_1 and u_2 around inside the plane, while the plane itself stays put. He says that changing one training example “in the fifth decimal place” can change the eigenvectors significantly.
That claim is true only under a condition the lecture leaves implicit. How far an eigenvector moves depends on the size of the perturbation relative to the gap between its eigenvalue and the next one. The generator tests it with data whose top two eigenvalues differ by an exact relative gap. The data are a regular twelve-sided polygon in a plane, stretched slightly along one axis, plus two points off the plane. Changing one coordinate of one point by 10^{-5} moves u_1 by 0.0009° when the gap is 10^{-1}, 0.08° when it is 10^{-3}, 9.6° when it is 10^{-5}, and 59° when it is 10^{-7}. The plane spanned by u_1, u_2 moves by less than 10^{-6} degrees in every case. So a fifth-decimal change matters only when the eigenvalues agree to about five decimals.
The more realistic version is the one Ng gives in answer to a follow-up question 57:56: a lab mate collects a slightly different data set. Then sampling noise, not rounding, is the perturbation. Figure 15.3 draws pairs of 200-point samples from the same three-dimensional distribution and compares their principal directions. When \lambda_2 / \lambda_1 = 0.5, the two samples’ u_1 differ by a median of 5°. At 0.9 they differ by 36°, and at 0.98 and above they are essentially unrelated, around 45–50°. Throughout, the two samples’ top-two subspaces differ by under 1°. High-dimensional data typically have long runs of similar eigenvalues, so this is the usual case. The subspace can be reported; the individual axes are an arbitrary choice of basis within it.






Figure 15.3: Median angle, over 200 pairs of samples of 200 points from the same three-dimensional distribution, between the two samples’ first eigenvectors (purple) and between their two-dimensional principal subspaces (teal), as the second eigenvalue approaches the first. The third eigenvalue is 0.01 throughout.



Two more questions close the PCA half. 56:21 Is there a probabilistic version? Yes: probabilistic PCA is factor analysis with the noise covariance constrained to \sigma^2 I, the spherical restriction of the last lecture, in place of a general diagonal \Psi. 56:33 Can PCA overfit? Ng’s answer is that it can when k is close to m, for instance a 1,000-dimensional subspace estimated from 1,000 examples. Then the subspace fits the sample, not the distribution.

title: 15  PCA and ICA
section: 15.7 A map of the unsupervised algorithms
text:
15.7 A map of the unsupervised algorithms
49:23 A student asks when to use PCA and when to use factor analysis. Ng answers by sorting the four unsupervised algorithms of the course along two axes: whether they model a density p(x), and whether they assume the data lie near a subspace or in clusters (“clumps”).



Table 15.1: The four unsupervised algorithms of lectures 13–15, after Ng’s board.






Models p(x)
No probabilistic model




Data near a subspace
factor analysis
PCA


Data in clusters
mixture of Gaussians
k-means






The left column is where EM lives. EM applies whenever there is a model p(x, z) with z unobserved, whether z is discrete (the mixture) or Gaussian (factor analysis). The density models are what you want for anomaly detection. The right column is for compression and for human understanding: PCA to see high-dimensional data, k-means to split customers into market segments or genes into groups. Ng adds that the mixture of Gaussians often works well on data that are not really clustered, so the table is a guide, not a rule.

title: 15  PCA and ICA
section: 15.8 Independent components analysis: the cocktail party
text:
15.8 Independent components analysis: the cocktail party
1:02:36 PCA looks for directions of high variance. ICA looks for directions that are statistically independent. The motivating problem is the cocktail party. Several people talk at once, and several microphones placed around the room each record a different mixture of their voices. Ng plays a demonstration with two microphones. Each one picks up a voice counting to ten in English mixed with another voice in Spanish. ICA, given only the two recordings and told nothing about voices, returns one track per speaker. A second example mixes the counting voice with music from a radio. Because this one was recorded in a real room, Ng notes, the separation is not perfect, but most of the music is gone.
1:07:32 The model is linear. Let s^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^n hold the n sources at time i, where s^{(i)}_j is the air-pressure deviation produced by speaker j. Microphone j records

x^{(i)}_j = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{jk}\, s^{(i)}_k, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad x^{(i)} = A s^{(i)},
\tag{15.3}
with an unknown, square mixing matrix A. Here x^{(i)} is the recording at time i, and the recordings must be time-aligned across microphones. The goal is the unmixing matrix W = A^{-1}, so that s^{(i)} = W x^{(i)}. Writing w_j^\top for the rows of W, source j is s^{(i)}_j = w_j^\top x^{(i)}. Asked whether there must be as many microphones as speakers, Ng says yes for now. The general case is deferred.
Two caveats are worth stating. First, Equation 15.3 is an idealisation. In a real room each voice reaches each microphone after a delay and with echoes, so a microphone records a sum of filtered copies of each source, not a single weighted sum. This is part of why the real-room demonstration separates imperfectly. Second, Ng remarks that “sound can only add”, and that some versions of ICA put sign constraints on A and W for that reason. That needs restating. The sources are pressure deviations, which are positive and negative. Sound waves superpose with signs, and cancellation is how noise-cancelling headphones work. What is plausibly non-negative is the gain from a speaker to a microphone, so a sign constraint, where one is used, belongs on the entries of A, not on the signals.
1:14:12 Why should recovery be possible at all? Ng’s picture (Figure 15.4) uses two sources that each emit an independent value uniform on [-1, 1] at every instant, so the pairs (s_1, s_2) fill a square. The mixing matrix shears the square into a parallelogram, and that is all the microphones see. The edges of the parallelogram reveal the directions of the original axes, and an unmixing matrix that turns the parallelogram back into an axis-aligned square recovers the sources.






Figure 15.4: The ICA problem with two uniform sources. Independent sources fill a square (left). Mixing by A gives the parallelogram the microphones observe (centre). Unmixing by W = PDA^{-1}, where P swaps the two rows and D flips one sign, gives a square again (right): the sources are recovered, but as (-s_2, s_1).



1:15:44 Recovery has unavoidable ambiguities. The first is order. Nothing in the data says which source is the person and which is the radio, so the sources come back in an arbitrary order. The second is sign. A square flipped horizontally or vertically is the same square, so a source can come back negated. For audio that is harmless, because -s_j sounds identical to s_j. The official notes add a third, scale. Multiplying a source by \alpha and the corresponding column of A by 1/\alpha leaves x unchanged, so the sources are determined only up to scale, and for audio that is only a volume. All three combine into W = P D A^{-1} with P a permutation and D diagonal, as in the right panel of Figure 15.4. The generator checks that every such W, including swaps, sign flips and rescalings by 2 and -\tfrac12, returns exactly the sources, permuted and rescaled.
The picture also shows what ICA depends on. A uniform square has corners, which mark the original axes. Lecture 16 shows that Gaussian sources, whose density is round, have no such corners, and that this ambiguity cannot be resolved. It then derives the algorithm that finds W by maximum likelihood.






NoteIn the official notes



PCA, with the variance derivation and the eigenvector solution, is cs229-notes10. The ICA model, its permutation, scaling and sign ambiguities, and the reason Gaussian sources cannot be separated are in cs229-notes11, section 1. The density of a linear transformation and the maximum-likelihood algorithm for W are in sections 2 and 3.

title: 16  Independent Component Analysis and RL
text:
16.1 Gaussian sources cannot be unmixed
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
The lecture has two halves that share nothing but a date. The first finishes independent components analysis. Chapter 15 set up the cocktail-party model x = As and showed that the sources can be recovered only up to order, sign and scale. This chapter adds the reason ICA needs non-Gaussian sources, writes down the likelihood of the unmixing matrix W, and derives the stochastic gradient rule that maximises it. The second half opens the last part of the course, reinforcement learning. It introduces the Markov decision process and the 11-state gridworld that lectures 16 and 17 use as their running example, and states the goal: a policy that maximises the expected discounted sum of rewards.
3:07 Chapter 15’s picture of why ICA works used sources uniform on [-1, 1]. Their joint distribution fills a square, the mixing matrix shears it into a parallelogram, and the corners of the parallelogram give away the directions of the original axes. Ng now asks what happens if the sources are Gaussian instead. Two independent standard Gaussians have a joint density with circular contours. A mixing matrix stretches the circle into an ellipse, and an unmixing matrix that maps the ellipse back to a circle is easy to find. But it is not unique, because every rotation of a circle is the same circle. If W turns the data back into independent unit Gaussians, so does RW for any rotation R, and nothing in the data can choose between them.
The official notes make this precise. If s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) then x = As is Gaussian with covariance AA^\top, and for any orthogonal R the mixing matrix AR gives x' = ARs with covariance ARR^\top A^\top = AA^\top. The two models produce the same distribution of recordings. The generator checks the same fact from the other side: with a Gaussian source prior, the log-likelihood of the 1,500-example dataset used below is unchanged, to rounding error, when the true unmixing matrix is rotated by 10°, 30°, 45° or 60°. Under the logistic prior introduced below it drops by 0.030 per example at 45°, so that likelihood does single out the right rotation.
6:44 Ng cites the theorem behind this informally: the Gaussian is the only distribution of independent components that is rotationally symmetric, and so ICA is possible exactly when the data are non-Gaussian. The careful version, due to Comon, is slightly weaker in its demand: the sources are identifiable up to order and scale as long as at most one of them is Gaussian. One Gaussian source has no other Gaussian to be confused with, and two or more can be rotated into one another.
crumbs: 16  Independent Component Analysis and RL

title: 16  Independent Component Analysis and RL
section: 16.2 The density of a linear transformation
text:
16.2 The density of a linear transformation
12:08 To fit W by maximum likelihood we need p_x, the density of the recordings, given p_s, the density of the sources, and the relation s = Wx. The tempting answer is p_x(x) = p_s(Wx). Since W is invertible, every x corresponds to exactly one s, so it seems the probability of seeing x is the probability of the matching s. Ng points out that this is correct for probability mass functions and wrong for densities.
14:31 His one-dimensional example shows why. Let s be uniform on [0, 1], so p_s(s) = 1 there, and let x = 2s, so A = 2 and W = \tfrac12. Then x is uniform on [0, 2], and a density spread over twice the width must be half as tall: p_x(x) = \tfrac12 on [0, 2]. The naive formula gives p_s(x/2) = 1 on [0, 2], which integrates to 2 (Figure 16.1, left). The missing factor is the determinant:

p_x(x) = p_s(Wx)\,\lvert W \rvert ,
\tag{16.1}
where \lvert W\rvert is the absolute value of the determinant of W. In one dimension it is just \lvert W\rvert = \tfrac12, and the generator confirms numerically that the corrected density integrates to 1 and the naive one to 2. The intuition carries to n dimensions. A maps the unit cube of source space to a parallelepiped of volume \lvert A\rvert, so probability spread over that volume has its density divided by \lvert A\rvert, that is, multiplied by \lvert W\rvert = 1/\lvert A\rvert.






Figure 16.1: Left: the density of s \sim U[0, 1], the density of x = 2s, and the naive p_s(x/2), which has area 2. Right: log densities of the three candidate source priors, all scaled to unit variance. The Gaussian falls off as a parabola, the logistic and Laplace densities linearly.
crumbs: 16  Independent Component Analysis and RL

title: 16  Independent Component Analysis and RL
section: 16.3 A prior for the sources: the sigmoid as a CDF
text:
16.3 A prior for the sources: the sigmoid as a CDF
18:22 The last modelling choice is p_s, the density of a single speaker’s signal. It must not be Gaussian. Ng specifies it through its cumulative distribution function F(s) = P(S \le s), which rises smoothly from 0 to 1, and recovers the density as p_s = F'. The question then becomes which familiar function rises smoothly from 0 to 1, and the sigmoid is the obvious answer. So the model takes F = g, with g(s) = 1/(1 + e^{-s}), and

p_s(s) = g'(s) = g(s)\,\bigl(1 - g(s)\bigr).

This is the logistic density. Ng’s argument for it is its tails. A Gaussian density falls like e^{-s^2/2}; the logistic falls like e^{-\lvert s\rvert}, so large values are far more likely, and that, he says, describes recorded speech and many natural signals better. The right panel of Figure 16.1 shows the difference on a log scale. At equal variance, the logistic density at four standard deviations is 9.6 times the Gaussian’s, and its excess kurtosis is 1.2 where the Gaussian’s is 0. Ng adds that a two-sided exponential, the Laplace density, works as well, and he has used it himself. Its tails are heavier still, with excess kurtosis 3. The sigmoid, he recalls, was simply the choice that early ICA researchers needed and tried, in Bell and Sejnowski’s information-maximisation algorithm, and it has stayed the default because it works.
28:24 A student asks why the joint density of two logistic sources is not also rotationally symmetric. Ng sketches the contours of a Laplace pair as diamonds and guesses that the logistic looks “a bit like that too”, inviting the class to plot it. The plot is Figure 16.2, and the guess is half right. Close to the origin the logistic density is nearly Gaussian, because \log g'(s) \approx -\log 4 - s^2/4 for small s, so the inner contours are almost circles: along the diagonal the innermost one reaches 0.98 of its distance along an axis. Farther out the linear tails take over and the contours become diamonds, with that ratio falling to 0.86 at the outermost level drawn. A Laplace pair has diamonds at every level, with ratio 1/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707, and a Gaussian pair has circles. What matters for ICA is only that the logistic contours are not circles. Any departure from rotational symmetry gives the likelihood a preferred orientation.






Figure 16.2: Contours of the joint density of two independent unit-variance sources under three priors, at the same four drops in log density from the peak. Gaussian contours are circles. Logistic contours are nearly round near the centre and become diamonds outward. Laplace contours are diamonds at every level.

title: 16  Independent Component Analysis and RL
section: 16.4 Maximum likelihood for the unmixing matrix
text:
16.4 Maximum likelihood for the unmixing matrix
21:39 With these pieces the likelihood is short. ICA’s central assumption is that the speakers are independent, so the joint source density is a product, p(s) = \prod_{j=1}^n p_s(s_j). Combining that with Equation 16.1 and s_j = w_j^\top x, where w_j^\top is the j-th row of W, gives

p(x) = \left(\prod_{j=1}^n p_s\!\left(w_j^\top x\right)\right) \lvert W \rvert .

For a training set x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(m)}, one microphone reading per instant, the log-likelihood of W is

\ell(W) = \sum_{i=1}^m \left( \sum_{j=1}^n \log g'\!\left(w_j^\top x^{(i)}\right) + \log \lvert W \rvert \right).
\tag{16.2}
26:02 Ng writes the derivative without deriving it. The official notes do the algebra, which needs the identity \nabla_W \lvert W\rvert = \lvert W\rvert (W^{-1})^\top. For one example it gives the stochastic gradient ascent rule

W := W + \alpha \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 2g(w_1^\top x^{(i)}) \\ \vdots \\ 1 - 2g(w_n^\top x^{(i)}) \end{bmatrix} x^{(i)\top} + \left(W^\top\right)^{-1} \right).
\tag{16.3}
The first term comes from the prior: \frac{d}{ds}\log g'(s) = 1 - 2g(s). The second comes from the determinant and keeps W from collapsing to zero, which would otherwise make every w_j^\top x zero and every source density maximal. A student catches a slip on the board here: the bracket should hold 1 - 2g, with g the sigmoid. The generator compares the analytic gradient with central finite differences of Equation 16.2, and they agree to 2 \times 10^{-10}.
27:12 The whole algorithm, then, is to initialise W, run gradient ascent on Equation 16.2, and read each source off as s^{(i)}_j = w_j^\top x^{(i)}. Playing s^{(1)}_1, \dots, s^{(m)}_1 through a speaker plays back speaker 1. Figure 16.3 runs it on 1,500 readings of two independent Laplace sources mixed by a fixed A. Batch gradient ascent from W = I raises the average log-likelihood from -3.736 to -3.109 and levels off. The product WA it ends with is \bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}1.310 & 0.051\\ -0.035 & 1.411\end{smallmatrix}\bigr], a scaled identity up to cross-talk of under 4%, and each recovered signal correlates with its source at 0.999 or above. The scale is not 1, because maximum likelihood rescales each source to suit the logistic prior. That is the scale ambiguity from chapter 15, resolved arbitrarily. The data here are generated exactly by the ICA model. Ng’s real-room recording separated less cleanly, for the reasons Section 15.8 gives.






Figure 16.3: ICA on two mixed Laplace sources. Left: the microphone readings, whose arms run along the columns of A. Centre: the same points multiplied by the W that gradient ascent finds; the arms now lie on the axes, so each coordinate is one source. Right: the average log-likelihood over 400 iterations of batch gradient ascent from W = I.









NoteIn the official notes



The density of a linear transformation and the full derivation of Equation 16.3 are in cs229-notes11, sections 2 and 3. The notes also remark that the data should have zero mean, which the sigmoid prior assumes, and that the training examples, being successive moments of audio, are not independent. The notes say this does not hurt the result, and that visiting the examples in a random order can speed up stochastic gradient ascent.

title: 16  Independent Component Analysis and RL
section: 16.5 Where ICA is used, and where it breaks
text:
16.5 Where ICA is used, and where it breaks
30:03 Asked for the closest nonlinear extension of ICA, Ng says there is no good answer yet and points to his own group’s work on stacking it. The large unsupervised network that learned to detect faces and cats in YouTube frames (Le et al., 2012) was trained layer by layer with an objective the paper calls reconstruction topographic ICA, a close relative of sparse coding. Ng’s view is that hierarchical versions of ICA and sparse coding lost attention when supervised deep learning took off, and deserve more of it than they get.
33:46 The standard application is cleaning electroencephalography (EEG) data. Electrodes on the scalp each record a weighted sum of the electrical activity of many brain processes at once: the heartbeat, eye blinks, everything else. That is a cocktail party in the head, and ICA unmixes it the same way. An analyst identifies the components that are heartbeat or blink artefacts, removes them, and remixes the rest (Jung et al., 2000). The clean signal is then the input to whatever comes next, such as a classifier that tries to tell from EEG whether a person is thinking of a person or an object. Run on small patches of natural images, ICA finds components that are localised, oriented edges (Bell and Sejnowski, 1997). The same result from sparse coding (Olshausen and Field, 1996) is one of the reasons neuroscientists ask whether the visual cortex learns its edge detectors this way.
40:41 A student had asked whether the number of microphones must equal the number of speakers. Ng’s answer is that more microphones than speakers is fine: run ICA, perhaps slightly modified, and some of the recovered sources come out silent. Fewer microphones than speakers is a research problem. With one microphone and two speakers, A is 1 \times 2 and cannot be inverted, so separation needs knowledge beyond independence. A low voice and a high voice can sometimes be pulled apart, two similar voices hardly at all.
The “slightly modified” matters more than it sounds. Run Equation 16.2 unchanged with ten microphones and five speakers, and W is 10 \times 10 while the recordings fill only a five-dimensional subspace. Any row w_j orthogonal to that subspace outputs exactly zero for every example, so it is one of the silent sources. Scaling that row by c leaves its \log g'(0) terms unchanged and multiplies \lvert W\rvert by c. The log-likelihood therefore grows by m \log c without bound. The generator confirms the exact m \log c gain for three microphones and two sources. So the silent sources are where the plain algorithm diverges, not a harmless by-product. The usual modification is to reduce the recordings to as many dimensions as there are sources, with PCA, before running ICA.
Ng’s other suggestion, from a student’s follow-up, is to parameterise the model by the rectangular mixing matrix A, 10 \times 5 here, instead of W. That avoids the problem but loses the convenient formula Equation 16.1, which needs a square W. How many sources to assume, he says, is like choosing k in k-means: try several and look for components that come out near-silent.

title: 16  Independent Component Analysis and RL
text:
16.6 Why reinforcement learning
49:52 The fourth and last part of the course is reinforcement learning. Ng motivates it with the autonomous helicopter from lecture 1. At every moment the helicopter is in some state, its position, orientation and velocity, and must choose how to move the control sticks. Supervised learning would need, for each state, the one correct stick position, and nobody can write that down. What a designer can write is a reward function: high when the helicopter flies the intended trajectory, very negative when it crashes. Ng compares it to training a dog. You cannot tell the dog what to do, but you can say “good dog” and “bad dog”, and it learns to do more of what earns the first. Games fit the same mould. Nobody knows the one best chess move in a given position, but a program can play and be rewarded with +1 for a win, -1 for a loss and 0 for a draw.
53:41 Such sparse feedback creates what Ng calls the credit assignment problem. A chess program checkmated on move 50 receives -1, but the losing blunder may have been on move 20, with the remaining 30 moves only playing out a lost position. A self-driving car that crashes usually made the decisive mistake seconds earlier, not at the instant of impact. Given only the final reward, the algorithm has to work out which of its earlier actions to do more of and which to do less of. Every algorithm in the rest of the course solves this problem, at least indirectly, and the value functions of lecture 17 are the main way they do it.

title: 16  Independent Component Analysis and RL
text:
16.8 Payoff, discounting and policies
1:05:15 The robot wakes in some state s_0 and chooses an action a_0. The world moves it to s_1 \sim P_{s_0 a_0}, it chooses a_1, moves to s_2 \sim P_{s_1 a_1}, and so on. Its total payoff is the discounted sum of the rewards along the way:

R(s_0) + \gamma R(s_1) + \gamma^2 R(s_2) + \cdots .
\tag{16.4}
The goal is to choose actions that maximise the expected total payoff, since the transitions are random. With \gamma around 0.99, a reward one step from now counts 0.99 as much as one now, and one a hundred steps away about 0.37 as much.
1:08:00 Ng gives two reasons for \gamma, and says plainly that the second is the real one. The first is the time value of money. A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year, because it can earn interest, and by the same logic a payment is better postponed than made now. So \gamma makes the robot hurry towards positive rewards and put off negative ones. The second is that with \gamma < 1 the algorithms provably converge, and with \gamma = 1 many of them do not, or are much harder to analyse. A student supplies the mechanism. Without discounting, the sum Equation 16.4 can grow or shrink without bound. With it, \lvert\text{payoff}\rvert \le R_{\max}/(1-\gamma). For a robot that loiters for ever at -0.02 per step with \gamma = 0.99, that is -2, a finite number an algorithm can reason about.
1:11:28 What a reinforcement learning algorithm produces is a policy, \pi : S \to A, a rule for which action to take in each state. Executing \pi means taking a = \pi(s) in whatever state the robot is in. Ng shows the optimal policy for the gridworld (Figure 16.4, right), computed offline. Lecture 17 derives value iteration, the algorithm that computes it. The generator runs it and reproduces, to two decimals, the values Ng later reads off the board.
1:14:44 The interesting cell is (3, 1). North is the direct route: two steps to (3, 3), then one East to the goal. But at (3, 2) a 0.1 chance of slipping East lands the robot on -1. West goes all the way round by (1, 1) and the top row, which costs more steps and more discounting, but never passes the -1. Ng’s point is that the answer is not obvious by eye, and the optimal policy takes the long, safe route. The generator measures how fine the distinction is. At (3, 1), the expected value of the next state is 0.736 for West against 0.674 for North, and the runner-up is not North but South, at 0.691: bumping into the wall and staying put is better than going North. The choice holds only while the step reward lies between 0 and -0.0368. Below that, loitering costs enough that the risky short route wins. Elsewhere the margins are smaller still. At (3, 2), North beats West by 0.0005, and only because the step reward is below -0.0196; at (4, 1), West beats South by 0.003. An MDP solver makes these distinctions exactly. A person eyeballing the grid would not.
1:16:13 Two last questions point ahead. Chess fits the framework if a “state” is the board when it is your turn: you move, the opponent moves, and the opponent’s unknown reply becomes the randomness in P_{sa}. And the probabilities 0.8, 0.1, 0.1 need not be given. For a real robot they are usually estimated from data, which is how lecture 17 ends. The number of policies is finite but large. Lecture 17 counts it as 4^{11}, though only the nine non-absorbing states need an action, so 4^9 = 262{,}144. Enumerating them is hopeless for any realistic MDP, and the next lecture’s value and policy iteration avoid enumeration altogether.






NoteIn the official notes



Markov decision processes, the five-tuple, the total payoff and policies are in cs229-notes12, section 1. The notes allow rewards that depend on the action, R(s, a), and mention finite-horizon MDPs. The lecture keeps to R(s) and infinite horizons.
