title: 17  MDPs and Value/Policy Iteration
text:
17.1 The value of a policy
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Lecture 16 defined a Markov decision process and claimed an optimal policy for the 11-state gridworld without saying where it came from. This lecture supplies the method. It defines three objects: V^\pi, the value of following a fixed policy; V^*, the best value any policy can achieve; and \pi^*, the policy that achieves it. Each satisfies a version of Bellman’s equation, and the two standard algorithms, value iteration and policy iteration, are two ways of solving those equations. The lecture then drops the assumption that the transition probabilities are known. It estimates them from the robot’s own experience, and this raises the question of how much the robot should explore.
6:46 For a policy \pi, the value function V^\pi : S \to \mathbb{R} gives the expected total payoff of starting in s and following \pi for ever:
V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}\left[ R(s_0) + \gamma R(s_1) + \gamma^2 R(s_2) + \cdots \;\middle|\; s_0 = s,\ \pi \right].
8:40 Ng’s example is deliberately poor. From some states it drives straight for the -1. The left half of Figure 17.1 uses a concrete policy of that kind, East from every state. On the top row it reaches the +1 and is worth about 0.6 to 0.76. Along the middle and bottom rows it runs into the -1, or stalls against the east wall paying -0.02 a step, and is worth about -0.3 to -1.1. The \pm 1 cells are absorbing: once the robot reaches one, it collects that reward and the world ends.
10:57 The equation that governs V^\pi comes from splitting the payoff after its first term. Factor one \gamma out of everything after R(s_0):
R(s_0) + \gamma \bigl( R(s_1) + \gamma R(s_2) + \cdots \bigr).
The bracket is the payoff of a robot that starts in s_1 and follows \pi. Its expectation is V^\pi(s_1), and s_1 is drawn from P_{s\pi(s)}, because in state s the policy takes action \pi(s). Writing s' for the next state gives Bellman’s equation for V^\pi:
V^\pi(s) = R(s) + \gamma \sum_{s' \in S} P_{s\pi(s)}(s')\, V^\pi(s').
\tag{17.1}
The first term is the immediate reward, which the robot gets just for waking up in s. The second is the discounted expected future reward.
19:42 For a fixed \pi, Equation 17.1 is linear in the unknowns V^\pi(s). For s = (3, 1), with \pi going North, it reads
V^\pi(3,1) = R(3,1) + \gamma\bigl[0.8\,V^\pi(3,2) + 0.1\,V^\pi(2,1) + 0.1\,V^\pi(4,1)\bigr],
and one such equation for each of the 11 states gives 11 linear equations in 11 unknowns. A linear solver handles that instantly. The generator solves the system for the East policy and checks the result against 5,000 sweeps of repeated substitution into Equation 17.1. The two agree to 10^{-9}.

title: 17  MDPs and Value/Policy Iteration
text: Figure 17.1: Left: the policy “always go East” and its value V^\pi, solved from the 11 Bellman equations. Right: the optimal policy and the optimal value function V^* for R = -0.02, \gamma = 0.99. Cell (3, 1), whose action the lecture works out by hand, is highlighted.

title: 17  MDPs and Value/Policy Iteration
section: 17.2 The optimal value function and the optimal policy
text:
17.2 The optimal value function and the optimal policy
24:47 The optimal value function is the best value any policy achieves from each state:

V^*(s) = \max_\pi V^\pi(s).

Ng flags a terminology trap. Both V^\pi and V^* are called “value functions”, but one belongs to a particular policy, good or bad, and the other to the best of them. The maximum is over a combinatorially large set, 4^9 policies even for this small grid, so the definition does not suggest how to compute V^*. Its Bellman equation does.
27:12 Run the same argument as for Equation 17.1, but let the robot choose its first action well. It collects R(s) for waking up in s. Whatever action a it takes, it then lands in s' \sim P_{sa} and can collect at most V^*(s') from there. The best first action is the one with the largest expected continuation, so

V^*(s) = R(s) + \max_{a \in A}\; \gamma \sum_{s' \in S} P_{sa}(s')\, V^*(s').
\tag{17.2}
29:44 If V^* were known, the optimal action would be the one that attains that maximum. Ng asks the room what to do in state s, and the answer is already in Equation 17.2:

\pi^*(s) = \arg\max_{a \in A} \sum_{s' \in S} P_{sa}(s')\, V^*(s').
\tag{17.3}
\gamma is dropped because a positive constant does not move an argmax. 32:50 Ng states, without proof, that this policy is optimal from every state at once: V^*(s) = V^{\pi^*}(s) \ge V^\pi(s) for every \pi and every s. One policy is best everywhere, so no state has to trade off against another. The generator checks both halves. The value of the greedy policy, solved from its own linear system, equals V^* to 10^{-9}, and V^* is at least V^\pi, state by state, for 3,000 random policies. The plan is therefore to find V^* and then read off \pi^* with Equation 17.3.

title: 17  MDPs and Value/Policy Iteration
text:
17.3 Value iteration
35:22 Value iteration treats Equation 17.2 as an update rule:

Initialise V(s) := 0 for every s.
Repeat until convergence: for every s, V(s) := R(s) + \max_a \gamma \sum_{s'} P_{sa}(s')\, V(s').

38:07 There are two ways to carry out step 2, and Ng compares them to gradient descent. A synchronous update computes the right-hand side for all 11 states from the old values, then overwrites all 11 at once. In vector form this is V := B(V), where B is called the Bellman backup operator. An asynchronous update sweeps through the states one at a time and overwrites each value as soon as it is computed, so later states in the sweep already use the new values. Both converge to V^*.
Ng’s default is the synchronous form, because it is a matrix operation and vectorises. He says “asynchronous” at this point in the recording, but the reason he gives, vectorisation, and the procedure he describes, compute all eleven and then update, are the synchronous one. The asynchronous form has the opposite advantage: it needs fewer sweeps. On the gridworld with \gamma = 0.99, the max-norm error falls below 10^{-6} after 21 asynchronous sweeps against 29 synchronous ones (Figure 17.2).
40:32 A student asks how to code the absorbing states. One way is to give them transition probabilities of zero to every state, so that their value is just R. Another is to add a twelfth, zero-reward “sink” state that they lead to and that loops on itself. Ng calls the second cleaner and the first more common. Both give the same values.
43:07 Why does it converge? The problem set shows that B is a contraction in the max norm: \lVert B(V) - B(V')\rVert_\infty \le \gamma \lVert V - V'\rVert_\infty. Since V^* = B(V^*), each synchronous sweep shrinks the error by at least a factor \gamma, so \lVert V_k - V^*\rVert_\infty \le \gamma^k \lVert V_0 - V^*\rVert_\infty. Ng turns this into a rule of thumb: at \gamma = 0.99, value iteration needs a few hundred iterations, and at \gamma = 0.9 a few dozen.
The bound is right but, for this MDP, very loose. Taken literally, it needs 1,375 sweeps per unit of initial error to reach 10^{-6} at \gamma = 0.99, and 132 at \gamma = 0.9. The gridworld gets there in 29 sweeps at \gamma = 0.99 and 21 at \gamma = 0.9. The generator asserts that every synchronous sweep is within the bound, so nothing here contradicts the theorem. The reason is the absorbing states. After k sweeps the remaining error is roughly the discounted value of what happens beyond step k. Under \pi^*, starting from (1, 1), the robot is still wandering after 10 steps with probability 0.04, and after 20 steps with probability essentially zero, so there is little left to discount. The factor \gamma only governs the rate when the process can run on for a long time without ending. The more useful fact for practice is that the policy converges before the values. With \gamma = 0.99, the greedy policy Equation 17.3 of the synchronous estimate is already exactly \pi^* after 11 sweeps, while the values are still off by as much as 0.08.






Figure 17.2: Value iteration on the gridworld: base-10 logarithm of the max-norm error against the number of sweeps, synchronous and asynchronous, at \gamma = 0.99 and \gamma = 0.9. Dotted lines are the guarantee \gamma^k \lVert V_0 - V^*\rVert_\infty, which every synchronous curve stays below, by a wide margin here because the robot is absorbed within a few steps.

title: 17  MDPs and Value/Policy Iteration
text:
17.4 Reading the policy off V^*
45:15 Ng writes the converged V^* on the board and uses it to justify the West arrow at (3, 1) that lecture 16 asserted. Going West reaches (2, 1) with probability 0.8, where V^* \approx 0.75. It slips North to (3, 2), worth 0.69, with probability 0.1, and South into the wall, staying at (3, 1), worth 0.71, with probability 0.1. The expected value is 0.740. Going North gives 0.8 \times 0.69 + 0.1 \times 0.75 + 0.1 \times 0.49 = 0.676, so West wins.
The generator’s V^* (Figure 17.1, right) matches the board values to two decimals: 0.746, 0.687, 0.709 and 0.491. Computed from the unrounded values, the two expectations are 0.736 and 0.674. Ng adds that a full check compares all four actions, and the full check is instructive. South, at 0.691, beats North: bumping into the wall and staying put is the second-best action, because North risks the slip into -1. East is last at 0.532.

title: 17  MDPs and Value/Policy Iteration
text:
17.5 Policy iteration
50:18 Policy iteration keeps a policy, not a value function, at the centre:

Initialise \pi randomly.
Repeat until \pi stops changing:

V := V^\pi, by solving the linear system Equation 17.1;
for every s, \pi(s) := \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} P_{sa}(s')\, V(s').


Step (b) pretends that the current V is optimal and acts greedily on it. Value iteration waits until V has converged to extract a policy. Policy iteration extracts a new one on every round. 54:44 The trade-off, as Ng puts it, is the linear solve in step (a). For 11 states, or a few hundred, it is trivial, and policy iteration is fast. For 10,000 states or a million, solving the system on every round is expensive, and he would use value iteration. He also notes a more academic difference. Value iteration approaches V^* and never exactly reaches it, as gradient descent approaches the minimum of a least-squares cost. Policy iteration stops after a finite number of rounds, at exactly \pi^* and exactly V^*, the way the normal equations jump straight to the answer. It must stop, because each round improves the policy, by the policy improvement theorem, and there are only finitely many policies to improve through.
The generator checks this on the gridworld. Started from 200 random policies, policy iteration needs between 2 and 8 evaluations, 5 on average, and always ends at the \pi^* of Figure 17.1. From “always East” it needs 3. The values never decrease from one round to the next, in any state. In practice, Ng says, he sees value iteration used more, because real problems are large. For small ones policy iteration may converge a little faster.






NoteIn the official notes



Both algorithms, the synchronous and asynchronous variants, and the statement that policy iteration terminates are in cs229-notes12, section 2. The contraction argument for value iteration is a homework problem in the course.

title: 17  MDPs and Value/Policy Iteration
text:
17.6 Learning the model
58:41 So far P_{sa} has been given. For a real robot, a helicopter or a chess opponent, it usually is not, and has to be estimated from experience. Run some policy for a while, count what happens, and use the maximum-likelihood estimate

\hat P_{sa}(s') = \frac{\#\{\text{times action } a \text{ was taken in } s \text{ and led to } s'\}}{\#\{\text{times action } a \text{ was taken in } s\}}.
\tag{17.4}
When the denominator is zero, because a has never been tried in s, the common heuristic is a uniform guess, \hat P_{sa}(s') = 1/\lvert S\rvert.
1:01:41 Laplace smoothing would also avoid the 0/0: add 1 to every numerator and \lvert S\rvert to every denominator. Ng says it is allowed but uncommon, because, unlike naive Bayes, MDP solvers are not badly hurt by zero estimates. The generator suggests a stronger statement: on the gridworld, smoothing makes things worse. It runs a uniformly random policy for a given number of moves, builds \hat P with and without smoothing, solves for the policy, and scores it by its true loss, the largest V^*(s) - V^{\hat\pi}(s) over states, averaged over 40 runs. The plain counts lose 0.078 after 1,000 moves and 0.010 after 10,000. With smoothing the losses are 0.263 and 0.023. The reason is visible in the formula. Smoothing gives every action a small probability of moving the robot to every state, including straight to the +1 or -1 from across the grid. With 11 states and only a few visits per state-action pair, that invented mass is large, and it is exactly the mass the optimal policy is most sensitive to. Exact recovery of \pi^* is rare either way, 14 runs in 40 even after 10,000 moves without smoothing, because of the 0.0005 margin at (3, 2) noted in lecture 16. Measuring the loss, not whether the policy is exactly \pi^*, is the fair test.
1:03:01 Put together, the practical loop is:

Take actions according to some policy \pi to gain experience in the MDP.
Update the estimates of P_{sa} from the counts, and of R if it is unknown.
Solve Bellman’s equations for the estimated MDP by value iteration, warm-started from the previous V if convenient, to get a new V.
Update \pi to be greedy with respect to V, and repeat.

1:06:03 The reward is usually part of the problem specification, but not always. For a trading application the reward is a day’s return, and for a car it might be a penalty for every pothole. Both are random functions of the state, so the same loop estimates the expected reward of each state by averaging what it observes.

title: 17  MDPs and Value/Policy Iteration
text:
17.7 Exploration versus exploitation
1:07:33 The loop above is greedy: it always acts on its current best estimate. Ng shows the trouble with a different MDP. A robot starts with a +1 nearby and a +10 farther away. If its first runs happen to reach the +1, the estimated model says that going there works, and the greedy policy keeps going there. Every trip ends at the +1, so the robot’s experience stays in that half of the state space, and the +10 is never found. Acting on what is known is exploitation. Trying actions that look worse to learn something new is exploration. The tension between them is not academic. Ng’s example is online advertising. Showing only the ads a user is predicted to click maximises short-term revenue. Showing occasional others is how the platform discovers interests nobody knew the user had.
1:13:28 The standard fix is ε-greedy exploration. On each step, with probability 1-\varepsilon take the action \pi(s), and with probability \varepsilon, for instance 0.1, take a random one. Ng points out that the name is backwards, since \varepsilon is the probability of acting randomly, not greedily, but it is the name everyone uses. With \varepsilon > 0 every action keeps being tried in every state the robot can reach, so the estimated model converges to the true one and the planned policy to \pi^*, though finding a remote reward by chance can take a long time.
Figure 17.3 makes Ng’s example concrete in one dimension, in a toy of our own: an eight-cell corridor with the +10 five steps to the left of the start and the +1 two steps to the right. Moves slip 20% of the time, each step costs 0.02, \gamma = 0.95, and the robot learns both P_{sa} and R as above. Going left is worth about 7.65 and going right 0.86, so the right answer is not close. Over 200 independent learners, the fraction whose policy heads for the +10 after 150 episodes is 0.62 for the greedy learner, 0.68 with \varepsilon = 0.1 and 0.78 with \varepsilon = 0.2. Two details are worth noticing. The greedy learner is not completely stuck: its curve keeps creeping up, presumably because slipping moves sometimes carry it left without being asked. And none of the curves has reached 1, which is Ng’s caveat about how long a remote reward can take to find.






Figure 17.3: A toy version of the lecture’s exploration example, not from the lecture. Left: the corridor, with the start between a distant +10 and a nearby +1. Right: over 200 learners that estimate the model from experience and re-plan after each episode, the fraction whose current policy heads for the +10, for ε = 0 (greedy), 0.1 and 0.2.



1:16:17 Asked whether \varepsilon should stay fixed, Ng says there are many heuristics, and a reasonable one is to start large and shrink it. Another is Boltzmann exploration. Instead of a uniformly random action with probability \varepsilon, choose action a with probability proportional to \exp\bigl(Q(s, a)/\tau\bigr), where Q(s, a) = \sum_{s'} P_{sa}(s') V(s') is the estimated value of taking a and \tau is a temperature. Actions that look nearly as good as the best are tried often, and actions that look terrible almost never. A student asks about rewarding the robot for visiting states it has never seen. That is intrinsic motivation, a research line Ng suggests looking up. And asked how often to re-plan, he says as often as the computation allows. It does no harm. With a physical robot or helicopter, where each flight is a session, re-planning between flights is the natural rhythm.






NoteIn the official notes



Estimating P_{sa} and R from experience, with the 1/\lvert S\rvert rule for untried actions and the warm-started value iteration loop, is in cs229-notes12, section 3. The notes do not treat exploration. Lecture 18 extends the framework to continuous states, covered in section 4 of the same notes.

title: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation
text:
18.1 States that are vectors
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Value iteration as lecture 17 left it keeps one number per state, so it needs a state space it can list. A car, a helicopter or a pole balanced on a cart has a state made of real numbers. This lecture gives two ways to cope. The first is to chop the state space into cells and pretend it is discrete. The second is to treat the value function as something to fit: sample states, compute what value iteration says their values should be, and run linear regression on features of the state to fill in everything between. That second method, fitted value iteration, needs a simulator it can query at any state, and Ng spends the middle of the lecture on where such a simulator comes from. His preferred answer is to learn one from a pilot’s flight logs.
3:43 Ng starts from three robots and asks, for each, what the state has to contain. A car seen from above needs its position (x, y) and its heading \theta. That is enough at walking pace, but at any real speed the next position depends on how fast the car is moving, so the state also carries the velocities \dot x, \dot y, \dot\theta: six numbers. Whether to add the steering-wheel angle or the wear on the tyres is a modelling choice that depends on what you are building. A helicopter moves in three dimensions, so it has position (x, y, z), an orientation given by roll, pitch and yaw (\phi, \theta,
\psi), and the six corresponding velocities: twelve numbers. The third robot is the classic toy of early reinforcement learning, the inverted pendulum: a cart on a rail with a pole hinged freely on top, which the controller must keep upright by pushing the cart left and right. Its state is (x, \theta, \dot x, \dot\theta), four numbers.
10:06 In all three, S = \mathbb{R}^n with n equal to 4, 6 or 12. Angles wrap around rather than run along the real line, which a mathematician would object to; for the algorithms in this lecture the distinction does not matter.
crumbs: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation

title: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation
text:
18.2 Discretization, and what it costs
10:55 The direct approach lays a grid over the state space, gives every cell a name, and treats the robot as being “in” a cell whenever its true state falls inside it. The continuous problem becomes a discrete MDP that value iteration can solve, and the policy for a continuous state is the policy of its cell. Ng is clear that this is often fine. For a low-dimensional problem it is the quickest thing to get working.
12:31 It has two weaknesses, and he makes the first one with the example the course opened with. Suppose you predicted house prices by cutting the size axis into five intervals and fitting a constant on each. You would get a staircase, a poor representation of a price that varies smoothly with size. Discretizing the state space does exactly this to the value function: V^* is approximated by a constant on every cell. The left of Figure 18.1 shows the staircase on a one-dimensional MDP of our own. The state s is a point on a line, the actions move it left, right or not at all by 0.25 with Gaussian slip of standard deviation 0.15, the reward is -s^2, and \gamma = 0.9. With six cells, the discretized value function misses the true V^* by up to 14.8. Doubling the cells halves the error, to 7.0, then 3.4 and 1.8 with 48 cells. The dashed curve is the method the rest of the lecture builds, which fits five numbers and lands within 1.8.






Figure 18.1: Left: the optimal value function of a one-dimensional MDP (purple), the staircase a six-cell discretization gives (teal), and fitted value iteration with features 1, s, \dots, s^4 (dashed). Right: the number of cells k^n needed to discretize each of n state variables into k values, on a log scale, with the lecture’s three robots marked.



14:35 The second weakness is the one Bellman named the curse of dimensionality. Discretizing each of n state variables into k values gives k^n cells. At a coarse k = 10 the pendulum needs 10^4 cells and the car 10^6. The helicopter needs 10^{12}, and the official notes’ example of a 10-dimensional state at 100 values each needs 10^{20} (right of Figure 18.1). Ng adds that the curse is not only about continuous states. A factory with 100 machines, each in one of k conditions, has k^{100} discrete states, and fitted value iteration can be the better algorithm there too.
17:25 His working rules for when to discretize are worth having as stated. In two or three dimensions, just do it. In four to six, think about it, and it will often still work. The pendulum is fine, and friends of his made a six-dimensional bicycle model work “if you put some work into it”. The usual trick in this range is to discretize unevenly, spending more values on the variables the policy is most sensitive to, because every value saved is saved in the exponent. At seven or eight dimensions he becomes nervous. Above that he would very seriously look for an algorithm that does not discretize. The official notes draw the line a little lower: they promise reliable results in one or two dimensions, four with care, and six only with luck.
crumbs: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation

title: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation
text:
18.3 Getting a model
23:20 Fitted value iteration needs a model, or simulator: a black box that takes a state s and an action a and returns a next state s' drawn from P_{sa}. For simplicity the action space is taken to be discrete. Ng points out that this is usually a mild assumption, because robots tend to have far fewer controls than state variables. The car has a six-dimensional state but two controls, steering and braking. The helicopter has twelve state variables and four controls, a stick under each hand that moves in two directions. The pendulum has four and one.
26:13 One way to get a simulator is physics. For the pendulum, Newtonian mechanics gives \dot s as a function of the state, the push and the masses and length of the parts. Ng shows the equation only as decoration. Stepping it forward as s' = s + \Delta t\,\dot s with \Delta t = 0.1 s simulates the system at 10 Hz. In practice nobody derives these by hand. You download an open-source physics engine and give it the dimensions. He once built a four-legged walking robot’s controller this way.
29:15 The way he uses more often is to learn the model from data. Take the helicopter into a field and have a human pilot fly it around while GPS, accelerometers and a compass log the state ten times a second, along with the stick positions. One flight gives a trajectory s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, \dots, s_T; repeat it m times. Predicting s_{t+1} from (s_t, a_t) is now a supervised learning problem. Its linear version is

s_{t+1} \approx A s_t + B a_t,
\qquad
\min_{A, B} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \bigl\lVert s^{(i)}_{t+1} - \bigl(A s^{(i)}_t + B a^{(i)}_t\bigr) \bigr\rVert^2,
\tag{18.1}
with A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} square and B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d} tall and thin when the action has d < n components. Ng’s verdict from experience is that this is “actually not a terrible model” for a helicopter flying slowly and roughly level, and a poor one for fast, aggressive manoeuvres. Nonlinear features \phi(s) and \phi'(a) can replace the raw state and action when the linear model is not enough.
Equation 18.1 looks like a new kind of regression because A and B are matrices. Ng’s remark that it is the same as running ordinary linear regression n times, once per state variable, is right: the squared norm is a sum over the n components, and each component involves only one row of [A\;B]. The notes add that the least-squares fit is also the maximum-likelihood one. That holds even if the noise in different state variables is correlated, which is the realistic case, because every equation shares the same regressors. The generator confirms all three routes on a simulated two-dimensional system with correlated noise. The joint fit, the n separate regressions and the Gaussian maximum-likelihood fit with the true covariance agree to 10^{-15}.
35:37 A student asks whether m short flights differ from one long one. For the algorithm, Ng says, they do not. In practice the helicopter burns fuel and gets lighter, and the wind changes, so several flights average over conditions a single one would not cover.
37:41 Having fitted A and B, there are two simulators to choose from. The deterministic one sets s_{t+1} = A s_t + B a_t. The stochastic one adds \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma), whose covariance can be estimated from the residuals, and draws a fresh \varepsilon_t on every step. This whole approach of learning a model and then planning in it is model-based reinforcement learning. The alternative, model-free RL, runs the learning algorithm on the real system directly. Ng’s view in 2018 is that model-based methods were taking off faster in robotics. A physical robot cannot afford to be crashed thousands of times while it learns, while a video game or a board game is its own perfect simulator and can be.
41:45 He ends this part with a lesson from many robots. A policy optimised against a deterministic simulator tends to be brittle. It exploits details of the simulator that the real machine does not share, and that is how a five-legged robot can walk beautifully in a video and fall over in the lab. A simulator is always a little wrong: it misses a wind gust, or banks a degree too far in a turn. If the policy has to work in a slightly noisy simulator, it is much more likely to work on the real robot. His advice is to always add noise. The exact distribution matters much less than remembering to add it. (He mentions in passing that his own PhD thesis used reinforcement learning to fly helicopters, and that he lived through the crashes.)
crumbs: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation

title: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation
text:
18.4 Fitted value iteration
46:13 With a simulator in hand, the value function is approximated the way a price is approximated in linear regression:

V(s) = \theta^\top \phi(s),
\tag{18.2}
where \phi(s) is a vector of features of the state chosen by hand. Ng’s advice on choosing them is to remember what a value is: the expected payoff from that state, so features should say how well the robot is doing. For the pendulum, a pole leaning far to the right is bad unless the cart is moving fast to the right to catch it. So the product of the pole angle and the cart velocity is a natural feature, alongside x, \dot x and squares. A model-based method also makes overfitting less of a worry than in ordinary supervised learning. The training data come from the simulator and cost nothing, so a generous set of features, some of which turn out useless, can be fitted from as many samples as the computer can afford.
50:14 The algorithm starts from value iteration’s update in continuous form,

V(s) := R(s) + \gamma \max_a \mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P_{sa}}\bigl[V(s')\bigr],
\tag{18.3}
and replaces the two things it cannot do. It cannot visit every state, so it visits a sample. It cannot store an arbitrary V, so it fits Equation 18.2 to the targets that Equation 18.3 produces at the sampled states:

Sample states s^{(1)}, \dots, s^{(m)} at random, and set \theta := 0.
Repeat:

For each i = 1, \dots, m and each action a: draw s'_1, \dots, s'_k \sim P_{s^{(i)} a} from the simulator and set q(a) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \bigl[ R(s^{(i)}) + \gamma V(s'_j) \bigr].
Set y^{(i)} = \max_a q(a).
Set \theta := \arg\min_\theta \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \bigl( \theta^\top \phi(s^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \bigr)^2.


56:46 Each q(a) is a sample-average estimate of the expectation in Equation 18.3, so y^{(i)} is an estimate of the whole right-hand side at s^{(i)}. 58:04 Discrete value iteration would now set V(s^{(i)}) := y^{(i)}, but a linear function cannot have its values set one point at a time. The best it can do is come as close as possible to all the targets at once, which is a least-squares fit. Step (c) is linear regression with s^{(i)} in the role of x and y^{(i)} in the role of the price. A student asks where V(s'_j) in step (a) comes from. 1:08:35 It is \theta^\top \phi(s'_j) with the \theta from the previous iteration, exactly as discrete value iteration uses the previous sweep’s values.
1:00:51 Two questions clarify the bookkeeping. The m here is the number of sampled states and has nothing to do with the m flights used to learn the model. Ng’s picture is one team flying the helicopter a thousand times and publishing a model, and another team running fitted value iteration on it. 1:03:06 He then asks the class how the algorithm simplifies with a deterministic simulator. The answer is that k = 1 suffices, since all k samples would be the same next state. The generator checks this mechanically: with the noise switched off, k = 1 and k = 5 give the same \theta to within 10^{-14}. On how large m should be, 1:05:38 he reasons as for any regression. With 50 features, 500 samples might do. But samples are free, so there is no harm in 5,000 or 100,000 beyond running time. 1:09:07 Finally, nothing requires the regression to be linear. Locally weighted regression works, and replacing it with a neural network is, he says only half joking, how you get deep reinforcement learning.
On the one-dimensional MDP of Figure 18.1, with 200 sampled states, k = 10 and five polynomial features, fitted value iteration lands within 1.8 of V^* everywhere. That is as good as the 48-cell discretization, using five numbers instead of 48. With only three features, 1, s, s^2, the error is 7.1. The true V^* is not exactly quadratic, and a fit can only be as good as its features.
What the lecture does not say, and the notes do in one sentence, is that fitted value iteration “cannot be proved to always converge”. Discrete value iteration converges because its update is a contraction in the max norm (Section 17.3). A least-squares fit is not a max-norm operation, and composing the two can expand distances instead of shrinking them. Tsitsiklis and Van Roy give the smallest example, reproduced in Figure 18.2. There are two states with no actions and no rewards; state 1 moves to state 2, which stays put, so V^* = 0. There is one feature, \phi = 1 in state 1 and \phi = 2 in state 2. The targets are y = \gamma \cdot 2\theta for both states, and the least-squares fit of \theta' \phi to them is

\theta' = \frac{1 \cdot 2\gamma\theta + 2 \cdot 2\gamma\theta}{1^2 + 2^2} = \frac{6\gamma}{5}\,\theta,

so \theta grows geometrically whenever \gamma > 5/6. This happens although the features represent V^* exactly at \theta = 0. The cause is that the fit weights both states equally while the dynamics send everything to state 2. The algorithm as written starts at \theta := 0, and in this example it would sit there for ever. Any nonzero start, or any noise in the targets, sets the divergence going.






Figure 18.2: Fitted value iteration on Tsitsiklis and Van Roy’s two-state chain, started at \theta = 1. At \gamma = 0.9 the parameter grows by a factor 6\gamma/5 = 1.08 per iteration and passes 1,000 after 90; at \gamma = 0.8 it shrinks. Ordinary value iteration on the same two states converges at \gamma = 0.9.



None of this makes the algorithm unusable. The notes say it usually converges or nearly converges in practice. At the start of lecture 19 Ng answers a student who asked whether it really works: it does, on a real helicopter at low speed. The counterexample is a reason to watch \theta across iterations rather than trust it.






NoteIn the official notes



Discretization, simulators, learning a linear model and fitted value iteration are in cs229-notes12, section 4, which also writes the update with an integral over s' and states the convergence caveat.
crumbs: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation

title: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation
section: 18.5 From a value function to an action
text:
18.5 From a value function to an action
1:10:37 Fitted value iteration returns \theta, and \pi^* is only implicit in it:

\pi(s) = \arg\max_a \mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P_{sa}}\bigl[V(s')\bigr].

On a helicopter this has to be computed ten times a second. The obvious method is to estimate the expectation from k simulator samples, as in training. Ng is reluctant to do that. He does not like the idea of a self-driving car with a random number generator in its control loop, where an unlucky draw could pick a bad action. 1:13:35 The common fix uses the form most simulators have, s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t) + \varepsilon_t. Train with the noise, so that the policy is robust, but at deployment set \varepsilon_t = 0 and k = 1:

\pi(s) = \arg\max_a V\bigl(f(s, a)\bigr).
\tag{18.4}
Each tenth of a second the controller simulates one step for every action, evaluates V at the predicted next states, and takes the best. Ng admits this is not rigorously justified. There is one case where it is exact. If V is quadratic and the noise is additive with a distribution that does not depend on the action, then

\mathbb{E}\bigl[V(f + \varepsilon)\bigr] = V(f) + \tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma)

for zero-mean noise with covariance \Sigma, where H is the (constant) Hessian of V. The second term is the same for every action, so dropping the noise cannot change the argmax. The generator confirms that the quadratic fit’s two read-outs agree at every one of 601 states. For other features the noise term depends on f(s, a), so the two can disagree, though in this toy the quartic fit still never did. This is a first glimpse of a fact lecture 19 makes central: for quadratic values and linear-Gaussian dynamics, the noise does not change the optimal action at all.
1:18:26 Asked about continuous actions, Ng says a car’s steering and braking can be discretized without much loss, but a helicopter’s controls usually are not. When f is smooth, the maximisation in Equation 18.4 can be done by a fast numerical optimiser in real time, which is the territory of model predictive control. 1:19:24 And to a student asking how the controller knows where it has got to after acting: it measures. A tenth of a second later a new GPS reading and new sensors give the new state, wind and model errors included, and the argmax is taken again from there.
crumbs: 18  Continuous State MDPs and Model Simulation

title: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator
text:
19.1 Rewards that depend on the action
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Fitted value iteration (Section 18.4) handles continuous states by approximating the value function. This lecture finds the one important case where no approximation is needed: if the dynamics are linear and the reward quadratic, the value function is exactly quadratic, the optimal policy is exactly linear, and both come out of a short matrix recursion however many state variables there are. Getting there takes two small generalizations of the MDP first, rewards that depend on the action and a finite horizon, because the algorithm, the linear quadratic regulator (LQR), is most naturally a backward pass over a fixed number of time steps. Ng’s summary is that LQR applies to a narrow set of problems, but when it applies it is the algorithm to use.
4:16 So far the reward has been a function of the state alone. Letting it depend on the action too, R : S \times A \to \mathbb{R}, makes the payoff
R(s_0, a_0) + \gamma R(s_1, a_1) + \gamma^2 R(s_2, a_2) + \cdots,
and it lets a problem say that actions have costs. A robot in a maze can be charged for moving and nothing for standing still. A helicopter can be charged for yanking the sticks hard, which makes it jerk around. A route planner can charge each road segment its own cost, and a factory can price sending a maintenance crew differently from doing nothing. 5:55 Bellman’s equation changes in one visible way:
V^*(s) = \max_a \Bigl[ R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P_{sa}(s') V^*(s') \Bigr],
\tag{19.1}
with the max now outside the immediate reward, since that reward depends on the action being chosen. A student checks that the max covers the whole bracket, and it does. Value iteration uses Equation 19.1 as its update unchanged, and the optimal policy is the argmax of the same bracket. The reward depends on the current state and action, not on the next state. Ng notes that other formulations exist and this is one convenient one.
crumbs: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator

title: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator
section: 19.2 Finite horizons and policies that watch the clock
text:
19.2 Finite horizons and policies that watch the clock
11:00 The second generalization replaces the discount factor with a horizon T. The MDP runs for T steps and then stops, and the payoff is the finite sum

R(s_0, a_0) + R(s_1, a_1) + \cdots + R(s_T, a_T),

usually without discounting, though discounting is still allowed. Ng’s example is a model helicopter with thirty minutes of fuel: the aim is to collect as much reward as possible before the clock runs out.
13:11 A finite horizon has a consequence that is easy to miss. The best action can depend on the time. Put a robot between a small +1 nearby and a large +10 farther off. With plenty of time it should go for the +10. With two or three steps left it should grab the +1, because the +10 is out of reach. So the optimal policy is written \pi^*_t(s), and is called non-stationary. 15:46 Ng points out what was implicit until now: in the infinite-horizon discounted setting of lectures 16 and 17 the optimal policy is stationary, the same at every step, because the future always looks the same.
16:31 Once the policy may change over time, so may the world. A non-stationary MDP has P^{(t)}_{sa} and R^{(t)}(s, a) indexed by time. Ng gives three examples. A long-haul airliner can burn a third of its take-off weight in fuel, so it handles differently on landing. A drive to San Francisco at 5 pm runs into rush hour, and into mud if the forecast says rain. And in a factory running round the clock, labour costs and availability change with the shift.
crumbs: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator

title: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator
text:
19.3 Solving it backwards
21:11 Define V^*_t(s) as the best expected payoff from state s at time t to the end. With nothing left after the last step, the base case is just the best immediate reward,

V^*_T(s) = \max_a R(s, a),

23:27 and each earlier step looks one step ahead to the next:

V^*_t(s) = \max_a \Bigl[ R(s, a) + \sum_{s'} P_{sa}(s') V^*_{t+1}(s') \Bigr],
\qquad
\pi^*_t(s) = \arg\max_a \Bigl[ \cdots \Bigr].
\tag{19.2}
This is no longer value iteration in the sense of repeating an update until it converges. It is dynamic programming: compute V^*_T, then V^*_{T-1} from it, then V^*_{T-2}, down to V^*_0, once each, and read \pi^*_t off at every step. Time-varying P^{(t)} and R^{(t)} slot into Equation 19.2 at no extra cost.
28:31 A student asks whether letting T \to \infty recovers ordinary value iteration. The two are closely related, but undiscounted sums can grow without bound as T grows. That is one reason discounting exists. If |R| \le R_{\max}, a discounted value is at most R_{\max}/(1-\gamma) in size, and a finite-horizon one at most (T+1) R_{\max}.
30:30 Ng sketches the +1/+10 corridor with deterministic moves. With two steps left, the values read like “10, 10, 10, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0”: cells within reach of the +10, cells only within reach of the +1, and cells that can reach neither. He suggests building the little simulator to watch the policy change as the clock runs down. Figure 19.1 does that for an eleven-cell corridor of our own, with the +10 in cell 0, the +1 in cell 8, and a state-action reward of -0.1 for each move, so that it uses both of this lecture’s generalizations. The generator checks the dynamic programme against brute force over every action sequence up to seven steps. Cell 5 shows the non-stationarity in full. With one or two steps left it stays put, since nothing is reachable and moving costs. With three or four it heads right for the +1. With five or more it heads left for the +10.






Figure 19.1: The optimal action in each cell of a corridor, for each number of steps left, from one at the bottom to twelve at the top, with the optimal value in each square. Cell 0 holds +10, cell 8 holds +1, and each move costs 0.1. Where moving now and moving later tie, as they often do when waiting is free and nothing is discounted, the figure shows the move.



The figure’s caption hides one more lesson. Without discounting and with waiting free, many cells have several optimal actions. Leaving for the +10 now or one step later gives the same total if there is time either way. Discounting is what makes sooner strictly better.
crumbs: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator

title: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator
text:
19.4 The LQR model
32:04 LQR is a finite-horizon MDP with continuous states S = \mathbb{R}^n, continuous actions A = \mathbb{R}^d, and two specific assumptions. The first is that the dynamics are linear with Gaussian noise:

s_{t+1} = A s_t + B a_t + w_t, \qquad w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma_w),
\tag{19.3}
with A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} and B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}. 34:27 Ng apologises for the notation. A is now both the set of actions and a matrix, because LQR comes from control theory in electrical and mechanical engineering and reinforcement learning from computer science, and when the two literatures met, their letters clashed. The same thing happens to V below. 36:30 The second assumption is a quadratic reward,

R(s, a) = -\bigl(s^\top U s + a^\top V a\bigr), \qquad U \succeq 0,\; V \succeq 0,
\tag{19.4}
with U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} and V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} positive semi-definite, so both terms are costs. For a helicopter that should hover at the origin, U = I and V = I give R = -\lVert s \rVert^2 - \lVert a \rVert^2. That penalises drifting from the hover point and penalises large control inputs. Time-varying A_t, B_t, U_t, V_t are allowed but not needed for the derivation.
40:43 Where do A and B come from? The first way was lecture 18’s (Equation 18.1): fly the helicopter, log m trajectories, and fit A and B by least squares. Ng says again that this gives a good model for slow flight.
crumbs: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator

title: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator
text:
19.5 Linearizing a nonlinear model
43:02 The second way starts from a nonlinear simulator s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t), from a physics engine or “a friend with a physics degree”. Ng tried the inverted pendulum’s equations himself and found them complicated. To make it linear, he draws the one-dimensional case. 45:31 Plot s_{t+1} = f(s_t) against s_t, pick a point \bar s_t, and replace f with its tangent line there:

s_{t+1} \approx f(\bar s_t) + f'(\bar s_t)\,(s_t - \bar s_t).

49:05 The tangent is good near \bar s_t and poor far away, so \bar s_t should be where the system spends its time: the hover point for a helicopter, the upright pole at rest for the pendulum. 50:37 With an action as well, linearize around a typical pair (\bar s_t, \bar a_t) using the Jacobians:

s_{t+1} \approx f(\bar s_t, \bar a_t)
+ \nabla_s f(\bar s_t, \bar a_t)\,(s_t - \bar s_t)
+ \nabla_a f(\bar s_t, \bar a_t)\,(a_t - \bar a_t).
\tag{19.5}
53:20 This is affine rather than linear, because of the constant terms. Ng’s fix is to add an intercept to the state, a component fixed at 1. Then Equation 19.5 takes the form s_{t+1} = A s_t + B a_t after “some algebraic munging”. When the linearization point is the origin and the system rests there, f(0, 0) = 0, as for the upright pendulum, the constants vanish and no intercept is needed.
Figure 19.2 does this for a pendulum on a motorised pivot, with the angle \theta measured from upright and a torque as the action. The only nonlinear term is gravity, (g/l)\sin\theta, and linearizing at \bar\theta = 0 replaces it with (g/l)\theta. The generator checks the hand-derived A and B against finite differences. The line is 1% too strong at 0.25 rad, 4% at 0.5 rad, 19% at 1 rad and 50% at 1.5 rad. The right panel runs the LQR controller designed on the linear model on the true pendulum. From 0.3 rad the real and predicted trajectories coincide. From 1.4 rad they come apart by up to 0.11 rad, but the controller still brings the pole up. Feedback forgives a model that is wrong in the right direction. Because the measured state is fed back every step, the controller corrects its own model errors as they appear. In this toy, with unlimited torque, it recovers even from 3 rad. A real motor’s torque limit would end that long before.






Figure 19.2: Left: the pendulum’s gravity term (g/l)\sin\theta and its tangent at the upright position. Right: the pole angle under the LQR controller designed on the linear model, on the true pendulum (solid) and as the linear model predicts it (dashed), from three starting angles.
crumbs: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator

title: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator
section: 19.6 The value function is exactly quadratic
text:
19.6 The value function is exactly quadratic
56:05 Now run the backward recursion Equation 19.2 on the LQR model. With continuous states, the sum over s' becomes an expectation over s_{t+1} \sim \mathcal{N}(A s_t + B a_t,
\Sigma_w). 57:07 The base case is immediate:

V^*_T(s_T) = \max_{a_T} \bigl[-s_T^\top U s_T - a_T^\top V a_T\bigr] = -s_T^\top U s_T,

because a^\top V a \ge 0, so the best last action is a_T = 0. A student notices that s^\top U s is also non-negative. It is, but it cannot be chosen: only a_T is maximised over.
59:09 The inductive step carries the whole method. Suppose

V^*_{t+1}(s) = s^\top \Phi_{t+1} s + \Psi_{t+1}

for some matrix \Phi_{t+1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} and scalar \Psi_{t+1}. This holds at t+1 = T with \Phi_T = -U and \Psi_T = 0. 1:04:23 Then

V^*_t(s_t) = \max_{a_t} \Bigl[ -s_t^\top U s_t - a_t^\top V a_t
+ \mathbb{E}_{s_{t+1} \sim \mathcal{N}(A s_t + B a_t,\, \Sigma_w)}\bigl[ s_{t+1}^\top \Phi_{t+1} s_{t+1} \bigr] + \Psi_{t+1} \Bigr].

The expectation of a quadratic under a Gaussian is a quadratic of the mean plus a constant, \mathbb{E}[s^\top \Phi s] = \mu^\top \Phi \mu + \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_w \Phi). So the bracket is a quadratic function of a_t, and since \Phi_{t+1} \preceq 0 and V \succeq 0 it is concave. 1:06:57 Setting its derivative to zero gives

a^*_t = -\bigl(B^\top \Phi_{t+1} B - V\bigr)^{-1} B^\top \Phi_{t+1} A \; s_t = L_t\, s_t .
\tag{19.6}
1:08:03 Ng stops on this. The optimal action is a linear function of the state. He stresses that this is not a function-approximation claim. Nobody fitted a line to the optimal action. Of all functions of the state, linear or not, the best one turns out to be linear. Substituting a^*_t back into the bracket gives another quadratic in s_t, which completes the induction. 1:09:45 The coefficients obey the discrete Riccati equations:

\begin{aligned}
\Phi_t &= A^\top \Bigl( \Phi_{t+1} - \Phi_{t+1} B \bigl(B^\top \Phi_{t+1} B - V\bigr)^{-1} B^\top \Phi_{t+1} \Bigr) A - U, \\
\Psi_t &= \Psi_{t+1} + \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma_w \Phi_{t+1}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{19.7}
1:11:04 The whole algorithm is to set \Phi_T = -U and \Psi_T = 0, then apply Equation 19.7 and Equation 19.6 for t = T-1 down to 0, and finally act with \pi^*_t(s) = L_t s. 1:14:08 What impresses Ng is that nothing in it is approximate. The approximation happens once, when a real system is forced into the form of a linear model with a quadratic cost, by regression or by linearization. After that, the value function really is quadratic and the policy really is linear, and the recursion computes both exactly.
The generator tests each claim by a second route on a cart with position and velocity at 10 Hz and a 60-step horizon. At 20 random times and states, a numerical maximisation of the Bellman bracket lands on L_t s and on s^\top \Phi_t s + \Psi_t to within 10^{-6}. None of 400 perturbed policies beats L_t s, and half of them add nonlinear terms of the state and time.






WarningTwo signs the 2018 notes get wrong



cs229-notes13 prints the optimal action without the leading minus sign in Equation 19.6. It also prints \Psi_t = -\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_t \Phi_{t+1}) + \Psi_{t+1}, and the board in the lecture shows the same minus sign. Both are wrong, and the notes’ own footnote, \mathbb{E}[w^\top \Phi w] = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma \Phi), gives the plus sign. The noise should make the value worse, and since \Phi_{t+1} \preceq 0, only +\operatorname{tr} does that. Monte Carlo settles it. From s_0 = (1, 0) with \Sigma_w = 0.25 I, 4,000 rollouts of the cart under L_t average -168.8 \pm 1.1. Equation 19.7 predicts -170.4, and the printed sign predicts +152.3, a positive value for a problem whose rewards are all negative. The action’s sign matters even more. Without the minus, the controller pushes the cart away from the origin, and the payoff of a single noiseless run is -1.4 \times 10^{14}. The notes also write B_t where B_t^\top is meant, and V_t and W_t for the same matrix.








NoteIn the official notes



Finite-horizon MDPs, LQR and linearization are cs229-notes13, sections 1, 2 and 3.1. Section 3.2 goes on to differential dynamic programming, which re-linearizes around a trajectory instead of a single point. Section 4 covers LQG, LQR when the state is observed only through noise, with the Kalman filter. The lecture covers neither.

title: 19  Finite-Horizon MDPs and the Linear Quadratic Regulator
section: 19.7 The noise does not change the policy
text:
19.7 The noise does not change the policy
1:15:22 Ng ends with a property he calls fun, and warns against generalizing. Look at what each quantity depends on. L_t in Equation 19.6 needs \Phi_{t+1} but not \Psi_{t+1}, which makes sense: adding a constant to every future value cannot change which action is best. \Phi_t in Equation 19.7 needs only \Phi_{t+1}. 1:17:36 The noise covariance \Sigma_w appears in exactly one place, the update for \Psi. Delete the \Psi line from the code and the optimal policy is computed perfectly without \Sigma_w ever being used. The optimal LQR policy does not depend on the noise. The value does: a helicopter in a gale does worse than one in still air. But the best response to any state is the same in both.
Figure 19.3 shows both effects on the cart. The gains computed with \Sigma_w = 0 and with \Sigma_w = 0.25 I are identical to the last bit, while \Psi_0 goes from 0 to -161.4. The figure also shows the finite horizon at work. For the first half of the horizon the gain is flat at L \approx (-2.76, -2.51), a stationary policy in all but name. Over the last 25 or so steps it relaxes to zero, because there is less and less future in which a correction would pay off. That is the clock-watching of Figure 19.1 in continuous form.






Figure 19.3: The two entries of the LQR gain L_t for the cart, on position and on velocity, against the time step for a 60-step horizon. Lines are for \Sigma_w = 0; circles, drawn every third step, are for \Sigma_w = 0.25 I.



1:19:00 Ng draws two lessons. The narrow one is that, when applying LQR, there is no need to work hard at estimating \Sigma_w. The broader one is about practice. For most MDPs the noise does change the policy, and the form of the noise matters. But in his experience of building robots, remembering to add noise matters more than getting its size exactly right. Ten per cent more or less rarely matters; a factor of two often does. That is the same advice as lecture 18’s (Section 18.3), now with one case where it can be proved.

title: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
text:
20.1 Debugging the helicopter, in RL notation
Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — CS229, Stanford University, Autumn 2018.
Every reinforcement-learning method in the course so far has been indirect: estimate the value function, then read the policy off it with an argmax. The last lecture introduces the other family. Direct policy search writes the policy down as a parametrised function, the way logistic regression writes down a hypothesis, and tunes its parameters by gradient ascent on the expected payoff, never computing a value function at all. The algorithm Ng derives, REINFORCE, gets an unbiased estimate of that gradient from a single run of the system. Unbiased is not the same as useful: the estimate is so noisy that REINFORCE is notoriously slow, and part of that noise comes from terms that average to zero and can be dropped. Before any of that, Ng finishes a promise from lecture 12 and restates the helicopter diagnostics in the notation the course has since introduced.
4:05 Lecture 12 walked through the diagnostics for Ng’s autonomous helicopter before the course had any reinforcement learning to describe them with (Section 12.5). The setup is now familiar. Build a simulator, a learned model s_{t+1} = A s_t + B a_t or something richer, as in Section 18.3. Choose a reward function, such as the negative squared distance from where the helicopter should be. Run a reinforcement-learning algorithm on the finite-horizon problem to get a policy \pi_{\text{RL}} that maximises \mathbb{E}[R(s_0) + \dots + R(s_T)] in the simulator. The first time, the controller flies much worse than the human pilot, and there are three things to try: improve the simulator, change the reward, or improve the RL algorithm. Ng is concrete about the last one. It means changing the discretization of a continuous state, or replacing the linear function approximator in fitted value iteration with a richer one such as a neural network.
The diagnostics are those of lecture 12 with the sign turned round, since the algorithm now maximises a payoff rather than minimising a cost. If \pi_{\text{RL}} flies well in simulation and badly in reality, the simulator is at fault. Otherwise, 8:28 record the human pilot’s flight and score it with the same reward. If the human’s payoff is higher, the algorithm failed to maximise the sum of rewards, because here is a policy that does better. If the algorithm’s payoff is higher and it still flies worse, maximising this reward is not the same as flying well, and the reward is what needs work.
13:12 A student asks whether the tests have an order. Ng checks the simulator first and turns to the other two only once it seems adequate. He also qualifies the whole procedure: the diagnostics look like a rigid decision rule, but in practice the answers are graded. The simulator is “kind of good”, the human beats the algorithm by a little, and the team looks at all three pieces of evidence together and decides where the next month goes. What he insists on is that the bottleneck moves as the project progresses, so the diagnostics are re-run after each round of work rather than once, and teams that prioritise this way move faster than teams that go by gut feel.
crumbs: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search

title: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
text:
20.2 Searching for the policy directly
17:01 Ng shows one more example of the indirect route first. Zico Kolter’s quadruped crossing rough terrain relied on an approximate value function that scored, for a given height map of the terrain, how good each position of the robot was; the robot moved towards higher value. That is value iteration’s way of thinking: learn V^*, or an approximation to it, then act greedily with \pi^*(s) = \arg\max_a \mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P_{sa}}[V^*(s')] (Section 17.4 and Section 18.5).
18:25 Direct policy search goes straight for the policy, with no value function in between. Its first step is the same as the first step of supervised learning. When logistic regression was introduced, Ng recalls, the form h_\theta(x) = g(\theta^\top x) was pulled out of a hat (Section 3.5), and the learning algorithm’s job was then to find the best \theta within that form. Policy search likewise starts by choosing a class of policies, parametrised by \theta, and its job is to find the best member of the class.
The running example is the inverted pendulum, a pole on a hinge atop a cart, with two actions: accelerate left or accelerate right. The state is

s = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ x \\ \dot x \\ \phi \\ \dot\phi \end{bmatrix},

the cart’s position and velocity and the pole’s angle and angular velocity, with a 1 for an intercept. The angle is \phi rather than the usual \theta, which is about to be taken by the parameters.
crumbs: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search

title: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
text:
20.3 Stochastic policies
22:51 The policies of lectures 16 to 19 were deterministic, a map from states to actions. Policy search uses a stochastic policy, a function \pi(s, a) giving the probability of taking action a in state s:

\pi(s, a) \ge 0, \qquad \sum_a \pi(s, a) = 1 \quad \text{for every } s .

On every step the agent draws its action from \pi(s, \cdot). 24:38 For the pendulum, Ng’s choice is logistic:

\pi_\theta(s, \text{right}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^\top s}}, \qquad
\pi_\theta(s, \text{left}) = 1 - \pi_\theta(s, \text{right}) .
\tag{20.1}
25:47 To see that this can express sensible behaviour, take \theta = (0, 0, 0, 1, 0). Then \theta^\top s = \phi, and the probability of accelerating right is 1/(1 + e^{-\phi}): the further the pole leans to the right, the likelier the cart is to accelerate right and get back under it. This ignores where the cart is, and a cart that keeps chasing the pole will run off the end of its track. 27:18 With \theta = (0, -0.5, 0, 1, 0) the position enters with a negative weight, so the further right the cart already is, the less likely it is to accelerate further right. The general problem is to find the five numbers that trade off position, velocity, angle and angular velocity best, and that is what the algorithm will do.
Figure 20.1 plots these policies. One thing the board example hides is scale. With a weight of 1 on an angle measured in radians, a pole tilted half a radian, nearly thirty degrees, still gets accelerated the right way only 62 % of the time: the policy is close to a coin flip over every angle a balancing controller would see. The signs in \theta say which way to lean; the magnitude says how decisively, and a weight of 10 turns the same policy into almost a step. The learning algorithm has to find both.






Figure 20.1: Probability of accelerating right against the pole angle, for the logistic policy Equation 20.1. Purple: Ng’s weight of 1 on the angle; teal: the same direction scaled by ten. Solid: the cart at x = 0; dashed: the cart at x = 1 with a weight of -0.5 times the angle weight on position, which shifts each curve right. Computed in figures/20-policy-search/make_diagrams.py.



49:04 Later, answering a question, Ng gives the reason for the switch to stochastic policies. A deterministic policy over two actions is a step function of \theta, either left or right, and there is no derivative to follow. Probabilities move smoothly with \theta, so the expected payoff becomes differentiable and gradient ascent applies.
crumbs: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search

title: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
text:
20.4 The objective
29:03 The goal is to choose \theta to maximise the expected payoff when the policy is run:

\max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}\left[R(s_0, a_0) + R(s_1, a_1) + \dots + R(s_T, a_T) \,\middle|\, \pi_\theta\right],
\tag{20.2}
in the finite-horizon setting of Section 19.2, with rewards that may depend on the action as in Section 19.1. For the pendulum the reward might be -1 whenever the pole falls over and 0 otherwise.
30:15 One difference from value iteration is easy to miss. V^* gives the optimal policy for every starting state at once, so a single \pi^* is simultaneously best from wherever the system begins. Policy search optimises from one fixed initial state s_0, or one fixed distribution over initial states, and the policy it finds is best for that start. A policy class too small to contain \pi^* forces a trade-off between states, and the initial distribution decides which states the trade-off favours.
crumbs: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search

title: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
text:
20.5 REINFORCE
32:02 To keep the board manageable, Ng sets T = 1: two states and two actions. The expectation in Equation 20.2 is then a sum over every state-action sequence, weighted by its probability:

\mathbb{E}[\text{payoff}] = \sum_{s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1}
P(s_0)\, \pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)\, P_{s_0 a_0}(s_1)\, \pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)
\left[R(s_0, a_0) + R(s_1, a_1)\right].
\tag{20.3}
The initial distribution P(s_0) and the transition probabilities P_{s_0 a_0}(s_1) do not depend on \theta; only the two policy factors do. Everything below carries over to longer horizons with longer products and sums.
34:58 The algorithm that climbs this objective is called REINFORCE, after Williams’ 1992 paper (Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms for connectionist reinforcement learning). Ng presents its core and notes that the original has a few further refinements, one of which comes up below. Each iteration does three things:

Run the system for T steps under the current policy, sampling each action from \pi_\theta, to get a sequence s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, \dots, s_T, a_T.
Compute the payoff, the sum of the rewards along it.
Update 
\theta := \theta + \alpha \left[\sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_t, a_t)}{\pi_\theta(s_t, a_t)}\right] \times \text{payoff}.
\tag{20.4}

37:48 Each update is random, because it depends on which states the system happened to visit and which actions the policy happened to draw. Ng’s picture is the one he drew for stochastic gradient descent on linear regression (Section 2.6): batch gradient descent heads straight for the optimum, while the stochastic version takes a jittery path that heads the right way on average. The claim is that REINFORCE is stochastic gradient ascent on the expected payoff: the expected value of the bracketed update is exactly the gradient of Equation 20.3.
crumbs: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search

title: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
section: 20.6 Why the update follows the gradient
text:
20.6 Why the update follows the gradient
40:05 The proof is three lines of calculus. Differentiate Equation 20.3. Inside the sum only the two \pi_\theta factors depend on \theta, so the product rule gives two terms:

\nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}[\text{payoff}] = \sum_{s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1}
P(s_0)\, P_{s_0 a_0}(s_1)
\left[\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)\, \pi_\theta(s_1, a_1) + \pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)\, \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)\right]
\times \text{payoff}.

43:58 Now multiply and divide the first term by \pi_\theta(s_0, a_0) and the second by \pi_\theta(s_1, a_1). Both terms then contain the full product P(s_0)\,\pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)\,P_{s_0 a_0}(s_1)\,\pi_\theta(s_1, a_1), which is the probability of the whole sequence, and it factors out:

\nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}[\text{payoff}] = \sum_{s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1}
P(s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1)
\left[\frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)}{\pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)} + \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)}{\pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)}\right]
\times \text{payoff}.
\tag{20.5}
That is a probability-weighted sum over sequences of exactly the quantity REINFORCE adds to \theta in Equation 20.4, so it is the expected value of that update. 48:03 With a small learning rate, many updates average out and the parameters drift along the gradient of the expected payoff. Each ratio \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta / \pi_\theta is \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta, the score of the action, which is the form the update is usually written in today. For the logistic policy Equation 20.1 it is the familiar (\mathbb{1}\{a = \text{right}\} - \pi_\theta(s, \text{right}))\, s, the same expression as the logistic-regression gradient (Section 3.6), now weighted by the payoff instead of the label error.
The generator for this chapter checks Equation 20.5 by two routes on a small pole-balancing problem described below. It enumerates every two-step trajectory to compute the expected REINFORCE update exactly, differentiates the expected payoff numerically through a dynamic programme, and finds the two agree to 10^{-8} at twenty random settings of \theta.
48:36 A student asks whether the derivation depends on the logistic form. It does not. Nothing in it used anything about \pi_\theta except that it is the probability of the action and that it is differentiable in \theta. A softmax over many actions works, and so does a logistic function of elaborate features of the state. 50:48 The same holds for continuous actions, which policy search handles without discretizing. If the action is a real number, the force on the cart or a car’s steering angle, a natural policy is a = \theta^\top s + \varepsilon with Gaussian \varepsilon; \pi_\theta(s, a) becomes a Gaussian density, and the same update applies with the density in place of the probability.
49:40 Another student asks why not skip all this and train the helicopter by supervised learning on a human pilot’s stick inputs, learning the map from state to the pilot’s action. Ng thinks that might fly a helicopter slowly without crashing it, but not well. Learning from rewards is what let the controller fly some manoeuvres better than the human pilots did, and imitation gives the controller no signal for doing better than the teacher it copies.
crumbs: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search

title: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
section: 20.7 Why REINFORCE is slow, and what helps
text:
20.7 Why REINFORCE is slow, and what helps
58:14 Ng is blunt about the cost. The expected update is exactly right, but each individual update is very noisy, so REINFORCE needs a small learning rate and a very large number of iterations. Papers that use it routinely report millions of them.
Part of that noise is self-inflicted, and the lecture’s form of the update shows where. Equation 20.4 multiplies the score of every action by the whole payoff, including rewards collected before the action was taken. The action at step t cannot have affected those, and the corresponding terms average to zero. The reason is an identity that holds in every state:

\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta(s, \cdot)}\left[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s, a)\right]
= \sum_a \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s, a) = \nabla_\theta \sum_a \pi_\theta(s, a) = \nabla_\theta 1 = 0 .

A reward from before step t is fixed by the time a_t is drawn, so its product with the score of a_t has mean zero. Those terms contribute nothing to the expected update and add variance to every individual one. Dropping them gives the update usually written for REINFORCE, with each action weighted only by the rewards that follow it:

\theta := \theta + \alpha \sum_{t=0}^{T} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s_t, a_t)
\left(\sum_{\tau = t}^{T} R(s_\tau, a_\tau) - b_t\right).
\tag{20.6}
The same identity licenses b_t, a baseline: any quantity that does not depend on the action a_t can be subtracted from the weight without changing the expected update. A good choice is the expected reward-to-go from step t, which turns the weight into a measure of whether the run went better or worse than usual from that point. That is one of the refinements in Williams’ original algorithm, whose update is written with a reinforcement baseline from the start.
The generator checks all three versions on a toy that keeps every expectation computable. The pole’s tilt is an integer from -2 to 2, and it falls, ending the reward, if it leaves that range. Gravity pushes a tilted pole further over with probability one half; an upright pole wobbles either way with probability a quarter each. Accelerating corrects the tilt by one step with probability 0.6. The reward is 1 for every step the pole is up, over 20 transitions, and the policy is \pi_\theta(s, \text{right}) = 1/(1 + e^{-(\theta_0 + \theta_1 s)}). At \theta = 0, the coin-flip policy, the expected payoff is 5.25 and the best deterministic policy gets 13.50. Averaged over 20,000 runs, all three estimators agree with the numerically differentiated gradient, \partial J / \partial \theta_1 = 2.34, within their standard errors. Their variances do not agree. On \theta_1, the lecture’s version has variance 174, the rewards-that-follow version 51, and with the baseline 19: nine times less noise for the same expected step.






Figure 20.2: Exact expected payoff of the current policy during REINFORCE on the toy balancing problem, averaged over 20 runs, for the lecture’s update Equation 20.4 (whole payoff), Equation 20.6 with b_t = 0 (rewards that follow), and Equation 20.6 with b_t the expected reward-to-go. Dashed: the best deterministic policy. Computed in figures/20-policy-search/make_diagrams.py.



Figure 20.2 shows what that buys. At step size \alpha = 0.01 all three approach the optimum, but the lecture’s version needs about 290 updates for its average run to reach 90 % of the best payoff, against 130 and 110 for the other two. At \alpha = 0.03 the lower-variance versions get there in about 100 and 40 updates. The lecture’s version does not get there at all on average: after 500 updates, 5 of its 20 runs are still below 90 % of the best payoff. Inspecting them shows how it fails. A single large, noisy step throws the intercept \theta_0 far from zero, the policy then pushes the same way in almost every state, and with the sigmoid saturated the scores, and so the further updates, are tiny. A larger step size is not available to an estimator this noisy, which is Ng’s point about small learning rates, and removing terms that average to zero is the cheapest way to make it available.
crumbs: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search

title: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
text:
20.8 Partial observability
52:24 Ng names two situations in which direct policy search is the better choice. The first is a partially observable MDP, or POMDP. Suppose the pendulum has a position sensor and an angle sensor but nothing that measures velocities, and both sensors are noisy. On each step the agent sees not the state but an observation

y = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ \phi \end{bmatrix} + \text{noise},

two noisy readings of four state variables, and it still has to choose an action.
Value-function methods are stuck here. 55:34 Even with V^* and \pi^* in hand, the policy \pi^*(s) needs the state, which the agent does not have. There is a large academic literature that extends value-based methods to POMDPs, but in Ng’s assessment those algorithms are very complicated and are not widely used in production. Policy search needs no extension. Define the policy on what the agent can see,

\pi_\theta(y, \text{right}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^\top y}},

and REINFORCE runs unchanged: nothing in Equation 20.5 required the policy’s input to be the state, only that the action’s probability be a differentiable function of \theta. The policy may not be as good as one that sees the state, but the algorithm finds the best one of this form.
57:00 The input can be any features of the history, not just the current reading. A common design is to run a state estimator, such as a Kalman filter, over all the measurements so far, which produces an estimate of the full state vector including the velocities, and feed that estimate to the policy as its features.

title: 20  RL Debugging and Direct Policy Search
text:
20.9 Policy or value function?
58:59 The second consideration is which object is simpler. Ng distinguishes low-level control tasks, the ones a skilled human does by feel with a joystick in a fraction of a second: hovering a helicopter, balancing an inverted pendulum, keeping a car in its lane on a straight road. For those a simple function of the state, often close to linear, is a good policy, so a small policy class contains a good answer, and direct policy search is promising. Chess and Go are the opposite: a good move depends on reasoning several steps ahead, no simple function of the board position plays well, and value-function approximation is the more promising route. Driving sits on both sides. Staying in the lane is low-level control; planning to overtake one car before a truck arrives in that lane is multi-step reasoning.
1:02:01 The helicopter went through both phases. Ng’s first controllers, including the one in the inverted-flight video at the start of the lecture, came from a direct policy search algorithm, a relative of REINFORCE rather than REINFORCE itself. More complicated manoeuvres called for methods closer to value-function approximation. The two families combine, too: Ng cites AlphaGo, which trained a policy network and a value network and used both in its search.
1:03:20 The course closes with where reinforcement learning was being applied in 2018. Game playing is the visible case, but Ng expects robotics to matter most, and mentions large-machine control in industry, factory optimisation, sequential medical decisions in which each test result decides the next step, and the execution of large stock trades in pieces small enough not to move the price. The common thread is the one the whole reinforcement-learning unit has been about: a sequence of decisions whose payoff arrives only over time.






NoteIn the official notes



The 2018 notes for this part of the course, cs229-notes12, cover MDPs, value and policy iteration and continuous-state MDPs, and end before policy search. The lecture is the source for REINFORCE here; Williams’ 1992 paper has the general form, including the baseline.
